chapters.title: Dedication. To M. Talleyrand Perigord, Late Bishop of Autun
paragraphs: Sir,

Having read with great pleasure the pamphlet on national education that you recently published, I dedicate this volume to you — the first dedication I have ever written — in order to induce you to read it attentively; and I do so because I think you will understand me, which I do not expect of the many impertinent little wits who may ridicule the arguments they cannot answer. But, sir, my respect for your understanding goes further still: so far that I am confident you will not toss my work aside and hastily conclude that I am wrong merely because you did not see the subject in the same light yourself. And forgive my frankness, but I must remark that you treated it too superficially, content to regard it as it had been regarded in the past, when the rights of man, to say nothing of woman, were trampled on as a fantasy. I therefore call on you now to weigh what I have put forward concerning the rights of woman and national education; and I call with the firm voice of humanity. For my arguments, sir, are dictated by a disinterested spirit: I plead for my sex, not for myself. I have long considered independence the great blessing of life, the basis of every virtue; and I will always secure my independence by reducing my needs, even if I had to live on a barren heath.

It is, then, affection for the whole human race that sends my pen darting swiftly across the page in support of what I believe to be the cause of virtue; and the same motive makes me earnestly wish to see woman placed in a position in which she would advance, rather than hold back, the progress of those glorious principles that give substance to morality. Indeed, my opinion on the rights and duties of woman seems to follow so naturally from these simple principles that I think it hardly possible that some of the broad minds who framed your admirable constitution will not agree with me.

In France there is undoubtedly a wider spread of knowledge than in any other part of Europe, and I attribute this largely to the social contact that has long existed between the sexes. It is true — I state my views freely — that in France the very essence of sensuality has been distilled to delight the pleasure-seeker, and a kind of sentimental lust has prevailed. Together with the system of duplicity taught by the whole character of their political and civil government, this has given the French character a sinister sort of shrewdness, properly called finesse, and a polish of manners that damages substance by driving sincerity out of society. And modesty, the fairest garment of virtue, has been more grossly insulted in France than even in England, until their women have come to treat as PRUDISH that attention to decency which animals observe by instinct.

Manners and morals are so closely related that they have often been confused; but although manners should be no more than the natural reflection of morals, when various causes have produced artificial and corrupt manners, which are picked up very early, morality becomes an empty word. The personal reserve and the sacred regard for cleanliness and delicacy in domestic life, which French women almost despise, are the graceful pillars of modesty. Yet far from despising them, if the pure flame of patriotism has reached their hearts, these women should work to improve the morals of their fellow citizens by teaching men not only to respect modesty in women but to acquire it themselves, as the only way to deserve women’s esteem.

In arguing for the rights of women, I build my main case on this simple principle: if woman is not prepared by education to become man’s companion, she will halt the progress of knowledge, for truth must be common to all, or it will have no effect on general practice. And how can woman be expected to co-operate unless she knows why she ought to be virtuous — unless freedom strengthens her reason until she understands her duty and sees how it is connected with her real good? If children are to be brought up to understand the true principle of patriotism, their mother must be a patriot; and the love of mankind, from which an orderly succession of virtues springs, can only be produced by considering the moral and civil interest of mankind. But woman’s present education and situation shut her out from such inquiries.

In this work I have put forward many arguments, which I found conclusive, to prove that the prevailing notion of a distinct sexual character undermines morality. I have argued that, to make the human body and mind more perfect, chastity must be far more widely practised, and that chastity will never be respected among men until a woman’s person stops being, as it were, idolized when little virtue or good sense adorns it with the noble marks of mental beauty or the touching simplicity of affection.

Consider these observations calmly, sir, for a glimpse of this truth seemed to open before you when you remarked “that to see one half of the human race excluded by the other from all participation of government, was a political phenomenon that, according to abstract principles, it was impossible to explain.” If so, what does your constitution rest on? If the abstract rights of man can withstand discussion and explanation, then by the same reasoning those of woman will not shrink from the same test — although a different opinion prevails in this country, founded on the very argument you use to justify the oppression of woman: prescription, the authority of long custom.

Consider — I address you as a legislator — whether, when men fight for their own freedom and for the right to judge for themselves what makes them happy, it is not inconsistent and unjust to subjugate women, even though you firmly believe you are acting in the way best suited to promote their happiness? Who made man the sole judge, if woman shares with him the gift of reason?

Tyrants of every kind argue in this style, from the weak king to the weak father of a family; they are all eager to crush reason, yet always claim that they usurp its throne only in order to be useful. Do you not play a similar part when you FORCE all women, by denying them civil and political rights, to stay walled up in their families, groping in the dark? For surely, sir, you will not claim that a duty can be binding if it is not founded on reason? If this really is their destiny, arguments for it may be drawn from reason; and, with such dignified support, the more understanding women acquire, the more attached they will be to their duty, because they will comprehend it. For unless they comprehend it, unless their morals rest on the same unchanging principles as man’s, no authority can make them carry it out virtuously. They may be convenient slaves, but slavery will have its constant effect, degrading both the master and the abject dependent.

But if women are to be shut out, without a voice, from sharing in the natural rights of mankind, then prove first, to fend off the charge of injustice and inconsistency, that they lack reason. Otherwise this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION, the first constitution founded on reason, will always show that man must, in one form or another, act like a tyrant; and tyranny, wherever in society it raises its brazen face, will always undermine morality.

I have repeatedly asserted, and supported with what seemed to me unanswerable arguments drawn from matters of fact, that women cannot be confined by force to domestic concerns. For however ignorant they are, they will meddle in weightier affairs, neglecting their private duties only to disrupt, with cunning tricks, the orderly plans of reason that rise above their comprehension.

Moreover, as long as women are brought up to acquire nothing but personal accomplishments, men will look for pleasure in variety, and unfaithful husbands will make unfaithful wives. Indeed, such ignorant beings will be very excusable when, never taught to respect the public good nor granted any civil right, they try to obtain justice for themselves by retaliation.
Once this box of mischief has been opened in society, what is left to preserve private virtue, the only safeguard of public freedom and universal happiness?

Let there be, then, no coercion ESTABLISHED in society, and as the ordinary law of gravity takes effect, the sexes will settle into their proper places. And now that fairer laws are shaping your citizens, marriage may become more sacred; your young men may choose their wives out of affection, and your young women may let love uproot vanity.

The father of a family will then no longer ruin his health and debase his feelings by visiting prostitutes, nor forget, while obeying the call of appetite, the purpose for which it was implanted in him; and the mother will not neglect her children to practise the arts of coquetry when good sense and modesty secure her husband’s friendship.

But until men pay attention to the duty of a father, it is useless to expect women to spend in the nursery the time that they, “wise in their generation,” choose to spend at their mirrors. For this exercise of cunning is only a natural instinct that enables them to obtain indirectly a little of the power in which they are unjustly denied a share; and if women are not permitted to enjoy legitimate rights, they will make both men and themselves vicious in order to obtain illicit privileges.

I wish, sir, to set some inquiries of this kind in motion in France; and should they end by confirming my principles, then when your constitution is revised, the rights of woman may be respected — if it is fully proved that reason calls for this respect and loudly demands JUSTICE for one half of the human race.
I am, sir,
Yours respectfully,
M. W.

chapters.title: Introduction
paragraphs: After studying the pages of history and viewing the living world with anxious concern, I have been weighed down by the most melancholy feelings of sorrowful indignation, and I have sighed when forced to admit either that nature has made a great difference between one man and another, or that the civilization the world has so far achieved has been very partial. I have looked through various books written on education, and I have patiently observed how parents behave and how schools are run; but what has been the result? A deep conviction that the neglected education of my fellow creatures is the chief source of the misery I lament, and that women in particular are made weak and wretched by a number of converging causes, all springing from one hasty conclusion. The conduct and manners of women plainly prove, in fact, that their minds are not in a healthy state. Like flowers planted in soil that is too rich, they sacrifice strength and usefulness to beauty; and the showy leaves, after pleasing a fastidious eye, wither unnoticed on the stalk long before the season when they should have reached maturity. One cause of this barren blooming I attribute to a false system of education, taken from the books on this subject written by men who, regarding females as women rather than as human creatures, have been more eager to make them alluring mistresses than rational wives. And the understanding of the sex has been so deceived by this hollow homage that the civilized women of this century, with a few exceptions, are anxious only to inspire love, when they ought to cherish a nobler ambition and command respect by their abilities and virtues.

In a treatise on the rights and manners of women, therefore, the works written specifically for their improvement must not be overlooked — especially when the claim is made in plain terms that women’s minds are weakened by false refinement; that the books of instruction written by men of genius have had the same effect as more frivolous works; and that, in the true Mahometan style, women are regarded only as females and not as part of the human species, even though improvable reason is admitted to be the dignified distinction that raises men above the animal creation and puts a natural sceptre in a feeble hand.

Yet I would not have my readers suppose, because I am a woman, that I intend to stir up violently the disputed question of the equality or inferiority of the sex. But since the subject lies in my path, and I cannot pass over it without exposing the main drift of my reasoning to misinterpretation, I shall pause for a moment to give my opinion in a few words. In the government of the physical world, it can be observed that the female is, in general, inferior to the male. The male pursues, the female yields — this is the law of nature, and it does not appear to be suspended or repealed in favour of woman. This physical superiority cannot be denied — and it is a noble prerogative! But not content with this natural pre-eminence, men try to sink us still lower, merely to make us alluring objects for a moment; and women, intoxicated by the adoration that men pay them under the sway of their senses, do not try to win a lasting place in men’s hearts, or to become the friends of the fellow creatures who find amusement in their company.

I can foresee an obvious objection. From every quarter I have heard outcries against masculine women; but where are they to be found? If men use this label to attack women’s enthusiasm for hunting, shooting and gambling, I shall join the outcry most heartily; but if it is aimed at the imitation of manly virtues, or, more properly speaking, at the attainment of those talents and virtues whose exercise ennobles the human character, and which raise females in the scale of animal being when they are included under the general term mankind — then all who view women with a philosophical eye must, I should think, wish with me that they may grow more and more masculine every day.

This discussion naturally divides the subject. I shall first consider women in the broad light of human creatures who, like men, are placed on this earth to develop their faculties; and afterwards I shall point out more particularly their own special calling.

I also wish to avoid an error into which many respectable writers have fallen, for the instruction so far addressed to women has been better suited to LADIES, if we except the little indirect advice scattered through Sandford and Merton. Addressing my sex in a firmer tone, however, I pay particular attention to those in the middle class, because they seem to be in the most natural state. Perhaps the seeds of false refinement, immorality and vanity have always been scattered by the great. Weak, artificial beings, lifted prematurely and unnaturally above the common needs and affections of their kind, undermine the very foundation of virtue and spread corruption through the whole mass of society! As a class of mankind, they have the strongest claim to pity! The education of the rich tends to make them vain and helpless, and the developing mind is not strengthened by the practice of those duties that give dignity to human character. They live only to amuse themselves, and by the same law that in nature invariably produces certain effects, they soon provide nothing but barren amusement.

But as I intend to look separately at the different ranks of society and at the moral character of women in each, this hint is enough for now; I have mentioned the subject only because it seems to me the very essence of an introduction to give a brief account of the contents of the work it introduces.

My own sex will, I hope, forgive me if I treat them as rational creatures instead of flattering their FASCINATING graces and regarding them as if they were in a state of perpetual childhood, unable to stand on their own. I earnestly wish to show what true dignity and human happiness consist in. I wish to persuade women to try to acquire strength of both mind and body, and to convince them that the soft phrases — susceptibility of heart, delicacy of sentiment and refinement of taste — are almost synonymous with terms for weakness, and that beings who are only the objects of pity, and of that kind of love which has been called its sister, will soon become objects of contempt.

Setting aside, then, those pretty feminine phrases that men condescendingly use to soften our slavish dependence, and scorning that weak elegance of mind, exquisite sensibility and sweet docility of manner supposed to be the sexual characteristics of the weaker vessel, I wish to show that elegance is inferior to virtue; that the first aim of worthy ambition is to earn a character as a human being, regardless of the distinction of sex; and that lesser aims should be tested against this simple touchstone.

This is a rough sketch of my plan; and if I express my conviction with the strong emotions I feel whenever I think of the subject, some of my readers will feel the force of what experience and reflection dictate. Inspired by this important aim, I shall disdain to pick my phrases or polish my style — I aim to be useful, and sincerity will keep me unaffected. Since I would rather persuade by the force of my arguments than dazzle by the elegance of my language, I shall not waste my time in rounding off sentences or in manufacturing the swollen bombast of artificial feelings, which, coming from the head, never reach the heart. I shall concern myself with things, not words! And, anxious to make my sex more respectable members of society, I shall try to avoid the flowery diction that has slid from essays into novels, and from novels into everyday letters and conversation.

These pretty nothings, these caricatures of the real beauty of sensibility, rolling glibly off the tongue, corrupt the taste and create a kind of sickly delicacy that turns away from plain, unadorned truth; and a flood of false sentiments and overstrained feelings, stifling the natural emotions of the heart, makes insipid those domestic pleasures that ought to sweeten the performance of the stern duties which educate a rational and immortal being for a nobler field of action.

The education of women has recently received more attention than it used to; yet women are still considered a frivolous sex, and are ridiculed or pitied by the writers who try to improve them through satire or instruction. It is admitted that they spend many of their early years acquiring a smattering of accomplishments, while strength of body and mind is sacrificed to libertine notions of beauty and to the desire to settle themselves in life by the only means through which women can rise in the world — marriage. And since this desire turns them into mere animals, when they marry they behave as such children may be expected to behave: they dress up, they paint their faces, and they nickname God’s creatures. Surely these weak beings are fit only for the harem! Can they manage a household, or look after the poor babies they bring into the world?

If, then, it can fairly be inferred from the present conduct of the sex, and from the prevailing love of pleasure that takes the place of ambition and of those nobler passions that open and enlarge the soul, that the instruction women have received has only tended, along with the constitution of civil society, to make them insignificant objects of desire — mere breeders of fools! — and if it can be proved that, in the attempt to give them accomplishments without cultivating their understanding, they are taken out of their sphere of duties and made ridiculous and useless once the short-lived bloom of beauty is over*, then I presume that RATIONAL men will excuse me for trying to persuade women to become more masculine and respectable.
(*Footnote. A lively writer, whose name I cannot remember, asks what business women over forty have in the world.)

Indeed, the word masculine is only a bogeyman. There is little reason to fear that women will acquire too much courage or fortitude, for their apparent inferiority in bodily strength must make them, to some degree, dependent on men in the various relationships of life. But why should this dependence be increased by prejudices that give virtue a sex and confuse simple truths with sensual daydreams?

Women are, in fact, so degraded by mistaken notions of female excellence that I do not mean to add a paradox when I assert that this artificial weakness produces a tendency to tyrannize and gives birth to cunning, the natural opponent of strength, which leads them to put on those contemptible childish airs that undermine esteem even while they arouse desire. Stop fostering these prejudices, and women will naturally settle into their subordinate, yet respectable, place in life.

It hardly seems necessary to say that I am now speaking of the sex in general. Many individual women have more sense than their male relatives; and since nothing tips the scale where there is a constant struggle for balance unless it naturally has more weight, some women govern their husbands without degrading themselves, because intellect will always govern.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Rights and Involved Duties of Mankind Considered
paragraphs: In the present state of society it seems necessary to go back to first principles in search of the simplest truths, and to contest every inch of ground with some prevailing prejudice. To clear my way, I must be allowed to ask a few plain questions; and the answers will probably seem as unambiguous as the axioms on which reasoning is built — though, when they become entangled with various motives for action, they are expressly contradicted by men’s words or conduct.
In what does man’s superiority over the animal creation consist? The answer is as clear as the fact that a half is less than the whole: in Reason.
What attainment raises one being above another? Virtue, we reply without a moment’s thought.
For what purpose were the passions implanted in us? So that man, by struggling with them, might attain a degree of knowledge denied to the animals: so whispers Experience.

Consequently, the perfection of our nature and our capacity for happiness must be measured by the degree of reason, virtue and knowledge that distinguishes the individual and directs the laws that bind society together. And it is equally undeniable, if mankind is viewed as a whole, that knowledge and virtue flow naturally from the exercise of reason.

With the rights and duties of man thus reduced to their simplest form, it seems almost impertinent to try to illustrate truths that appear so indisputable. Yet such deep-rooted prejudices have clouded reason, and such counterfeit qualities have taken the name of virtues, that it is necessary to follow the course of reason as it has been confused and entangled in error by various chance circumstances, comparing the simple axiom with the accidental departures from it.

Men in general seem to use their reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed without knowing how, rather than to root them out. It takes a strong mind to form its own principles resolutely, for a kind of intellectual cowardice prevails that makes many men shrink from the task, or do it only halfway. Yet the imperfect conclusions reached in this way are often very plausible, because they rest on partial experience — on views that are accurate, though narrow.

When we go back to first principles, vice, in all its native ugliness, slinks away from close examination; but a set of shallow reasoners are forever exclaiming that such arguments prove too much, and that a measure rotten at the core may still be expedient. So expediency is constantly set against simple principles, until truth is lost in a fog of words, virtue in outward forms, and knowledge is turned into an empty noise by the plausible prejudices that take its name.

That the wisest form of society is the one whose constitution is founded on the nature of man strikes every thinking being so forcibly, in the abstract, that it seems presumptuous to try to offer proofs. Yet proof must be offered, or reason will never storm the stronghold of prescription; and to cite prescription as an argument for depriving men (or women) of their natural rights is one of the absurd sophistries that insult common sense every day.

The civilization of most of the people of Europe is very partial; indeed, it may be questioned whether, in exchange for their innocence, they have gained any virtues that make up for the misery produced by the vices plastered over their unsightly ignorance, and for the freedom they have traded for splendid slavery. The desire to dazzle by wealth, the surest pre-eminence a man can obtain, the pleasure of commanding flattering sycophants, and many other intricate, base calculations of doting self-love have all helped to crush the mass of mankind and to make liberty a convenient pretext for sham patriotism. For while rank and titles are held to be of the utmost importance, and Genius “must hide its diminished head” before them, it is, with few exceptions, very unfortunate for a nation when a man of ability, without rank or property, pushes himself forward into public notice. Alas! What unheard-of misery have thousands suffered to buy a cardinal’s hat for some scheming, obscure adventurer who longed to be ranked with princes, or to lord it over them by seizing the triple crown!

Such, indeed, has been the wretchedness that has flowed from hereditary honours, wealth and monarchy that men of lively sensibility have almost uttered blasphemy in trying to justify the ways of providence. Man has been portrayed as independent of the power of his Maker, or as a lawless planet darting out of its orbit to steal the heavenly fire of reason; and the vengeance of heaven, lurking in that subtle flame, amply punished his rashness by bringing evil into the world.

Struck by this view of the misery and disorder that pervaded society, and weary of jostling against artificial fools, Rousseau fell in love with solitude; and, being at the same time an optimist, he labours with uncommon eloquence to prove that man was by nature a solitary animal. Misled by his respect for the goodness of God — who certainly (for what man of sense and feeling can doubt it!) gave life only in order to communicate happiness — he regards evil as something positive, and as the work of man, not realizing that he was exalting one attribute at the expense of another that is equally necessary to divine perfection.

Resting on a false hypothesis, his arguments for a state of nature are plausible but unsound. I call them unsound because to claim that a state of nature is better than civilization in all its possible perfection amounts to putting supreme wisdom on trial; and the paradoxical cry that God made everything right, and that evil was brought in by the creature he formed, knowing what he was forming, is as unphilosophical as it is impious.

That wise Being who made us and set us here, when he beheld the fair idea, willed — by permitting it to be so — that our reason should be unfolded by the passions, since he could foresee that present evil would yield future good. Could the helpless creature he summoned out of nothing break loose from his providence and, without his permission, boldly learn to know good by practising evil? No. How could that energetic advocate of immortality reason so inconsistently? If mankind had stayed forever in the brutish state of nature — which not even his magic pen can depict as a condition in which a single virtue took root — it would have been plain, though not to the sensitive, unreflecting wanderer, that man was born to go round the cycle of life and death and to ornament God’s garden for some purpose hard to reconcile with his attributes.

But if, to crown the whole, rational creatures were to be produced, allowed to rise in excellence by exercising powers implanted for that purpose; if benevolence itself saw fit to call into existence a creature above the animals, one who could think and improve himself, why should that priceless gift — for a gift it was, if man was so created as to be capable of rising above the state in which sensation produced brutish ease — be called, in so many words, a curse? It might be reckoned a curse if our whole existence were limited to our time in this world; for why should the gracious fountain of life give us passions and the power of reflection only to embitter our days and fill us with mistaken notions of dignity? Why should he lead us from love of ourselves to the sublime emotions excited by the discovery of his wisdom and goodness, if these feelings were not set in motion to improve our nature, of which they form a part, and to make us capable of enjoying a more godlike share of happiness? Firmly convinced that no evil exists in the world that God did not design to take place, I build my belief on the perfection of God.
Rousseau exerts himself to prove that all WAS right originally; a crowd of authors, that all IS right now; and I, that all WILL BE right.

But, true to his first position, Rousseau celebrates barbarism as the next best thing to a state of nature; and, addressing the shade of Fabricius, he forgets that the Romans, in conquering the world, never dreamed of setting their own liberty on a firm basis or of extending the reign of virtue. Eager to support his system, he brands every effort of genius as vicious; and, pronouncing the deification of savage virtues, he raises to the rank of demigods men who were scarcely human — the brutal Spartans, who, in defiance of justice and gratitude, slaughtered in cold blood the slaves who had shown themselves to be men by rescuing their oppressors.

Disgusted with artificial manners and virtues, the citizen of Geneva, instead of sifting the subject properly, threw out the wheat with the chaff, without stopping to ask whether the evils from which his ardent soul turned in indignation were the result of civilization or the remnants of barbarism. He saw vice trampling on virtue, and the appearance of goodness taking the place of the reality; he saw talents bent by power to sinister ends, and never thought of tracing this gigantic mischief back to arbitrary power — back to the hereditary distinctions that clash with the mental superiority that naturally raises one man above his fellows. He did not see that royal power, within a few generations, brings idiocy into the noble line, and holds out bait that makes thousands idle and vicious.

Nothing can show the royal character in a more contemptible light than the various crimes that have raised men to the highest rank. Vile intrigues, unnatural crimes and every vice that degrades our nature have been the steps to this exalted eminence; yet millions of men have passively allowed the feeble limbs of the descendants of such rapacious prowlers to rest undisturbed on their bloodstained thrones.

What but a poisonous vapour can hang over society when its chief director has been taught nothing but the invention of crimes, or the stupid routine of childish ceremonies? Will men never be wise? Will they never stop expecting corn from tares, and figs from thistles?

No man, even when the most favourable circumstances combine, can acquire enough knowledge and strength of mind to perform the duties of a king entrusted with unchecked power. How, then, must those duties be violated when his very elevation is an insuperable barrier to gaining either wisdom or virtue — when all his feelings as a man are stifled by flattery, and reflection is shut out by pleasure! Surely it is madness to make the fate of thousands depend on the whim of a weak fellow creature whose very station sinks him NECESSARILY below the lowest of his subjects! But one power should not be thrown down in order to raise up another — for all power intoxicates weak man, and its abuse proves that the more equality is established among men, the more virtue and happiness will reign in society. Yet this, and any similar maxim drawn from simple reason, raises an outcry: the church or the state is in danger if faith in the wisdom of antiquity is not unquestioning; and those who, roused by the sight of human suffering, dare to attack human authority are reviled as despisers of God and enemies of man. These are bitter slanders, yet they reached one of the best of men (Dr. Price), whose ashes still preach peace, and whose memory calls for a respectful pause whenever subjects so close to his heart are discussed.

After attacking the sacred majesty of kings, I shall hardly cause surprise by adding my firm conviction that every profession whose power rests on a strict hierarchy of rank is highly damaging to morality.

A standing army, for example, cannot coexist with freedom, since subordination and rigour are the very sinews of military discipline, and despotism is required to give vigour to undertakings directed by one will. A spirit fired by romantic notions of honour — a sort of morality based on the fashion of the day — can be felt by only a few officers, while the bulk of the army must be moved by command, like the waves of the sea; for the strong wind of authority drives the mass of subordinates forward in headlong fury, though they hardly know or care why.

Moreover, nothing can do so much harm to the morals of people in country towns as the occasional quartering among them of a set of idle, superficial young men whose sole occupation is gallantry, and whose polished manners make vice all the more dangerous by concealing its ugliness beneath bright, decorative drapery. An air of fashion — merely a badge of slavery, and proof that the soul has no strong character of its own — so overawes simple country people that they imitate the vices when they cannot catch the elusive graces of polite behaviour. Each regiment is a chain of despots who, obeying and tyrannizing without using their reason, hang as dead weights of vice and folly on the community. A man of rank or fortune, certain of advancement through connections, has nothing to do but chase some extravagant whim; while the needy GENTLEMAN, who must rise, as the phrase goes, on his merit, turns into a servile parasite or a vile pimp.

Sailors — the naval gentlemen — fit the same description, except that their vices take a different and coarser form. They are more thoroughly idle when they are not carrying out the ceremonial duties of their station, whereas the trivial fluttering of soldiers might be called active idleness. Confined more to the company of men, sailors acquire a taste for broad humour and mischievous pranks; soldiers, who frequently mix with well-bred women, pick up a sentimental cant. But mind is equally out of the question, whether they indulge in the horse-laugh or the polite simper.

May I extend the comparison to a profession in which more mind is certainly to be found? For the clergy have better opportunities for improvement, though subordination cramps their faculties almost as much. The blind submission to forms of belief imposed at university serves as an apprenticeship for the curate who, if he means to rise in his profession, most obsequiously respects the opinion of his rector or patron. Perhaps there can be no more striking contrast than that between the servile, dependent gait of a poor curate and the courtly bearing of a bishop. And the respect and the contempt they inspire make the performance of their separate functions equally useless.

It is very important to observe that every man’s character is, to some degree, formed by his profession. A man of sense may have only a professional cast of features that wears off as you trace his individuality, whereas the weak, common man scarcely ever has any character except what belongs to his corps; at least, all his opinions have been so steeped in the vat consecrated by authority that the faint spirit yielded by the grape of his own vine cannot be distinguished.
As society grows more enlightened, therefore, it should take great care not to set up bodies of men who are bound to be made foolish or vicious by the very constitution of their profession.

When society was in its infancy and men were only just emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests, who worked the two most powerful springs of savage conduct — hope and fear — must have held boundless sway. Naturally, then, aristocracy is the first form of government. But clashing interests soon lose their balance; out of the confusion of ambitious struggles a monarchy and a church hierarchy emerge, and feudal tenures secure the foundations of both. This seems to be the origin of royal and priestly power, and the dawn of civilization. Such combustible materials, however, cannot stay pent up for long; they find an outlet in foreign wars and internal uprisings, and in the tumult the people gain some power, which forces their rulers to cover their oppression with a show of right. So, as wars, agriculture, commerce and literature broaden the mind, despots are driven to hold, by hidden corruption, the power that was once seized by open force.* And this deadly, lurking gangrene is spread fastest by luxury and superstition, the sure dregs of ambition. The idle puppet of a court first turns into a luxurious monster or a fastidious sensualist, and then uses the contagion spread by his unnatural condition as the instrument of tyranny.

(*Footnote. Men of ability scatter seeds that grow up and have a great influence on the formation of opinion; and once public opinion gains the upper hand, through the exercise of reason, the overthrow of arbitrary power is not far off.)

It is this pestilential royal purple that makes the progress of civilization a curse and distorts the understanding, so that men of sensibility come to doubt whether the growth of the intellect yields more happiness or more misery. Yet the nature of the poison indicates its antidote. Had Rousseau gone one step further in his inquiry, or had his eye been able to see through the foggy air he almost scorned to breathe, his active mind would have leapt ahead to contemplate man’s perfection in the founding of true civilization, rather than taking his ferocious flight back into the night of sensual ignorance.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Prevailing Opinion of a Sexual Character Discussed
paragraphs: Many ingenious arguments have been put forward to account for and excuse the tyranny of man, arguments meant to prove that in acquiring virtue the two sexes ought to aim at quite different characters. To put it plainly, women are not granted enough strength of mind to acquire anything that truly deserves the name of virtue. Yet, if we allow that they have souls, it would seem that providence has appointed only one way to lead MANKIND to either virtue or happiness.

If, then, women are not a swarm of triflers who live, like mayflies, for a single day, why should they be kept ignorant under the plausible name of innocence? Men complain, and rightly, of the follies and whims of our sex, when they are not busy savagely satirizing our headstrong passions and grovelling vices. Look, I would answer, at the natural effect of ignorance! A mind with nothing but prejudices to rest on will always be unstable, and a current will rush on with destructive fury when there are no barriers to break its force. From infancy women are told, and taught by their mothers’ example, that a little knowledge of human weakness (rightly called cunning), a soft temper, OUTWARD obedience and a scrupulous attention to a childish sort of propriety will win them the protection of man; and that if they are beautiful, nothing else is needed, for at least twenty years of their lives.

That is how Milton describes our first frail mother. Yet when he tells us that women are formed for softness and sweet attractive grace, I cannot understand what he means, unless, in the true Mahometan manner, he meant to deny us souls and to hint that we were beings designed, by sweet attractive grace and docile blind obedience, solely to gratify the senses of man when he can no longer soar on the wing of contemplation.

How grossly they insult us who advise us in this way to make ourselves nothing more than gentle domestic animals! Consider, for example, that winning softness, so warmly and so often recommended, which governs by obeying. What childish language! And how insignificant is the being — can it be an immortal one? — who will stoop to govern by such underhand methods! “Certainly,” says Lord Bacon, “man is of kin to the beasts by his body: and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit, he is a base and ignoble creature!” Men, it seems to me, act in a thoroughly unphilosophical way when they try to secure the good conduct of women by trying to keep them forever in a state of childhood. Rousseau was more consistent when he wished to halt the progress of reason in both sexes; for if men eat of the tree of knowledge, women will come in for a taste. But since their understandings now receive only an imperfect cultivation, all they acquire is a knowledge of evil.

Children, I grant, should be innocent; but applied to men or women, the word is merely a polite name for weakness. For if we allow that Providence destined women to acquire human virtues, and, by exercising their understandings, to gain that stability of character which is the firmest ground for our hopes of the future, then they must be permitted to turn to the fountain of light itself, and not be forced to steer by the twinkling of a mere satellite. Milton, I grant, thought very differently, for he bows only to the indefeasible right of beauty; though it would be hard to reconcile the two passages I now intend to set side by side. But great men are often led by their senses into inconsistencies of this kind: —

“To whom thus Eve with perfect beauty adorned: My author and disposer, what thou bidst Unargued I obey; so God ordains; God is thy law, thou mine; to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge and her praise.”

These are precisely the arguments I have used with children, except that I have added: “Your reason is growing stronger now, and until it reaches some degree of maturity you must look up to me for advice; after that you ought to THINK, and to rely on God alone.”
Yet in the following lines Milton seems to agree with me, when he has Adam remonstrate with his Maker in these words: —

“Hast thou not made me here thy substitute, And these inferior far beneath me set? Among unequals what society Can sort, what harmony or delight? Which must be mutual, in proportion due Given and received; but in disparity The one intense, the other still remiss Cannot well suit with either, but soon prove Tedious alike: of fellowship I speak Such as I seek fit to participate All rational delight.”

In discussing the conduct and character of women, therefore, let us set sensual arguments aside and work out what we should try to make of them, so that they may co-operate, if the expression is not too bold, with the Supreme Being.

By individual education I mean — for the sense of the term has not been precisely fixed — the kind of attention to a child that will gradually sharpen the senses, shape the temper, regulate the passions as they begin to stir, and set the understanding to work before the body is mature; so that the grown man need only continue the important task of learning to think and reason, not begin it.

To prevent any misreading, I must add that I do not believe a private education can work the wonders that some over-hopeful writers have credited it with. Men and women must be educated, to a great extent, by the opinions and customs of the society they live in. In every age a current of popular opinion has swept all before it and given the century, as it were, a family likeness. We may fairly infer, then, that until society is differently constituted, not much can be expected from education. For my present purpose, however, it is enough to assert that, whatever effect circumstances have on the abilities, every being can become virtuous by exercising its own reason. For if even one being were created with vicious inclinations — that is, positively bad — what could save us from atheism? Or, if we worship a God, would that God not be a devil?

It follows that the most perfect education, in my view, is the kind of exercise of the understanding best suited to strengthen the body and form the heart — or, in other words, to enable the individual to acquire such habits of virtue as will make it independent. Indeed, it is a farce to call any being virtuous whose virtues do not spring from the exercise of its own reason. Rousseau held this opinion about men; I extend it to women, and I confidently assert that they have been drawn out of their proper sphere by false refinement, not by any effort to acquire masculine qualities. Still, the royal homage they receive is so intoxicating that, until the morals and customs of the age change and come to rest on more reasonable principles, it may be impossible to convince them of two things: that the illegitimate power they gain by degrading themselves is a curse, and that they must return to nature and equality if they wish to secure the calm contentment that natural, unspoiled affections bring. But for that era we must wait — wait, perhaps, until kings and nobles, enlightened by reason and preferring the real dignity of man to childish pomp, throw off their gaudy inherited trappings; and if even then women do not give up the arbitrary power of beauty, they will prove that they have LESS mind than man. I may be accused of arrogance, yet I must declare what I firmly believe: every writer on female education and manners, from Rousseau to Dr. Gregory, has helped to make women more artificial and weaker in character than they would otherwise have been, and consequently more useless members of society. I could have stated this conviction in a gentler tone; but I fear that would have been the whine of affectation, not a faithful expression of my feelings and of the clear conclusion that experience and reflection have led me to draw. When I come to that part of the subject, I shall turn to the passages I most particularly object to in the works of the authors just mentioned; but I must first point out that my objection covers the whole drift of those books, which tend, in my opinion, to degrade one half of the human species and to make women pleasing at the cost of every solid virtue.

Yet, to reason on Rousseau’s own ground: if a man did reach a degree of mental perfection when his body reached maturity, it might then be right, in order to make a man and his wife ONE, for her to rely entirely on his understanding; and the graceful ivy clinging to the oak that supported it would form a whole in which strength and beauty stood out equally. But alas! husbands, like their helpmates, are often no more than overgrown children — indeed, thanks to early debauchery, hardly men even in outward form; and if the blind lead the blind, no one need come down from heaven to tell us the result.

In the present corrupt state of society, many causes combine to enslave women by cramping their understandings and sharpening their senses. One of them, which perhaps does more silent harm than all the rest, is their disregard of order.

Doing everything in an orderly way is a most important rule. Yet women, who generally receive only a disorderly sort of education, seldom keep to it with the exactness of men, who are trained to method from infancy. This careless guesswork — for what other word describes the random efforts of a kind of instinctive common sense that has never been tested by reason? — prevents them from drawing general conclusions from facts, so that they do today what they did yesterday, simply because they did it yesterday.

This contempt for the understanding in early life has more damaging effects than is commonly supposed. For the little knowledge that women of strong minds do acquire is, for various reasons, more haphazard than that of men, and it is gained more from sheer observation of real life than from comparing individual observations with the results of experience generalized by reflection. Since their dependent position and domestic occupations draw them more into company, they learn in snatches; and because learning is, in general, only a secondary concern for them, they do not pursue any single branch of it with the persevering ardour needed to give vigour to the faculties and clarity to the judgment. In the present state of society a little learning is required to keep up the character of a gentleman, and boys are made to submit to a few years of discipline. In the education of women, however, the cultivation of the understanding always gives way to acquiring some physical accomplishment; and even then, weakened by confinement and false notions of modesty, the body is kept from attaining the grace and beauty that slack, half-formed limbs never show. Besides, in youth their faculties are not drawn out by rivalry; and since they have no serious scientific study, whatever natural shrewdness they possess is turned too early upon life and manners. They dwell on effects and variations without tracing them back to causes; and complicated rules for regulating behaviour are a poor substitute for simple principles.

As proof that it is education which gives females this appearance of weakness, we may point to the example of military men, who, like women, are sent out into the world before their minds have been furnished with knowledge or strengthened by principles. The results are similar. Soldiers pick up a little superficial knowledge, snatched from the muddy stream of conversation, and by constantly mixing in company they acquire what is called a knowledge of the world; and this familiarity with manners and customs has often been mistaken for a knowledge of the human heart. But does the raw fruit of casual observation, never tested by a judgment formed through comparing theory with experience, deserve such an honour? Soldiers, like women, practise the minor virtues with meticulous politeness. Where, then, is the difference of sex, when the education has been the same? All the difference I can see arises from the greater advantage of liberty, which lets soldiers see more of life.
It may be a digression from my present subject to make a political remark; but since it arose naturally from the course of my reflections, I shall not pass over it in silence.

Standing armies can never be made up of resolute, robust men. They may be well-drilled machines, but they will seldom include men moved by strong passions or possessed of very vigorous faculties. As for any depth of understanding, I will venture to say that it is as rarely found in the army as among women; and the cause, I maintain, is the same. It may further be noted that officers, too, pay particular attention to their appearance and are fond of dancing, crowded rooms, adventures and ridicule. Like the FAIR sex, they make gallantry the business of their lives. They were taught to please, and they live only to please. Yet they keep their rank in the distinction between the sexes, for they are still thought superior to women — though what that superiority consists in, beyond what I have just described, is hard to discover.

The great misfortune is that they both acquire manners before morals, and a knowledge of life before reflection has given them any acquaintance with the grand ideal outline of human nature. The result is only natural. Content with human nature as it commonly appears, they fall prey to prejudices; and since they take all their opinions on trust, they submit blindly to authority. So if they have any good sense, it is a sort of instinctive glance that takes in proportions and passes judgment on manners, but that fails whenever arguments must be pursued below the surface or opinions analysed.

May not the same remark be applied to women? Indeed, the argument may be pushed further still, for both are thrown out of any useful station by the unnatural distinctions established in civilized life. Riches and hereditary honours have turned women into ciphers, mere zeros that lend importance to the figure standing before them; and idleness has bred in society a mixture of gallantry and despotism which leads the very men who are slaves to their mistresses to tyrannize over their sisters, wives and daughters. This, it is true, merely keeps them in rank and file. Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and blind obedience will come to an end; but since power always seeks blind obedience, tyrants and sensualists are quite right to try to keep women in the dark, for the former want only slaves and the latter a plaything. The sensualist, indeed, has been the most dangerous of tyrants; and women have been duped by their lovers, as princes are by their ministers, while dreaming that they ruled over them.

I am now chiefly alluding to Rousseau, for his character of Sophia is undoubtedly a captivating one, though it strikes me as grossly unnatural. What I intend to attack, however, is not the superstructure but the foundation of her character: the principles on which her education was built. Indeed, warmly as I admire the genius of that able writer, whose opinions I shall often have occasion to cite, when I read his voluptuous reveries indignation always takes the place of admiration, and the stern frown of insulted virtue wipes away the smile of pleasure that his eloquent sentences usually raise. Is this the man who, in his ardour for virtue, would banish all the gentle arts of peace and almost carry us back to Spartan discipline? Is this the man who delights in painting the useful struggles of passion, the triumphs of good dispositions, and the heroic flights that carry the glowing soul beyond itself? How these mighty sentiments are lowered when he describes the pretty foot and enticing airs of his little favourite! But I set the subject aside for now; and, rather than severely rebuking the passing outpourings of overweening sensibility, I shall only observe that anyone who has looked on society with a benevolent eye must often have been gratified by the sight of humble mutual love, neither dignified by sentiment nor strengthened by shared intellectual pursuits. The domestic trifles of the day have supplied matter for cheerful talk, and innocent caresses have softened labours that called for no great exercise of mind or stretch of thought. Yet has not the sight of this modest happiness stirred more tenderness than respect? It is an emotion like the one we feel when children are playing or animals frolicking; whereas the contemplation of the noble struggles of suffering merit has raised our admiration and carried our thoughts to that world where sensation will give way to reason.
Women, therefore, must be regarded either as moral beings, or as so weak that they must be wholly subjected to the superior faculties of men.

Let us examine this question. Rousseau declares that a woman should never for a moment feel herself independent; that she should be ruled by fear so as to exercise her NATURAL cunning; and that she should be made a coquettish slave so that she may be a more alluring object of desire, a SWEETER companion to man whenever he chooses to relax. He pushes still further the arguments that he claims to draw from the indications of nature, and hints that truth and fortitude, the cornerstones of all human virtue, should be cultivated only within certain limits, because, where the female character is concerned, obedience is the great lesson that must be impressed with unrelenting rigour.

What nonsense! When will some great man appear with strength of mind enough to blow away the fumes with which pride and sensuality have clouded this subject! If women are inferior to men by nature, their virtues must nonetheless be of the same quality, if not of the same degree, or else virtue becomes a merely relative idea; it follows that their conduct ought to rest on the same principles and aim at the same goal.

Bound to man as daughters, wives and mothers, women may have their moral character judged by the way they fulfil those simple duties; but the end, the great end, of their efforts should be to unfold their own faculties and acquire the dignity of conscious virtue. They may try to make their road pleasant, but, like men, they ought never to forget that life does not yield the happiness that can satisfy an immortal soul. I do not mean to suggest that either sex should become so lost in abstract reflection or distant prospects as to forget the affections and duties that lie before them, which are in truth the means appointed to produce the fruit of life. On the contrary, I would warmly recommend them, even while I assert that they give the most satisfaction when they are seen in their true, subordinate light.

The prevailing opinion that woman was created for man may well have originated in Moses’s poetic story. Yet since very few people, one presumes, who have given the subject any serious thought have ever supposed that Eve was literally one of Adam’s ribs, the inference must be allowed to collapse; or it may be admitted only so far as it proves that man, from the remotest antiquity, found it convenient to use his strength to subjugate his companion, and his ingenuity to show that her neck ought to be bent under the yoke, because she, like the brute creation, was created to do his pleasure.

Let no one conclude that I wish to turn the order of things upside down. I have already granted that, from the constitution of their bodies, men seem designed by Providence to attain a greater degree of virtue. I speak collectively of the whole sex; but I see not the shadow of a reason to conclude that their virtues should differ in nature. Indeed, how could they, if virtue has only one eternal standard? If I reason consistently, therefore, I must maintain as firmly that they have the same simple direction as that there is a God.

It follows, then, that cunning should not be set up against wisdom, petty cares against great exertions, or insipid softness, varnished over with the name of gentleness, against the fortitude that only grand views can inspire.

I shall be told that woman would then lose many of her particular graces, and the opinion of a well-known poet may be quoted to refute my unqualified assertions. For Pope has said, speaking for the whole male sex,
“Yet ne’er so sure our passions to create, As when she touch’d the brink of all we hate.”

I leave it to the judicious to decide in what light this sally places men and women; for the present I shall be content to observe that I cannot see why, unless they are mortal, females should always be degraded by being made subordinate to love or lust.

To speak disrespectfully of love is, I know, high treason against sentiment and fine feelings; but I wish to speak the plain language of truth, and to appeal to the head rather than the heart. Trying to reason love out of the world would be to outdo Cervantes in Quixotism, and would be just as great an offence against common sense; but an attempt to restrain this tumultuous passion, and to prove that it should not be allowed to dethrone the higher powers or to seize the sceptre that the understanding should always wield with composure, seems less wild.

In both sexes youth is the season for love; but during those days of thoughtless enjoyment, provision ought to be made for the weightier years of life, when sensation gives way to reflection. Yet Rousseau, and most of the male writers who have trodden in his footsteps, have warmly taught that the entire tendency of female education should be aimed at a single point: to make women pleasing.

Let me reason with those supporters of this opinion who have any knowledge of human nature: do they imagine that marriage can uproot the habits of a lifetime? The woman who has been taught only to please will soon find that her charms are slanting rays of sunlight, and that they can have little effect on her husband’s heart once they are seen every day, when summer is past and gone. Will she then have enough inner energy to look into herself for comfort and cultivate her dormant faculties? Or is it not more reasonable to expect that she will try to please other men, and, in the excitement raised by the hope of new conquests, try to forget the humiliation her love or pride has suffered? When the husband ceases to be a lover — and that time will inevitably come — her desire to please will then grow languid or turn into a source of bitterness; and love, perhaps the most fleeting of all passions, gives way to jealousy or vanity.

I am speaking now of women who are held back by principle or prejudice. Such women would shrink from an affair with real horror, yet they still wish to be persuaded, by the homage of gallant admirers, that their husbands cruelly neglect them; or they spend days and weeks dreaming of the happiness enjoyed by kindred souls, until their health is undermined and their spirits are broken by discontent. How, then, can the great art of pleasing be so necessary a study? It is useful only to a mistress. The chaste wife and serious mother should regard her power to please merely as the polish on her virtues, and her husband’s affection as one of the comforts that make her task less difficult and her life happier. But whether she is loved or neglected, her first wish should be to make herself worthy of respect, and not to rest all her happiness on a being subject to the same weaknesses as herself.
The amiable Dr. Gregory made a similar mistake. I respect his heart, but I wholly disapprove of his celebrated Legacy to his Daughters.

He advises them to cultivate a fondness for dress because, he asserts, a fondness for dress is natural to them. I cannot understand what either he or Rousseau means when they so often use this vague term. If they told us that in some earlier existence the soul was fond of dress and brought the inclination with it into a new body, I should listen with a half smile, as I often do when I hear someone hold forth about innate elegance. But if he meant only that the exercise of the faculties will produce this fondness, I deny it. It is not natural; like false ambition in men, it springs from a love of power.

Dr. Gregory goes much further: he actually recommends pretence, advising an innocent girl to belie her own feelings and not to dance with spirit, even when gaiety of heart would make her feet eloquent without making her movements immodest. In the name of truth and common sense, why should one woman not admit that she can take more exercise than another — in other words, that she has a sound constitution? And why, to dampen innocent liveliness, must she be darkly told that men will draw conclusions she little suspects? Let the libertine draw whatever inference he likes; but I hope that no sensible mother will check the natural frankness of youth by instilling such indecent warnings. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh; and one wiser than Solomon has said that the heart should be made clean, rather than that trivial ceremonies be observed — ceremonies that are not very hard to perform with scrupulous exactness while vice reigns in the heart.

Women ought to strive to purify their hearts; but how can they, when their uncultivated understandings leave them wholly dependent on their senses for occupation and amusement; when no noble pursuit lifts them above the petty vanities of the day, or enables them to curb the wild emotions that shake a reed at the mercy of every passing breeze? Is affectation needed to win the affections of a virtuous man?

Nature has given woman a weaker frame than man. But consider a wife who, by exercising her mind and body while discharging the duties of daughter, wife and mother, has allowed her constitution to keep its natural strength and her nerves a healthy tone: to ensure her husband’s affections, must she, I say, stoop to use art and feign a sickly delicacy in order to secure his affection? Weakness may arouse tenderness and flatter the arrogant pride of man; but the lordly caresses of a protector will not satisfy a noble mind that longs to be respected and deserves to be. Doting fondness is a poor substitute for friendship!

In a seraglio, I grant, all these arts are necessary; the epicure must have his palate tickled, or he will sink into apathy. But have women so little ambition that they are content with such a condition? Can they idly dream their lives away in the lap of pleasure or the languor of weariness, instead of asserting their claim to pursue rational pleasures and distinguishing themselves by practising the virtues that dignify mankind? Surely she has no immortal soul who can idle her life away, occupied solely in adorning her person so that she may amuse the listless hours and soften the cares of a fellow creature who is willing to be enlivened by her smiles and tricks once the serious business of life is over.

Moreover, the woman who strengthens her body and exercises her mind will, by managing her household and practising various virtues, become her husband’s friend, not his humble dependant; and if such solid qualities earn her his regard, she will not find it necessary to hide her affection, or to pretend to an unnatural coldness of constitution in order to arouse his passions. Indeed, if we look back at history, we shall find that the women who have distinguished themselves were neither the most beautiful nor the gentlest of their sex.

Nature — or, to speak with strict correctness, God — has made all things right; but man has sought out many inventions to spoil the work. I am referring now to the part of Dr. Gregory’s treatise in which he advises a wife never to let her husband know the extent of her sensibility or affection. A sensualist’s precaution, and as futile as it is absurd! Love, by its very nature, must be transitory. To look for a secret that would make it constant would be as wild a search as the hunt for the philosopher’s stone or the universal remedy; and the discovery would be just as useless, or rather harmful, to mankind. The most sacred bond of society is friendship. A shrewd satirist has well said “that rare as true love is, true friendship is still rarer.”
This is an obvious truth, and since its cause does not lie deep, even a slight inquiry will find it.

Love, the common passion, in which chance and sensation take the place of choice and reason, is felt to some degree by the mass of mankind; for there is no need at present to speak of the emotions that rise above love or sink below it. This passion, naturally heightened by suspense and obstacles, draws the mind out of its usual state and exalts the affections. But once the security of marriage lets the fever of love subside, a healthy temperature is thought insipid only by those who lack the intellect to put the calm tenderness of friendship and the confidence of respect in the place of blind admiration and the sensual emotions of fondness.

This is, and must be, the course of nature: friendship or indifference inevitably follows love. And this arrangement seems to harmonize perfectly with the system of government that prevails in the moral world. Passions spur us to action and open the mind; but once the object is gained and the satisfied mind rests in enjoyment, they sink into mere appetites, a personal and momentary gratification. The man who had some virtue while he was fighting for a crown often becomes a voluptuous tyrant once it adorns his brow; and when the lover is not lost in the husband, the dotard, a prey to childish whims and doting jealousies, neglects the serious duties of life, and the caresses that should build confidence in his children are lavished on the overgrown child, his wife.

To fulfil the duties of life, and to be able to pursue with vigour the various occupations that form the moral character, the master and mistress of a family ought not to go on loving each other with passion. I mean that they ought not to indulge those emotions that disturb the order of society and absorb thoughts which should be employed otherwise. The mind that has never been absorbed by a single object lacks vigour; but if it can remain so absorbed for long, it is weak.

A mistaken education, a narrow, uncultivated mind and many prejudices about sex tend to make women more constant than men; but for the present I shall not touch on this branch of the subject. I will go further still and put forward, without any thought of paradox, the claim that an unhappy marriage is often very beneficial to a family, and that the neglected wife is, in general, the best mother. And this would nearly always be the result if the female mind were more enlarged. For it seems to be the ordinary rule of Providence that whatever we gain in present enjoyment is deducted from that treasure of life, experience; and that while we are gathering the flowers of the day and revelling in pleasure, we cannot at the same time seize the solid fruit of toil and wisdom. The road lies before us, and we must turn right or left; whoever passes his life bounding from one pleasure to another must not complain if he gains neither wisdom nor a respectable character.

Suppose for a moment that the soul is not immortal and that man was created only for the present scene: I think we should then have reason to complain that love, that childish doting, ever grew insipid and lost its savour. Let us eat, drink and love, for tomorrow we die, would then indeed be the language of reason and the morality of life; and who but a fool would give up a reality for a fleeting shadow? But if, awed by observing the capacity of the mind for improvement, we scorn to confine our wishes or thoughts to so comparatively low a field of action, which appears grand and important only as it is connected with a boundless prospect and sublime hopes, what need is there for falsehood in conduct? And why must the sacred majesty of truth be violated to hold on to a deceptive good that undermines the very foundation of virtue? Why must the female mind be tainted with coquettish arts to gratify the sensualist, and to keep love from subsiding into friendship or compassionate tenderness, when there are no qualities on which friendship can be built? Let the honest heart show itself, and let REASON teach passion to submit to necessity; or let the dignified pursuit of virtue and knowledge raise the mind above those emotions which, when they are not kept within due bounds, embitter the cup of life rather than sweeten it.

I do not mean to refer to the romantic passion that accompanies genius. Who can clip its wings? But that grand passion, out of proportion to the puny enjoyments of life, is true only to the sentiment and feeds on itself. The passions celebrated for their durability have always been unhappy ones. They have gained strength from absence and from a melancholy temperament. Fancy has hovered around a form of beauty dimly seen — but familiarity might have turned admiration into disgust, or at least into indifference, and left the imagination free to start fresh game. On this view of things, Rousseau quite fittingly makes Eloisa, the mistress of his soul, love St. Preux when life was fading before her; but this is no proof that the passion is immortal.

Dr. Gregory’s advice about delicacy of sentiment is of the same kind: he advises a woman not to acquire it if she has made up her mind to marry. Yet this resolution, though perfectly consistent with his earlier advice, he calls INDELICATE, and he earnestly urges his daughters to hide it, even though it may govern their conduct — as if it were indelicate to have the ordinary appetites of human nature.

Noble morality! and consistent with the cautious prudence of a little soul that cannot see beyond the tiny portion of existence now before it. If all the faculties of a woman’s mind are to be cultivated only in so far as they concern her dependence on man; if, once she has obtained a husband, she has reached her goal and, basely proud, is content with so paltry a crown, then let her grovel contentedly, raised by her occupations scarcely above the animal kingdom. But if she is striving for the prize of her high calling, let her cultivate her understanding without stopping to consider what sort of character the husband she is destined to marry may have. Let her simply resolve, without being too anxious about present happiness, to acquire the qualities that ennoble a rational being; then a rough, unrefined husband may offend her taste without destroying her peace of mind. She will not shape her soul to suit her companion’s failings, but to bear them: his character may be a trial, but not an obstacle to virtue.

If Dr. Gregory meant his remark to apply only to romantic expectations of constant love and kindred feelings, he should have remembered that experience will banish what advice can never make us stop wishing for, when imagination is kept alive at the expense of reason.

I admit that it often happens that women who have nursed a romantic, unnatural delicacy of feeling waste their lives IMAGINING how happy they would have been with a husband who could love them with an ardent affection that grew every day and all day long. But they might as well pine married as single, and would not be one bit more unhappy with a bad husband than they are longing for a good one. That a proper education — or, to be more exact, a well-stocked mind — would enable a woman to bear a single life with dignity, I grant; but for her to avoid cultivating her taste in case her husband should occasionally offend it is to give up the substance for the shadow. To tell the truth, I do not see what use a cultivated taste is, if it does not make the individual more independent of the accidents of life; if it does not open new sources of enjoyment that depend only on the solitary workings of the mind. People of taste, married or single alike, will always be repelled by various things that do not touch less observant minds. The argument must not be allowed to turn on this conclusion; but, taking the whole sum of enjoyment into account, should taste be called a blessing?

The question is whether it brings more pain or more pleasure. The answer will settle whether Dr. Gregory’s advice is sound, and will show how absurd and tyrannical it is to lay down a system of slavery in this way, or to try to educate moral beings by any rules other than those derived from pure reason, which apply to the whole species.

Gentleness of manner, forbearance and long-suffering are such lovable, godlike qualities that sublime poetry has clothed the Deity in them; and perhaps no picture of his goodness takes so strong a hold on human affections as those that show him abounding in mercy and ready to pardon. Seen in this light, gentleness bears on its face every mark of grandeur, joined with the winning graces of condescension. But how different it looks when it is the submissive bearing of dependence, the prop of a weakness that loves because it needs protection, and forbears because it must endure injuries in silence, smiling under the lash at which it dare not snarl. Abject as this picture seems, it is the portrait of an accomplished woman, according to the accepted idea of female excellence, which plausible reasoners have separated from human excellence. Or else they (see Rousseau and Swedenborg) kindly restore the rib and make one moral being of a man and a woman, not forgetting to give her all the “submissive charms.”

We are not told how women are to exist in that state where there is to be neither marrying nor giving in marriage. For although moralists agree that the course of life seems to prove that MAN is being prepared by various circumstances for a future state, they consistently join in advising WOMAN to provide only for the present. On this basis gentleness, docility and a spaniel-like affection are, consistently enough, recommended as the cardinal virtues of the sex; and one writer, ignoring the arbitrary economy of nature, has declared that it is masculine for a woman to be melancholy. She was created to be man’s toy, his rattle, and it must jingle in his ears whenever he chooses to set reason aside and be amused.

To recommend gentleness on broad grounds is, indeed, strictly philosophical. A frail being should work at being gentle. But when forbearance confuses right and wrong, it ceases to be a virtue; and however convenient it may prove in a companion, that companion will always be regarded as an inferior and will inspire only an insipid tenderness that easily sinks into contempt. Still, if advice could really make gentle a being whose natural disposition did not allow of so fine a polish, some progress toward order would be made. But if, as could quickly be shown, this indiscriminate counsel produces only affectation, and puts a stumbling block in the way of gradual improvement and genuine betterment of temper, then the sex gains little by sacrificing solid virtues to acquire superficial graces, even if for a few years these may win the individual a royal sway.

As a philosopher, I read with indignation the plausible epithets that men use to soften their insults; and as a moralist, I ask what is meant by such mismatched pairings as fair defects, amiable weaknesses, etc.? If there is only one standard of morals, only one archetype for man, women seem to be suspended by destiny, like Mahomet’s coffin in the popular tale: they have neither the unerring instinct of brutes, nor are they permitted to fix the eye of reason on a perfect model. They were made to be loved, and must not aim at respect, for fear of being hunted out of society as masculine.

But let us look at the subject from another side. Do passive, indolent women make the best wives? Confining our discussion to the present life, let us see how such weak creatures play their part. Do the women who have strengthened the prevailing prejudice by acquiring a few superficial accomplishments merely add to their husbands’ happiness? Do they display their charms merely to amuse them? And have women who absorbed notions of passive obedience early in life enough character to run a household or educate children? So far from it that, after surveying the history of woman, I cannot help agreeing with the severest satirist and regarding the sex as both the weakest and the most oppressed half of the species. What does history reveal but marks of inferiority, and how few women have freed themselves from the galling yoke of sovereign man? So few that the exceptions remind me of an ingenious conjecture about Newton: that he was probably a being of a higher order, accidentally caged in a human body. In the same spirit I have been led to imagine that the few extraordinary women who have shot off in eccentric directions out of the orbit prescribed to their sex were MALE spirits, confined by mistake in a female frame. But if it is not philosophical to think of sex when the soul is mentioned, then the inferiority must depend on the organs; or else the heavenly fire that is to ferment the clay is not given out in equal portions.

However, avoiding, as I have so far, any direct comparison of the two sexes taken collectively, or frankly admitting the inferiority of woman as things now appear, I shall insist only on this: that men have increased that inferiority until women have sunk almost below the standard of rational creatures. Give their faculties room to unfold and their virtues room to gain strength, and then decide where the whole sex must stand on the intellectual scale. Yet let it be remembered that I am not asking a place for a small number of distinguished women.
