It is hard for us short-sighted mortals to say to what heights human discoveries and improvements may rise once the gloom of despotism, which makes us stumble at every step, has lifted. But when morality comes to rest on a more solid basis, then, without claiming the gift of prophecy, I will venture to predict that woman will be either the friend or the slave of man. We shall not, as we do now, doubt whether she is a moral agent or the link that joins man to the brutes. But should it then appear that, like the brutes, women were created chiefly for man’s use, he will let them bite the bridle patiently and not mock them with empty praise; or, should their rationality be proved, he will not hinder their improvement merely to gratify his sensual appetites. He will not, with all the graces of rhetoric, advise them to submit their understandings unquestioningly to the guidance of man. He will not, when he writes on the education of women, assert that they ought never to have the free use of reason; nor would he recommend cunning and dissimulation to beings who, just as he does, are acquiring the virtues of humanity.

Surely, if morality has an eternal foundation, there can be only one rule of right; and whoever sacrifices virtue, strictly so called, to present convenience, or whose DUTY it is to act in that way, lives only for the passing day and cannot be an accountable creature.
The poet, then, ought to have dropped his sneer when he says,
“If weak women go astray, The stars are more in fault than they.”

For it is quite certain that they are bound by the unbreakable chain of destiny, if it is proved that they are never to exercise their own reason, never to be independent, never to rise above opinion or to feel the dignity of a rational will that bows only to God — a will that often forgets that the universe contains any being but itself and the model of perfection on which its ardent gaze is fixed, adoring attributes that, softened into virtues, may be imitated in kind, though their degree overwhelms the enraptured mind.

If, I say — for I would not try to impress by declamation when reason offers her sober light — if they are really capable of acting like rational creatures, do not treat them like slaves, or like the brutes who depend on the reason of man when they live alongside him. Instead, cultivate their minds, give them the wholesome, sublime restraint of principle, and let them attain a conscious dignity by feeling themselves dependent on God alone. Teach them, like man, to submit to necessity, rather than giving morals a sex in order to make women more pleasing.

Further, should experience prove that they cannot attain the same degree of strength of mind, perseverance and fortitude, let their virtues still be the same in kind, even though they may struggle in vain for the same degree; the superiority of man will be just as clear, if not clearer, and truth, being a simple principle that admits of no modification, would be common to both. Indeed, the order of society as it is now regulated would not be turned upside down, for woman would then hold only the rank that reason assigned her, and no arts could be practised to even the balance, much less to tip it.

These may be called Utopian dreams. Thanks be to that Being who impressed them on my soul and gave me strength of mind enough to dare to use my own reason, until, having become dependent on him alone for the support of my virtue, I look with indignation on the mistaken notions that enslave my sex.

I love man as my fellow creature; but his sceptre, whether real or usurped, does not reach me, unless the reason of an individual demands my homage; and even then I submit to reason, not to man. Indeed, the conduct of an accountable being must be governed by the workings of its own reason; otherwise, on what foundation does the throne of God rest?

It seems to me necessary to dwell on these obvious truths, because females have been, as it were, insulted; and while they have been stripped of the virtues that should clothe humanity, they have been decked out with artificial graces that enable them to exercise a short-lived tyranny. Since love takes the place in their hearts of every nobler passion, their sole ambition is to be beautiful, to stir emotion rather than to inspire respect; and this ignoble desire, like the servility found in absolute monarchies, destroys all strength of character. Liberty is the mother of virtue; and if women are slaves by their very constitution, and not allowed to breathe the sharp, bracing air of freedom, they must forever languish like hothouse plants and be reckoned beautiful flaws in nature. Let it also be remembered that they are the only flaw.

As for the argument drawn from the subjection in which the sex has always been held, it turns back upon man. The many have always been held in thrall by the few; and monsters who have shown scarcely any discernment of human excellence have tyrannized over thousands of their fellow creatures. Why have men of superior gifts submitted to such degradation? For is it not universally acknowledged that kings, taken as a group, have always been inferior in ability and virtue to the same number of men drawn from the common mass of mankind — and yet have they not been, and are they not still, treated with a reverence that is an insult to reason? China is not the only country where a living man has been made a God. MEN have submitted to superior strength so as to enjoy the pleasure of the moment with impunity — WOMEN have only done the same. Therefore, until it is proved that the courtier who servilely gives up the birthright of a man is not a moral agent, it cannot be demonstrated that woman is essentially inferior to man because she has always been subjugated.

Brute force has so far governed the world; and that the science of politics is still in its infancy is plain from the fact that philosophers hesitate to give the knowledge most useful to man that definite distinction.
I shall pursue this argument no further than is needed to establish one obvious inference: that as sound politics spread liberty, mankind, including woman, will become wiser and more virtuous.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Same Subject Continued
paragraphs: Bodily strength, once what distinguished heroes, has now fallen into such undeserved contempt that men and women alike seem to think it unnecessary: women because it detracts from their feminine graces and from that lovely weakness which is the source of their undue power; men because it seems incompatible with the character of a gentleman.

It can easily be shown that both, in moving away from one extreme, have run into the other; but first it may be proper to point out that a common error has gained a degree of acceptance and has lent force to a false conclusion, one in which an effect has been mistaken for a cause.

People of genius have very often damaged their health by study or by careless neglect of it, and because the violence of their passions is proportioned to the vigour of their intellects, the saying that the sword wears out the scabbard has become almost proverbial. From this, superficial observers have concluded that men of genius usually have weak constitutions — or, to use a more fashionable word, delicate ones. Yet I believe the facts will prove the opposite; for, having inquired diligently, I find that in most cases strength of mind has gone together with superior strength of body — a natural soundness of constitution, that is, not the robust nerves and powerful muscles that come from physical labour while the mind lies idle or merely directs the hands.

In the preface to his biographical chart, Dr. Priestley has observed that most great men have lived past forty-five. And considering how thoughtlessly they squandered their strength — wasting the lamp of life in pursuit of a favourite science, forgetful of the midnight hour; or, lost in poetic dreams, letting fancy people the scene until the passions that meditation had stirred disturbed the soul and shook the constitution, while the objects of those passions, the baseless fabric of a vision, faded before the exhausted eye — they must have had frames of iron. Shakespeare did not grasp the airy dagger with a feeble hand, and Milton did not tremble when he led Satan far from the borders of his dreary prison. These were not the ravings of feebleness or the sickly outpourings of disordered brains; they were the overflowing of an imagination that, wandering “in a fine phrenzy,” was not constantly reminded of its material chains.

I know that this argument would take me further than people may suppose I wish to go; but I follow the truth, and, holding to my first position, I will grant that bodily strength seems to give man a natural superiority over woman; and this is the only solid ground on which the superiority of his sex can be built. But I still insist that the two sexes should have not only the same virtue but the same KNOWLEDGE in kind, if not in degree; and that women, regarded as rational as well as moral creatures, should try to acquire human virtues (or perfections) by the SAME means as men, instead of being brought up as a fanciful sort of HALF being, one of Rousseau’s wild chimeras.

But if men can, with some show of reason, boast of their bodily strength, why are women so infatuated as to take pride in a defect? Rousseau has supplied them with a plausible excuse — one that could only have occurred to a man whose imagination had been allowed to run wild and to embroider the impressions made on his exquisite senses — so that they might, forsooth, have a pretext for yielding to a natural appetite without violating a romantic kind of modesty that flatters the pride and libertinism of man.

Misled by these sentiments, women sometimes boast of their weakness, and cunningly gain power by playing on the WEAKNESS of men; and well they may glory in their illicit rule, for, like Turkish pashas, they hold more real power than their masters. But virtue is sacrificed to passing gratifications, and the respectability of a lifetime to the triumph of an hour.

Women, like despots, perhaps now have more power than they would have if the world, divided and subdivided into kingdoms and families, were governed by laws derived from the exercise of reason; but, to continue the comparison, in gaining that power they degrade their character, and licentiousness spreads through the whole of society. The many become a pedestal for the few. I will therefore venture to assert that until women are educated more rationally, the progress of human virtue and the advance of knowledge must be continually held back. And if it is granted that woman was not created merely to gratify man’s appetite, or to be the upper servant who provides his meals and looks after his linen, it follows that the first concern of those mothers or fathers who genuinely attend to the education of girls should be, if not to strengthen the body, then at least not to ruin the constitution with mistaken notions of beauty and female excellence. Nor should girls ever be allowed to absorb the harmful idea that a defect can, by some chemical process of reasoning, turn into an excellence. On this point I am glad to find that the author of one of the most instructive books our country has produced for children agrees with me; I shall quote his apt remarks, so that the force of his respected authority may support reason.*

(*Footnote. A respected old man gives the following sensible account of the method he followed in educating his daughter. “I endeavoured to give both to her mind and body a degree of vigour, which is seldom found in the female sex. As soon as she was sufficiently advanced in strength to be capable of the lighter labours of husbandry and gardening, I employed her as my constant companion. Selene, for that was her name, soon acquired a dexterity in all these rustic employments which I considered with equal pleasure and admiration. If women are in general feeble both in body and mind, it arises less from nature than from education. We encourage a vicious indolence and inactivity, which we falsely call delicacy; instead of hardening their minds by the severer principles of reason and philosophy, we breed them to useless arts, which terminate in vanity and sensuality. In most of the countries which I had visited, they are taught nothing of an higher nature than a few modulations of the voice, or useless postures of the body; their time is consumed in sloth or trifles, and trifles become the only pursuits capable of interesting them. We seem to forget, that it is upon the qualities of the female sex, that our own domestic comforts and the education of our children must depend. And what are the comforts or the education which a race of beings corrupted from their infancy, and unacquainted with all the duties of life, are fitted to bestow? To touch a musical instrument with useless skill, to exhibit their natural or affected graces, to the eyes of indolent and debauched young men, who dissipate their husbands’ patrimony in riotous and unnecessary expenses: these are the only arts cultivated by women in most of the polished nations I had seen. And the consequences are uniformly such as may be expected to proceed from such polluted sources, private misery, and public servitude.

“But, Selene’s education was regulated by different views, and conducted upon severer principles; if that can be called severity which opens the mind to a sense of moral and religious duties, and most effectually arms it against the inevitable evils of life.” — Mr. Day’s “Sandford and Merton,” Volume 3.)

But even if it were proved that woman is naturally weaker than man, how does it follow that it is natural for her to strive to become weaker still than nature meant her to be? Arguments of this kind insult common sense and smack of passion. In this enlightened age, one may hope, the DIVINE RIGHT of husbands, like the divine right of kings, can be challenged without danger; and though conviction may not silence many noisy disputants, whenever a prevailing prejudice is attacked the wise will reflect on it, and leave the narrow-minded to rail with thoughtless vehemence against innovation.

A mother who wishes to give her daughter true dignity of character must ignore the sneers of ignorance and follow a plan diametrically opposed to the one that Rousseau has recommended with all the beguiling charms of eloquence and philosophical sophistry; for his eloquence makes absurdities look plausible, and his dogmatic conclusions bewilder, without convincing, those who lack the ability to refute them.

Throughout the animal kingdom every young creature needs almost constant exercise, and, following this hint, children should spend their infancy in harmless romping that exercises the feet and hands without demanding close direction from the head or the constant attention of a nurse. Indeed, the care needed for self-preservation is the first natural exercise of the understanding, just as little inventions to amuse the passing moment unfold the imagination. But these wise designs of nature are defeated by misguided doting or blind zeal. The child — a girl especially — is not left to its own direction for a single moment, and is thus made dependent; and then dependence is called natural.

To preserve personal beauty — woman’s glory! — the limbs and faculties are cramped by worse than Chinese bindings, and the sedentary life girls are condemned to lead, while boys frolic in the open air, weakens their muscles and slackens their nerves. As for Rousseau’s remarks, since echoed by several writers, that girls naturally — that is, from birth and independently of education — love dolls, dressing up and talking, they are too childish to deserve serious refutation. It is indeed very natural that a girl condemned to sit for hours on end listening to the idle chatter of weak-minded nurses, or to wait on her mother while she dresses, should try to join in the conversation; and it is undoubtedly a most natural consequence that she should imitate her mother or aunts and amuse herself by decking out her lifeless doll just as they deck her out, poor innocent baby! For even men of the greatest abilities have seldom had strength enough to rise above the atmosphere around them; and if the page of genius has always been blurred by the prejudices of its age, some allowance should be made for a sex that, like kings, always sees things through a distorting medium.

In this way the fondness for dress so conspicuous in women can easily be explained, without supposing that it springs from a desire to please the sex on which they depend. In short, the absurdity of supposing that a girl is a coquette by nature, and that a desire connected with nature’s impulse to propagate the species should appear even before a faulty education has heated the imagination and called it forth prematurely, is so unphilosophical that so shrewd an observer as Rousseau would never have adopted it had he not been in the habit of making reason give way to his love of singularity, and truth to a favourite paradox.

Yet to give the mind a sex in this way was hardly consistent with the principles of a man who argued so warmly, and so well, for the immortality of the soul. But what a weak barrier truth is when it stands in the way of a hypothesis! Rousseau respected — almost adored — virtue, and yet he allowed himself to love with sensual fondness. His imagination was forever supplying inflammable fuel to his inflammable senses; but, in order to reconcile this with his respect for self-denial, fortitude and those heroic virtues that a mind like his could not admire coolly, he labours to turn the law of nature upside down, and puts forward a doctrine full of mischief and insulting to the character of supreme wisdom.

His ridiculous stories, meant to prove that girls are NATURALLY attentive to their appearance, without giving any weight to daily example, are beneath contempt. And the tale of a little miss with such correct taste that she gave up the pleasant amusement of making O’s merely because she saw it was an ungraceful posture deserves to be filed alongside the anecdotes of the learned pig.*

(*Footnote. “I once knew a young person who learned to write before she learned to read, and began to write with her needle before she could use a pen. At first indeed, she took it into her head to make no other letter than the O: this letter she was constantly making of all sizes, and always the wrong way. Unluckily one day, as she was intent on this employment, she happened to see herself in the looking glass; when, taking a dislike to the constrained attitude in which she sat while writing, she threw away her pen, like another Pallas, and determined against making the O any more. Her brother was also equally averse to writing: it was the confinement, however, and not the constrained attitude, that most disgusted him.” Rousseau’s “Emilius.”)

I have probably had more opportunity than J. J. Rousseau to observe girls in their infancy. I can remember my own feelings, and I have looked steadily about me; yet, far from agreeing with him about the first dawn of the female character, I will venture to state that a girl whose spirits have not been dampened by inactivity, and whose innocence has not been tainted by false shame, will always be a romp, and the doll will never catch her interest unless confinement leaves her no alternative. In short, girls and boys would play together harmlessly if the distinction of sex were not drummed into them long before nature makes any difference. I will go further and state, as an indisputable fact, that most of the women I have observed who have behaved like rational creatures, or shown any vigour of intellect, have by chance been allowed to run wild — as some of the elegant shapers of the fair sex would put it.

The harmful consequences of neglecting health in infancy and youth reach further than is supposed. Dependence of body naturally produces dependence of mind; and how can a woman be a good wife or mother when most of her time is spent guarding against illness or enduring it? Nor can we expect a woman to try resolutely to strengthen her constitution and to refrain from enfeebling indulgences if artificial notions of beauty and false descriptions of sensibility have been tangled up with her motives for action from an early age. Most men are sometimes obliged to put up with bodily discomfort and occasionally to endure harsh weather; but genteel women are, quite literally, slaves to their bodies, and they glory in their subjection.

I once knew a weak woman of fashion who was more than usually proud of her delicacy and sensibility. She thought a discriminating taste and a puny appetite the height of all human perfection, and she behaved accordingly. I have watched this weak, artificial creature neglect every duty of life, and yet recline complacently on a sofa and boast of her lack of appetite as proof of a delicacy that extended to — or perhaps sprang from — her exquisite sensibility; for it is hard to make such ridiculous jargon intelligible. Yet at that same moment I have seen her insult a worthy old gentlewoman whom unexpected misfortunes had made dependent on her showy charity, and who, in better days, had a claim on her gratitude. Could a human creature have become so weak and depraved a being unless, as with the Sybarites dissolved in luxury, everything resembling virtue had been worn away, or had never been instilled by precept — a poor substitute, it is true, for cultivation of the mind, though it does serve as a fence against vice?

Such a woman is no more irrational a monster than some of the Roman emperors, who were corrupted by lawless power. Yet since kings have been placed more under the restraint of law, and under the curb of honour, however weak, the records of history are no longer filled with such unnatural examples of folly and cruelty; nor does the despotism that kills virtue and genius in the bud hang over Europe with the destructive blast that lays Turkey waste and makes its men, as well as its soil, barren.

Women everywhere are in this deplorable state; for, in order to preserve their innocence — as ignorance is politely called — truth is hidden from them, and they are made to put on an artificial character before their faculties have gained any strength. Taught from infancy that beauty is woman’s sceptre, the mind shapes itself to the body and, roaming about its gilded cage, seeks only to decorate its prison. Men have various occupations and pursuits that engage their attention and give character to the developing mind; but women, confined to one, and with their thoughts constantly turned to the most insignificant part of themselves, seldom look beyond the triumph of the hour. But if their understanding were once freed from the slavery to which they have been subjected by the pride and sensuality of man and by their own short-sighted desire for present sway — like the tyrant’s desire for dominion — we should probably read of their weaknesses with surprise. I must be allowed to pursue the argument a little further.

Perhaps, if we allowed the existence of an evil being who, in the allegorical language of Scripture, goes about seeking whom he may devour, he could find no more effective way to degrade human character than by giving a man absolute power.

This argument branches out in various directions. Birth, riches and every intrinsic advantage that raise a man above his fellows without any mental effort in fact sink him below them. The weaker he is, the more he is manipulated by scheming men, until the bloated monster has lost every trace of humanity. And that whole tribes of men should quietly follow such a leader, like flocks of sheep, is an absurdity that only a desire for present enjoyment and a narrow understanding can explain. Where shall we find men, brought up in slavish dependence and enfeebled by luxury and idleness, who will stand up to assert the rights of man, or claim the privilege of moral beings, who should have only one road to excellence? Slavery to monarchs and ministers, from which the world will take a long time to free itself, and whose deadly grip halts the progress of the human mind, has not yet been abolished.

Let men, then, in the pride of power, not use the same arguments that tyrannical kings and corrupt ministers have used, and falsely claim that woman ought to be subjugated because she always has been. But when man, governed by reasonable laws, enjoys his natural freedom, let him despise woman if she does not share it with him; and until that glorious time arrives, when he holds forth on the folly of the female sex, let him not overlook his own.

It is true that women who gain power by unjust means, by practising or encouraging vice, plainly lose the rank that reason would assign them, and become either abject slaves or capricious tyrants. In acquiring power they lose all simplicity and all dignity of mind, and they act as men are seen to act when they have been raised up by the same means.

It is time to bring about a revolution in female manners — time to restore women’s lost dignity, and to make them, as part of the human species, work to reform the world by reforming themselves. It is time to separate unchanging morals from local customs. If men are demigods, then by all means let us serve them! And if the dignity of the female soul is as questionable as that of animals — if women’s reason does not give them enough light to guide their conduct, while unerring instinct is denied them — then they are surely the most miserable of all creatures, and, bowed beneath the iron hand of destiny, must resign themselves to being a FAIR DEFECT in creation. But the subtlest casuist would be at a loss to justify the ways of providence towards them by pointing to some irrefutable reason for making so large a part of mankind at once accountable and not accountable.

The only solid foundation for morality seems to be the character of the Supreme Being, whose harmony arises from a balance of attributes; and, to speak with reverence, one attribute seems to imply the NECESSITY of another. He must be just because he is wise; he must be good because he is omnipotent. For to exalt one attribute at the expense of another equally noble and necessary bears the mark of man’s warped reason — the homage paid by passion. Man, used to bowing down to power in his savage state, can rarely shake off this barbarous prejudice, even when civilization shows how far mental strength surpasses bodily strength; and these crude opinions cloud his reason even when he thinks of the Deity. God’s omnipotence is made to swallow up or overrule his other attributes, and those mortals who think his power must be governed by his wisdom are accused of irreverently limiting it.

I reject the kind of humility that, having investigated nature, stops short at its author. The high and lofty One, who inhabiteth eternity, no doubt possesses many attributes of which we can form no idea; but reason tells me that they cannot conflict with those I adore, and I am bound to listen to her voice.

It seems natural for man to seek excellence, and either to trace it in the object he worships or to wrap that object blindly in perfection as in a garment. But what good can this second kind of worship do for the moral conduct of a rational being? He bows to power; he adores a dark cloud that may open a bright prospect to him, or may burst in angry, lawless fury on his doomed head, he knows not why. And if the Deity is supposed to act on the vague impulse of an undirected will, man too must follow his own will, or act by rules derived from principles he rejects as irreverent. Enthusiasts and cooler thinkers alike have fallen into this dilemma when they have tried to free men from the wholesome restraints imposed by a just conception of God’s character.

It is not impious to examine the attributes of the Almighty in this way; indeed, who that uses his faculties can avoid doing so? For to love God as the fountain of wisdom, goodness and power seems to be the only worship of use to a being who wishes to acquire either virtue or knowledge. A blind, unsettled affection may, like human passions, fill the mind and warm the heart, while to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with our God is forgotten. I shall take this subject further when I consider religion in a light opposite to the one Dr. Gregory recommends, for he treats it as a matter of sentiment or taste.

To return from this apparent digression: it is to be wished that women would cherish an affection for their husbands founded on the same principle on which devotion ought to rest. There is no other firm foundation under heaven; so let them beware of the deceptive light of sentiment, too often used as a gentler word for sensuality. It follows, then, I think, that from infancy women should either be shut away like Eastern princes or educated so that they can think and act for themselves.
Why do men waver between two opinions and expect what is impossible? Why do they look for virtue in a slave, or in a being whom the constitution of civil society has made weak, if not vicious?

Still, I know it will take a considerable time to root out the firmly established prejudices that sensualists have planted. It will also take some time to convince women that, on a broad view, they act against their real interest when they cherish or affect weakness under the name of delicacy; and to convince the world that the poisoned source of female vices and follies — if custom obliges me to use those synonymous terms loosely — has been the sensual homage paid to beauty, that is, to beauty of features. For a German writer has shrewdly observed that men of every description generally acknowledge a pretty woman to be pretty, as an object of desire; while a fine woman, who inspires loftier emotions by displaying intellectual beauty, may be overlooked or regarded with indifference by those men who find their happiness in gratifying their appetites. I foresee an obvious reply: as long as man remains the imperfect being he appears to have been so far, he will be more or less the slave of his appetites; and since the women who gain most power are those who gratify his predominant appetite, the sex is degraded by a physical, if not a moral, necessity.

This objection has some force, I grant; but while so sublime a precept exists as “be pure as your heavenly father is pure;” it would seem that man’s virtues are not limited by the Being who alone could limit them, and that he may press forward without asking whether such a noble ambition takes him out of his sphere. To the wild billows it has been said, “thus far shalt thou go, and no further; and here shall thy proud waves be stayed.” In vain, then, do they beat and foam, held back by the power that keeps the struggling planets in their orbits; matter yields to the great governing Spirit. But an immortal soul, not bound by mechanical laws, and struggling to free itself from the shackles of matter, adds to the order of creation instead of disturbing it when, working together with the Father of spirits, it tries to govern itself by the unchanging rule by which the universe is regulated, to a degree before which our imagination faints.

Besides, if women are educated for dependence — that is, to act according to the will of another fallible being and to submit to power, right or wrong — where are we to stop? Are they to be regarded as deputies, allowed to rule over a small domain and answerable for their conduct to a higher tribunal that is itself liable to error?

It will not be hard to prove that such delegates will behave like men ruled by fear, and will make their children and servants bear their tyrannical oppression. Since they submit without reason, and have no fixed rules by which to regulate their conduct, they will be kind or cruel just as the whim of the moment dictates; and we should not be surprised if, chafed by their heavy yoke, they sometimes take a malicious pleasure in laying it on weaker shoulders.

But suppose a woman trained to obedience is married to a sensible man who guides her judgment without making her feel the servility of her subjection, so that she acts by this reflected light with as much propriety as can be expected when reason is borrowed at second hand; even so, she cannot guarantee her protector’s life. He may die and leave her with a large family.

A double duty then falls on her: to bring the children up in the character of both father and mother, to form their principles and to secure their property. But, alas, she has never thought for herself, much less acted for herself. She has learned only to please men and to depend on them gracefully; yet, burdened with children, how is she to find another protector — a husband to take the place of reason? A rational man (for we are not treading on romantic ground), though he may think her a pleasing, docile creature, will not choose to marry a FAMILY for love when the world contains many other pretty creatures. What, then, is to become of her? Either she falls easy prey to some base fortune hunter, who cheats her children of their father’s inheritance and makes her miserable, or she becomes the victim of discontent and blind indulgence. Unable to educate her sons or to inspire their respect — for it is no mere play on words to say that people who are not respectable are never respected, however important the position they fill — she pines in the anguish of useless, powerless regret. The serpent’s tooth enters her very soul, and the vices of licentious youth bring her to the grave in sorrow, if not in poverty as well.
This is not an overdrawn picture; on the contrary, it is an entirely possible case, and something like it must have come before every attentive eye.

I have, however, taken it for granted that she meant well, though experience shows that the blind may as easily be led into a ditch as along the beaten road. But suppose — and it is not a very improbable guess — that a being taught only to please must still find her happiness in pleasing: what an example of folly, not to say vice, she will set her innocent daughters! The mother will be lost in the coquette, and instead of making friends of her daughters she will look at them askance, for they are rivals — rivals crueller than any others, because they invite comparison and drive from the throne of beauty a woman who has never thought of taking a seat on the bench of reason.

No lively brush, and no sharp outline of caricature, is needed to sketch the domestic miseries and petty vices that such a mistress of a household spreads around her. Yet she is only acting as a woman ought to act who has been raised according to Rousseau’s system. No one can ever reproach her with being masculine or with stepping out of her sphere; indeed, she may observe another of his grand rules and, carefully keeping her reputation spotless, be counted a good sort of woman. Yet in what respect can she be called good? It is true that she refrains, without much struggle, from committing gross crimes; but how does she fulfil her duties? Duties! — in truth she has enough to think about in adorning her body and nursing a weak constitution.

As for religion, she never presumed to judge for herself, but conformed, as a dependent creature should, to the ceremonies of the church in which she was raised, piously believing that wiser heads than hers have settled that business; and never to doubt is her idea of perfection. So she pays her tithe of mint and cummin, and thanks her God that she is not as other women are. These are the blessed effects of a good education! These are the virtues of man’s helpmate! I must relieve my feelings by drawing a different picture.

Let the imagination now present a woman of reasonable understanding — for I do not wish to leave the level of the ordinary — whose constitution, strengthened by exercise, has let her body reach its full vigour, while her mind has gradually expanded to grasp the moral duties of life and what human virtue and dignity consist in. Shaped in this way by the duties arising from her relations to others in her station, she marries for affection without losing sight of prudence. Looking beyond the happiness of marriage, she secures her husband’s respect before it becomes necessary to use base arts to please him and to feed a dying flame, which nature doomed to go out once its object became familiar, when friendship and forbearance take the place of a more ardent affection. This is the natural death of love, and domestic peace is not destroyed by struggles to prevent its end. I also suppose the husband to be virtuous; otherwise she has even greater need of independent principles.

Fate, however, breaks this bond. She is left a widow, perhaps without sufficient means; but she is not desolate! She feels nature’s pang; but once time has softened grief into melancholy resignation, her heart turns to her children with redoubled tenderness, and, in her anxiety to provide for them, affection gives her maternal duties a sacred and heroic character. She thinks that her virtuous efforts are seen not only by the One from whom all her comfort must now flow, and whose approval is life; her imagination, a little withdrawn and exalted by grief, also dwells on the fond hope that the eyes her trembling hand closed may still see how she masters every wayward passion to fulfil the double duty of being father as well as mother to her children. Raised to heroism by misfortune, she suppresses the first faint stirrings of a natural inclination before it ripens into love, and in the bloom of life she forgets her sex — forgets the pleasure of an awakening passion that might have been inspired and returned once more. She no longer thinks of pleasing, and a sense of her own dignity keeps her from priding herself on the praise her conduct deserves. Her children have her love, and her brightest hopes lie beyond the grave, where her imagination often wanders.

I think I see her surrounded by her children, reaping the reward of her care. Their intelligent eyes meet hers, while health and innocence smile on their chubby cheeks; and as they grow up, their grateful attention eases the cares of life. She lives to see the virtues she tried to plant on principle become fixed as habits, and to see her children reach a strength of character that enables them to endure adversity without forgetting their mother’s example.
Her life’s task thus fulfilled, she calmly awaits the sleep of death, and, rising from the grave, may say: Behold, thou gavest me a talent, and here are five talents.

I wish to sum up what I have said in a few words, for here I throw down my gauntlet and deny that there are any sexual virtues — virtues peculiar to one sex — not excepting modesty. For man and woman, truth, if I understand the meaning of the word, must be the same; yet the fanciful female character, so prettily drawn by poets and novelists, demands the sacrifice of truth and sincerity, and so virtue becomes a relative idea, with no foundation but utility — and men claim the right to judge that utility arbitrarily, shaping it to suit their own convenience.
Women, I grant, may have different duties to fulfil; but they are HUMAN duties, and I firmly maintain that the principles that should govern how they are carried out must be the same.

To become respectable, women must exercise their understanding; there is no other foundation for independence of character. I mean to say explicitly that they must bow only to the authority of reason, instead of being the MODEST slaves of opinion.

In the upper ranks of life, how rarely do we meet a man of superior abilities, or even of ordinary attainments? The reason seems clear to me: the state they are born into is an unnatural one. Human character has always been formed by the occupations that the individual or the class pursues; and if the faculties are not sharpened by necessity, they must stay dull. The argument can fairly be extended to women; for, seldom occupied with serious business, they pursue pleasure, and this gives their character the insignificance that makes the society of the GREAT so insipid. The same lack of firmness, arising from a similar cause, drives both to flee from themselves into noisy pleasures and artificial passions, until vanity takes the place of every social affection and the characteristics of humanity can hardly be made out. Such are the blessings of civil governments as they are now organized that wealth and female softness both tend to debase mankind, and both are produced by the same cause. But if women are allowed to be rational creatures, they should be encouraged to acquire virtues they can call their own; for how can a rational being be ennobled by anything that it has not gained by its OWN efforts?

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Observations on the State of Degradation to Which Woman Is Reduced by Various Causes
paragraphs: That woman is either naturally weak or degraded by a combination of circumstances is, I think, clear. But I shall simply set this position against a conclusion that I have often heard sensible men draw in favour of an aristocracy: that the mass of mankind cannot amount to anything, or else the obsequious slaves who patiently let themselves be penned up would feel their own importance and spurn their chains. Men, these observers add, everywhere submit to oppression when they need only lift up their heads to throw off the yoke; yet, instead of asserting their birthright, they quietly lick the dust and say, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Women, I argue by analogy, are degraded by the same inclination to enjoy the present moment, and in the end they despise the freedom that they lack the virtue to struggle for. But I must speak more plainly.

Where the cultivation of the heart is concerned, everyone agrees that sex does not enter into it; but the line of subordination in the powers of the mind must never be crossed. Woman is allowed to be only “absolute in loveliness,” and the share of rationality granted to her is very meagre indeed; for once genius and judgment are denied her, it is hard to guess what is left to make up an intellect.

The seed of immortality, if I may use the phrase, is the capacity of human reason to be perfected. For if man had been created perfect, or if at maturity such a flood of knowledge had broken in upon him that error became impossible, I should doubt whether his existence would continue after the body dissolved. But as things now stand, every moral difficulty that eludes human discussion, and that baffles alike the probing of deep thought and the lightning glance of genius, is an argument on which I build my belief in the immortality of the soul. Reason, then, is simply the power of improvement; or, more properly, the power of discerning truth. In this respect every individual is a world in itself. More of it may be visible in one being than in another; but the nature of reason must be the same in all, if it is an emanation of the divine, the tie that binds the creature to the Creator. For can a soul bear the stamp of the heavenly image if it is not perfected by the exercise of its own reason? Yet the soul of woman, outwardly decorated with elaborate care and adorned to delight man, “that with honour he may love,” (See Milton) is denied this distinction; and since man is always placed between her and reason, she is always represented as created only to see through a coarse medium and to take things on trust. But let us set aside these fanciful theories and consider woman as a whole, whatever that whole may be, rather than as a part of man. The question then is whether she has reason or not. If she has, which for the moment I will take for granted, then she was not created merely to be man’s comfort, and the sexual character should not destroy the human one.

Men have probably been led into this error by seeing education in a false light: not as the first step in forming a being that advances gradually toward perfection (the word is not quite accurate, but I cannot find a better), but merely as a preparation for life. On this sensual error, for I must call it that, the false system of female manners has been built, a system that robs the whole sex of its dignity and ranks women, dark and fair alike, with the smiling flowers whose only use is to adorn the land. Men have always spoken this language, and the fear of departing from a supposed sexual character has led even women of superior sense to adopt the same views. So understanding, strictly speaking, has been denied to woman, and instinct, refined into wit and cunning for the purposes of daily life, has been put in its place.

The power of generalizing ideas, of drawing broad conclusions from particular observations, is the only acquisition for an immortal being that truly deserves the name of knowledge. Merely to observe, without trying to account for anything, may serve (very imperfectly) as the common sense of everyday life; but where is the store laid up that is to clothe the soul when it leaves the body?

Not only has this power been denied to women; writers have insisted that, with a few exceptions, it is incompatible with their sexual character. Let men prove this, and I shall concede that woman exists only for man. I must first point out, however, that the power of generalizing ideas to any great extent is not very common among either men or women. But this exercise is the true cultivation of the understanding, and everything conspires to make that cultivation harder in the female world than in the male.
This assertion leads me naturally to the main subject of this chapter, and I shall now try to point out some of the causes that degrade the sex and keep women from generalizing their observations.

I shall not go back to the remote records of antiquity to trace the history of woman; it is enough to grant that she has always been either a slave or a despot, and to note that each of these conditions equally holds back the progress of reason. The chief source of female folly and vice has always seemed to me to be narrowness of mind; and the very constitution of civil governments has put almost insurmountable obstacles in the way of cultivating the female understanding. Yet virtue can be built on no other foundation! The same obstacles are placed in the way of the rich, and the same results follow.

Necessity has proverbially been called the mother of invention; the saying may be extended to virtue. Virtue is something acquired, and acquired at the cost of pleasure; and who gives up a pleasure within reach unless adversity has opened and strengthened his mind, or necessity has driven him on in the pursuit of knowledge? How fortunate people are when they have the cares of life to struggle with, for these struggles keep them from falling prey, out of mere idleness, to vices that sap their strength! But if men and women are placed from birth in a torrid zone, with the noonday sun of pleasure beating straight down on them, how can they brace their minds enough to carry out the duties of life, or even to enjoy the affections that draw them out of themselves?

As society is at present arranged, pleasure is the business of a woman’s life, and while it remains so, little can be expected of such weak beings. Having inherited, in direct line of descent from the first fair defect in nature, the sovereignty of beauty, women have given up, in order to keep their power, the natural rights that the exercise of reason might have won them; they have chosen to be short-lived queens rather than labour for the sober pleasures that come from equality. Raised up by their very inferiority (this sounds like a contradiction), they constantly demand homage as women, although experience ought to teach them that the men who pride themselves on paying this arbitrary, insolent respect to the sex with the most scrupulous precision are the most inclined to tyrannize over, and despise, the very weakness they cherish. They often echo Mr. Hume’s sentiments, when, comparing the French and Athenian character, he alludes to women: “But what is more singular in this whimsical nation, say I to the Athenians, is, that a frolic of yours during the Saturnalia, when the slaves are served by their masters, is seriously continued by them through the whole year, and through the whole course of their lives; accompanied too with some circumstances, which still further augment the absurdity and ridicule. Your sport only elevates for a few days, those whom fortune has thrown down, and whom she too, in sport, may really elevate forever above you. But this nation gravely exalts those, whom nature has subjected to them, and whose inferiority and infirmities are absolutely incurable. The women, though without virtue, are their masters and sovereigns.”

Ah! why do women (I write with affectionate concern) stoop to accept from strangers a kind of attention and respect that differs from the mutual civility which humanity dictates, and civilized politeness permits, between one man and another? And why do they not see, when “in the noon of beauty’s power,” that they are treated like queens only so that hollow respect can deceive them, until they are led to give up, or never take up, their natural prerogatives? Shut up in cages like birds, they have nothing to do but preen themselves and strut with mock majesty from perch to perch. It is true that they are given food and clothing for which they neither toil nor spin; but health, liberty and virtue are handed over in exchange. Yet where among mankind has anyone been found with enough strength of mind to give up these accidental privileges, someone who rose above opinion with the calm dignity of reason and dared to be proud of the privileges inherent in being human? And it is useless to expect it while hereditary power stifles the affections and nips reason in the bud.

Men’s passions have in this way set women on thrones; and until mankind grows more reasonable, it is to be feared that women will make use of the power they gain with the least effort and hold most securely. They will smile, yes, they will smile, though they are told that —
“In beauty’s empire is no mean, And woman either slave or queen, Is quickly scorn’d when not ador’d.”
But the adoration comes first, and no one foresees the scorn.

Lewis the Fourteenth in particular spread artificial manners and, by plausible means, caught the whole nation in his net; for in setting up an ingenious chain of despotism, he made it in the interest of each person among the people at large to respect his position and uphold his power. And women, whom he flattered with a childish gallantry toward the whole sex, gained during his reign that princely distinction which is so fatal to reason and virtue.

A king is always a king, and a woman always a woman (and, it might be added, a wit always a wit; for the vain antics by which wits and beauties seek attention and make conquests are much on a level). His authority and her sex always stand between them and rational conversation. With a lover, I grant, she should be a woman, and her sensibility will naturally lead her to try to stir his emotions, to satisfy not her vanity but her heart. This I do not count as coquetry; it is the unaffected impulse of nature. I protest only against the sexual appetite for conquest when the heart has nothing to do with it.

This appetite is not confined to women. “I have endeavoured,” says Lord Chesterfield, “to gain the hearts of twenty women, whose persons I would not have given a fig for.” Beside this cold-hearted scoundrel, the libertine who takes advantage of unsuspecting tenderness in a rush of passion is a saint; for I like to use words that mean something. Yet women, taught only to please, are always on the lookout to please, and with truly heroic zeal they try to win hearts merely to give them up or spurn them once the victory is decided and plain for all to see.
I must come down to the small details of the subject.

I regret that women are systematically degraded by accepting the trivial attentions that men think it manly to pay to the sex, when in fact the men are insultingly asserting their own superiority. To bow to an inferior is no condescension. These ceremonies seem to me so absurd, in fact, that I can hardly keep a straight face when I see a man spring up with eager and earnest concern to pick up a handkerchief or shut a door, when the LADY could have done it herself had she only taken a step or two.

A wild wish has just flown from my heart to my head, and I will not stifle it, though it may provoke a coarse laugh. I earnestly wish to see the distinction of sex erased in society, except where love inspires the behaviour. For I am firmly convinced that this distinction is the foundation of the weakness of character attributed to woman. It is the reason the understanding is neglected while accomplishments are acquired with painstaking care; and the same cause explains why women prefer the graceful virtues to the heroic ones.

Mankind of every kind wants to be loved and respected for SOMETHING; and the common herd will always take the shortest road to getting what it wants. The respect paid to wealth and beauty is the surest and least ambiguous, and so it will naturally always catch the vulgar eye of ordinary minds. Ability and virtue are absolutely necessary to lift men of the middle rank of life into notice; and the natural result is well known: the middle rank contains the most virtue and ability. Men thus have, in one station at least, an opportunity to exert themselves with dignity and to rise through the efforts that truly improve a rational creature. But the whole female sex, until their character is formed, is in the same condition as the rich. For they are born (I speak now of a civilized state) with certain sexual privileges, and while these are granted to them for nothing, few will ever think of doing more than is required in order to win the esteem of a small number of superior people.

When do we hear of women who emerge from obscurity and boldly claim respect for their great abilities or daring virtues? Where are they to be found? “To be observed, to be attended to, to be taken notice of with sympathy, complacency, and approbation, are all the advantages which they seek.” True! my male readers will probably exclaim; but before they draw any conclusion, let them remember that this was not originally written as a description of women, but of the rich. In Dr. Smith’s Theory of Moral Sentiments I have found a general portrait of people of rank and fortune which, in my opinion, could with complete aptness be applied to the female sex. I refer the discerning reader to the whole comparison; but I must be allowed to quote a passage to support an argument that I intend to press, as the most conclusive of all against a sexual character. For if no great men of any kind, apart from warriors, have ever appeared among the nobility, may we not fairly infer that their particular situation swallowed up the man and produced a character like that of women, who are LOCALIZED, if I may use the word, by the rank in which they are placed by COURTESY? Women, commonly called Ladies, must not be contradicted in company and are not allowed to use any physical strength; and only the negative virtues are expected of them, when any virtues are expected at all: patience, docility, good humour and pliancy, virtues incompatible with any vigorous exercise of intellect. Besides, because they live more in each other’s company and are seldom entirely alone, they are governed more by sentiments than by passions. Solitude and reflection are needed to give wishes the force of passions, and to enable the imagination to magnify their object and make it the most desirable of all. The same may be said of the rich: they do not deal enough in general ideas, gathered by impassioned thought or calm inquiry, to acquire the strength of character on which great resolutions are built. But listen to what a sharp observer says of the great.

“Do the great seem insensible of the easy price at which they may acquire the public admiration? or do they seem to imagine, that to them, as to other men, it must be the purchase either of sweat or of blood? By what important accomplishments is the young nobleman instructed to support the dignity of his rank, and to render himself worthy of that superiority over his fellow citizens, to which the virtue of his ancestors had raised them? Is it by knowledge, by industry, by patience, by self-denial, or by virtue of any kind? As all his words, as all his motions are attended to, he learns an habitual regard for every circumstance of ordinary behaviour, and studies to perform all those small duties with the most exact propriety. As he is conscious how much he is observed, and how much mankind are disposed to favour all his inclinations, he acts, upon the most indifferent occasions, with that freedom and elevation which the thought of this naturally inspires. His air, his manner, his deportment all mark that elegant and graceful sense of his own superiority, which those who are born to an inferior station can hardly ever arrive at. These are the arts by which he proposes to make mankind more easily submit to his authority, and to govern their inclinations according to his own pleasure: and in this he is seldom disappointed. These arts, supported by rank and pre-eminence, are, upon ordinary occasions, sufficient to govern the world. Lewis XIV. during the greater part of his reign, was regarded, not only in France, but over all Europe, as the most perfect model of a great prince. But what were the talents and virtues, by which he acquired this great reputation? Was it by the scrupulous and inflexible justice of all his undertakings, by the immense dangers and difficulties with which they were attended, or by the unwearied and unrelenting application with which he pursued them? Was it by his extensive knowledge, by his exquisite judgment, or by his heroic valour? It was by none of these qualities. But he was, first of all, the most powerful prince in Europe, and consequently held the highest rank among kings; and then, says his historian, ‘he surpassed all his courtiers in the gracefulness of his shape, and the majestic beauty of his features. The sound of his voice noble and affecting, gained those hearts which his presence intimidated. He had a step and a deportment, which could suit only him and his rank, and which would have been ridiculous in any other person. The embarrassment which he occasioned to those who spoke to him, flattered that secret satisfaction with which he felt his own superiority.’ These frivolous accomplishments, supported by his rank, and, no doubt, too, by a degree of other talents and virtues, which seems, however, not to have been much above mediocrity, established this prince in the esteem of his own age, and have drawn even from posterity, a good deal of respect for his memory. Compared with these, in his own times, and in his own presence, no other virtue, it seems, appeared to have any merit. Knowledge, industry, valour, and beneficence, trembling, were abashed, and lost all dignity before them.”
Woman too, thus “in herself complete” through possessing all these FRIVOLOUS accomplishments, so alters the nature of things,

— “That what she wills to do or say Seems wisest, virtuousest, discreetest, best; All higher knowledge in HER PRESENCE falls Degraded. Wisdom in discourse with her Loses discountenanc’d, and like folly shows; Authority and reason on her wait.” —
And all of this rests on her loveliness!

In the middle rank of life, to continue the comparison, men are trained for professions in their youth, and marriage is not regarded as the main feature of their lives; women, on the other hand, have no other project to sharpen their faculties. Their attention is not absorbed by business, large plans or any of the far-ranging flights of ambition; no, their thoughts are not occupied in raising such noble structures. To rise in the world and be free to run from pleasure to pleasure, they must marry well; to this end their time is sacrificed, and their persons are often legally prostituted. A man entering any profession keeps his eye steadily on some future advantage (and the mind gains great strength when all its efforts are directed to one point), and, absorbed in his business, he regards pleasure as mere relaxation; women, by contrast, seek pleasure as the main purpose of existence. Indeed, given the education that society gives them, the love of pleasure may be said to govern them all; but does this prove that souls have a sex? It would be just as rational to declare that the courtiers of France, once a ruinous system of despotism had formed their character, were not men, because they sacrificed liberty, virtue and humanity to pleasure and vanity. Fatal passions, which have always tyrannized over the WHOLE race!

The same love of pleasure, encouraged by the whole drift of their education, gives a trivial cast to women’s conduct in most situations. For example, they are always anxious about secondary matters, and on the lookout for adventures instead of being busy with their duties.

A man setting out on a journey generally has its purpose in view; a woman thinks more about the incidents along the way, the strange things that might possibly happen on the road and the impression she may make on her fellow travellers. Above all, she is anxiously absorbed in looking after the finery she carries with her, which is more than ever a part of herself when she is going to make a figure in new surroundings; when, to use an apt French turn of phrase, she is going to produce a sensation. Can dignity of mind coexist with such petty cares?

In short, women in general, like the rich of both sexes, have acquired all the follies and vices of civilization and missed its useful fruit. I need not always state beforehand that I am speaking of the condition of the whole sex and leaving exceptions aside. Their senses are inflamed and their understandings neglected; as a result they become the prey of their senses, which is delicately called sensibility, and are blown about by every passing gust of feeling. They are therefore much worse off than they would be if they lived in a state closer to nature. Always restless and anxious, their overworked sensibility not only makes them uncomfortable themselves but, to put it mildly, troublesome to others. All their thoughts turn on things designed to stir emotion; and since they feel when they ought to reason, their conduct is unstable and their opinions waver, not with the wavering that comes from deliberation or developing views, but from contradictory emotions. By fits and starts they grow ardent about many pursuits; yet this ardour, never concentrated into perseverance, soon burns itself out. Either it evaporates in its own heat, or it meets some other fleeting passion to which reason has never given any real weight, and indifference follows. Wretched indeed must be the being whose cultivation of mind has served only to inflame its passions! A distinction should be drawn between inflaming the passions and strengthening them. When the passions are pampered in this way while the judgment is left unformed, what can be expected to follow? Undoubtedly, a mixture of madness and folly!
This observation should not be restricted to the FAIR sex; for the present, however, I intend to apply it only to them.

Novels, music, poetry and gallantry all tend to make women creatures of sensation, and their character is formed in this way during the years in which they are acquiring accomplishments, the only improvement their position in society encourages them to pursue. This overstrained sensibility naturally weakens the other powers of the mind and keeps the intellect from gaining the command it ought to have if a rational creature is to be useful to others and content with its own station. For the exercise of the understanding, as life goes on, is the only means nature has provided for calming the passions.

Satiety has a very different effect, and I have often been powerfully struck by a vivid description of damnation, in which the spirit is shown forever hovering with thwarted eagerness around the defiled body, unable to enjoy anything without the organs of sense. Yet women are made slaves to their senses, because it is through their sensibility that they gain their present power.

And will moralists presume to claim that this is the condition in which half the human race should be encouraged to remain, in listless idleness and stupid acquiescence? Kind instructors! what were we created for? To remain innocent, it may be said; by which they mean in a state of childhood. We might as well never have been born, unless it was necessary for us to be created so that man could acquire the noble privilege of reason, the power of telling good from evil, while we lie down in the dust from which we were taken, never to rise again.

It would be an endless task to trace all the varieties of pettiness, care and sorrow into which women are plunged by the prevailing opinion that they were made to feel rather than to reason, and that whatever power they gain must be gained through their charms and their weakness;
“Fine by defect, and amiably weak!”

And since this amiable weakness makes them wholly dependent on man, apart from what they gain by illicit influence, not only for protection but for advice, is it surprising that they neglect the duties that reason alone points out, shrink from the trials designed to strengthen their minds, and exert themselves only to give their defects a graceful covering? That covering may heighten their charms in the eyes of the sensualist, though it sinks them below the scale of moral excellence.

Fragile in every sense of the word, they are forced to look to man for every comfort. In the most trivial dangers they cling to their support with parasitic tenacity, pitifully begging for help; and their NATURAL protector stretches out his arm or raises his voice to guard the lovely trembler — from what? Perhaps from the frown of an old cow or the leap of a mouse; a rat would be a serious danger. In the name of reason, and even of common sense, what can save such beings from contempt, however soft and fair they may be?

These fears, when they are not put on, may be very pretty; but they show a degree of feebleness that degrades a rational creature in a way women do not realize, for love and esteem are very different things.

I am fully convinced that we should hear nothing of these childish airs if girls were allowed enough exercise and were not shut up in stuffy rooms until their muscles grow slack and their digestion is ruined. To take the point further: if fear in girls, instead of being cherished and perhaps even created, were treated as cowardice is treated in boys, we should soon see women with a more dignified bearing. It is true that they could not then so fittingly be called the sweet flowers that smile along man’s path; but they would be more respectable members of society and would carry out the important duties of life by the light of their own reason. “Educate women like men,” says Rousseau, “and the more they resemble our sex the less power will they have over us.” This is exactly what I aim at. I do not wish them to have power over men, but over themselves.

I have heard men argue in the same vein against educating the poor; for aristocracy takes many forms. “Teach them to read and write,” they say, “and you take them out of the station assigned them by nature.” An eloquent Frenchman has answered them, and I will borrow his thoughts. They do not realize, when they turn man into a brute, that they may at any moment see him transformed into a savage beast. Without knowledge there can be no morality!

Ignorance is a flimsy foundation for virtue! Yet the writers who have argued most vehemently for the superiority of man, a superiority not of degree but of essence, have insisted that ignorance is the condition for which woman was designed. To soften the argument, however, they have laboured with chivalrous generosity to prove that the sexes ought not to be compared: man was made to reason, woman to feel; and together, as flesh and spirit, they make the most perfect whole, happily blending reason and sensibility into one character.

And what is sensibility? “Quickness of sensation; quickness of perception; delicacy.” That is how Dr. Johnson defines it, and the definition gives me no idea of anything but the most exquisitely polished instinct. I see not a trace of the image of God in either sensation or matter. Refine them seventy times seven, and they are still material; intellect does not live there, and fire will never turn lead into gold!

I come back to my old argument: if woman is granted an immortal soul, she must have an understanding to develop as the work of her life. And when, to make the present state more complete — though everything shows it to be only a fraction of a mighty sum — she is lured by present gratification into forgetting her great destiny, nature is thwarted; or else she was born only to procreate and rot. Or, if we grant brutes of every kind a soul, though not a rational one, the exercise of instinct and sensibility may be the step they are to take in this life towards attaining reason in the next; so that through all eternity they will lag behind man, who, for reasons we cannot tell, was given the power to attain reason in his first mode of existence.

When I discuss the particular duties of women, as I would discuss the particular duties of a citizen or a father, it will be seen that I do not mean to suggest that they should be taken out of their families — speaking, that is, of the majority. “He that hath wife and children,” says Lord Bacon, “hath given hostages to fortune; for they are impediments to great enterprises, either of virtue or mischief. Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.” I say the same of women. But the welfare of society does not rest on extraordinary exertions; and if society were more reasonably organized, there would be even less need for great abilities or heroic virtues. Running a family and educating children particularly require understanding, in a plain, unsophisticated sense: strength of both body and mind. Yet the men who have laboured most earnestly in their writings to domesticate women have tried, with arguments dictated by a gross appetite that satiety had made fastidious, to weaken their bodies and cramp their minds. But even if, by these sinister methods, they really PERSUADED women, by working on their feelings, to stay at home and fulfil the duties of a mother and mistress of a family, I would oppose only with caution opinions that led women to right conduct by prevailing on them to make the performance of a duty the business of life, even though reason were insulted. Yet — and I appeal to experience — if, when their understanding is neglected, women are drawn away from these domestic duties as much as, or even more than, they could be by the most serious intellectual pursuit (though it may be observed that the mass of mankind will never pursue an intellectual object vigorously), I may be allowed to infer that reason is absolutely necessary for a woman to perform any duty properly; and I must repeat once more that sensibility is not reason.

The comparison with the rich still comes to my mind; for when men neglect the duties of humanity, women will do the same; a common current sweeps them both along with thoughtless speed. Wealth and honours prevent a man from enlarging his understanding and sap all his powers, by reversing the order of nature, which has always made true pleasure the reward of labour. Pleasure — enervating pleasure — is likewise within woman’s reach without her having to earn it. But until inherited property is spread more widely, how can we expect men to take pride in virtue? And until they do, women will govern them by the most direct means, neglecting their dull domestic duties to seize the pleasure that flies past on the wing of time.

“The power of women,” says some author, “is her sensibility;” and men, not seeing where this leads, do all they can to make this power swallow up every other. Those who constantly exercise their sensibility will have the most of it: poets, painters and composers, for example. Yet when sensibility is increased in this way at the expense of reason, and even of imagination, why do philosophical men complain of women’s fickleness? Man’s sexual attention acts on female sensibility in particular, and this sympathy has been exercised in women ever since their youth. A husband cannot keep up those attentions for long with the passion needed to excite lively emotions; and the heart, used to lively emotions, turns to a new lover, or pines in secret, a prey to virtue or prudence. I mean, when the heart has really been made susceptible and the taste formed; for I am inclined to conclude, from what I have seen in fashionable life, that the kind of education and the dealings between the sexes which I have condemned foster vanity more often than sensibility; and that coquetry springs more often from vanity than from the inconstancy that overstrained sensibility naturally produces.

Another argument that has weighed heavily with me must, I think, carry some force with every thoughtful and benevolent heart. Girls who have been educated in this weak way are often cruelly left by their parents without any provision, and so they depend not only on the reason but on the generosity of their brothers. These brothers, to take the most favourable view of the matter, are decent enough men, and give as a favour what children of the same parents had an equal right to. A docile woman may remain in this ambiguous, humiliating situation for some time with a tolerable degree of comfort. But when the brother marries, as he probably will, she goes from being regarded as the mistress of the family to being viewed with averted looks as an intruder, an unnecessary burden on the benevolence of the master of the house and his new partner.

Who can count up the misery that many unfortunate beings, weak alike in mind and body, suffer in such situations — unable to work and ashamed to beg? The wife, a cold-hearted, narrow-minded woman (and this is not an unfair supposition, for the present kind of education does no more to enlarge the heart than the understanding), is jealous of the little kindness her husband shows his relations; and since her sensibility does not rise as far as humanity, she is displeased to see the property of HER children squandered on a helpless sister.

These are facts that have come before my eyes again and again. The result is obvious: the wife resorts to cunning to undermine the habitual affection she is afraid to oppose openly; and neither tears nor caresses are spared until the spy is worked out of her home and thrown on the world, unprepared for its difficulties; or else sent off, as a great effort of generosity or out of some regard for propriety, with a small allowance and an uncultivated mind, into joyless solitude.

These two women may be much on a level in reason and humanity; and had they changed places, each might have played exactly the same selfish part. But had they been educated differently, the case would also have been very different. The wife would not have had that sensibility which centres on self, and reason might have taught her not to expect her husband’s affection, nor even to be flattered by it, if it led him to violate prior duties. She would wish to love him not merely because he loved her, but for his virtues; and the sister might have been able to fend for herself instead of eating the bitter bread of dependence.

I am indeed convinced that the heart, as well as the understanding, is opened by cultivation; and also — though this may seem less obvious — by strengthening the organs. I am not speaking now of momentary flashes of sensibility, but of affections. And perhaps the hardest task in educating both sexes is to adjust instruction so that it neither narrows the understanding while the heart is warmed by the generous juices of spring, just raised by the electric fermentation of the season, nor dries up the feelings by occupying the mind with inquiries remote from life.

As for women, when they are given a careful education, they are made either into fine ladies, brimming with sensibility and teeming with capricious fancies, or into mere notable women — busy, capable housewives. The latter are often friendly, honest creatures, with a shrewd kind of good sense joined to worldly prudence, which often makes them more useful members of society than the fine sentimental lady, though they have neither greatness of mind nor taste. The intellectual world is closed to them; take them out of their family or neighbourhood and they come to a standstill, for the mind finds nothing to do; literature offers a fund of amusement that they have never tried to enjoy, and have often despised. The sentiments and taste of more cultivated minds seem ridiculous to them, even in those whom chance and family ties have led them to love; and in mere acquaintances they think it all affectation.

A man of sense can love such a woman only because of her sex, and respect her because she is a trustworthy servant. To keep his own peace, he lets her scold the servants and go to church in clothes made of the very best materials. A man whose understanding was the same size as hers would probably not get on so well with her, for he might want to encroach on her prerogative and manage some household matters himself. Yet women whose minds have not been enlarged by cultivation, and whose natural selfishness of sensibility has not been widened by reflection, are very unfit to manage a family; for, stretching their power beyond its due, they are always tyrannizing to support a superiority that rests only on the arbitrary distinction of fortune. Sometimes the evil is more serious: servants are deprived of innocent pleasures and made to work beyond their strength so that the notable woman can keep a better table and outshine her neighbours in finery and display. If she attends to her children, it is generally to dress them expensively; and whether this attention springs from vanity or from doting fondness, it is equally harmful.

Besides, how many women of this kind spend their days, or at least their evenings, in discontent. Their husbands admit that they are good managers and chaste wives, but leave home to look for more agreeable — if I may use an expressive French word — piquant company; and the patient drudge who performs her task like a blind horse in a mill is cheated of her just reward; for the wages due to her are her husband’s caresses, and women with so few resources in themselves do not bear this deprivation of a natural right very patiently.

A fine lady, on the other hand, has been taught to look down with contempt on the ordinary occupations of life, though she has been encouraged only to acquire accomplishments that rise one degree above mere sense; for even bodily accomplishments cannot be acquired with any precision unless the understanding has been strengthened by exercise.
