Without a foundation of principles, taste is superficial, and grace must spring from something deeper than imitation. Her imagination, however, is inflamed, and her feelings made fastidious, if not corrupted by artifice; or else no counterweight of judgment is acquired while the heart still remains guileless, though it grows too tender.

These women are often amiable, and their hearts really are more responsive to general benevolence, more alive to the sentiments that civilize life, than the square-elbowed family drudge; but, lacking a due proportion of reflection and self-government, they only inspire love. They are their husbands’ mistresses for as long as they keep any hold on their affections, and the platonic friends of his male acquaintances. These are the fair defects in nature: the women who seem to have been created not to enjoy the companionship of man, but to save him from sinking into absolute brutality by rubbing off the rough corners of his character, and by playful dalliance to lend some dignity to the appetite that draws him to them. Gracious Creator of the whole human race! Have you created such a being as woman, who can trace your wisdom in your works and feel that you alone are by your nature exalted above her — for no better purpose? Can she believe that she was made only to submit to man, her equal, a being who, like her, was sent into the world to acquire virtue? Can she consent to be occupied merely with pleasing him, merely with adorning the earth, when her soul is capable of rising to you? And can she rest in supine dependence on man for reason, when she ought to climb with him the steep and arduous heights of knowledge?

Yet if love is the supreme good, then educate women only to inspire it, and polish every charm until it intoxicates the senses; but if they are moral beings, give them a chance to become intelligent, and let their love for man be only one part of that glowing flame of universal love which, having encircled humanity, rises to God like grateful incense.

Fulfilling domestic duties takes a great deal of resolution, and a serious kind of perseverance that needs firmer support than emotions, however lively and true to nature they may be. To set an example of order, which is the soul of virtue, a person must adopt a certain austerity of behaviour, hardly to be expected from a being who has been made the weathercock of its own sensations since infancy. Anyone who rationally intends to be useful must have a plan of conduct; and in carrying out even the simplest duty we are often obliged to act against the immediate impulse of tenderness or compassion. Severity is often the surest, as well as the most sublime, proof of affection; and the lack of this power over the feelings, and of that lofty, dignified affection which makes a person prefer the future good of the loved one to a present gratification, is the reason so many doting mothers spoil their children. It has also made it doubtful whether neglect or indulgence does more harm; but I am inclined to think that indulgence has done the most.

Mankind seem to agree that children should be left in the care of women during their early years. Now, from all the observation I have been able to make, women of sensibility are the least fit for this task, because, carried away by their feelings, they will infallibly spoil a child’s temper. Managing the temper, the first and most important branch of education, requires the sober, steady eye of reason, and a plan of conduct equally far from tyranny and from indulgence; yet these are the very extremes into which people of sensibility fall by turns, always overshooting the mark. I have pursued this line of reasoning much further, until I have concluded that a person of genius is the most unsuitable person to employ in education, whether public or private. Minds of this rare kind see things too much in the mass, and seldom, if ever, have an even temper. That habitual cheerfulness we call good humour is perhaps as rarely joined to great mental powers as to strong feelings. And those who follow the flights of genius with interest and admiration, or who, with cooler approval, absorb the instruction the profound thinker has laboriously prepared for them, should not be disgusted if they find the former irritable and the latter morose; for liveliness of imagination and a tenacious grasp of mind are hardly compatible with that pliant courtesy which leads a man at least to bend to the opinions and prejudices of others instead of roughly confronting them.

But when we treat of education or of morals and customs, minds of a superior class need not be considered; they may be left to chance. It is the multitude of moderate abilities who need instruction, and who take on the colour of the atmosphere they breathe. This respectable body of people, men and women alike, should not, I maintain, have their sensations heightened in the hothouse of luxurious idleness at the expense of their understanding; for unless they carry the ballast of understanding they will never become either virtuous or free: an aristocracy founded on property, or on sterling talents, will always sweep before it the slaves of feeling, who are timid and ferocious by turns.

To look at the subject from another angle, countless arguments have been brought forward with a show of reason, because they are supposed to be drawn from nature, which men have used to degrade the sex both morally and physically. I must take note of a few.

The female understanding has often been spoken of with contempt on the ground that it reaches maturity sooner than the male. I shall not answer this argument by pointing to the early evidence of reason, as well as genius, in Cowley, Milton and Pope (many other names might be added), but shall simply appeal to experience to decide whether young men who are introduced early into society (and examples now abound) do not acquire the same precocity. This fact is so well known that merely mentioning it must call up, for anyone who mixes in the world at all, the image of a crowd of swaggering apes of men whose understandings have been narrowed by being brought into the company of men when they should have been spinning a top or twirling a hoop.

Some naturalists have also asserted that men do not reach their full growth and strength until thirty, whereas women are mature by twenty. I suspect that they are reasoning on false ground, misled by the male prejudice which counts beauty as the perfection of woman — mere beauty of feature and complexion, in the common sense the world gives the word — while male beauty is allowed to have some connection with the mind. Strength of body, and that character of face which the French call a physionomie, women no more acquire before thirty than men do. The little unaffected tricks of children, it is true, are especially pleasing and attractive; yet once the pretty freshness of youth has worn off, these unaffected graces turn into studied airs and disgust every person of taste. In girls’ faces we look only for vivacity and bashful modesty; but when the springtime of life is over, we look for soberer sense in the face, and for traces of passion in place of the dimples of high spirits, expecting to see individuality of character, which alone fastens the affections. We then want to converse, not to fondle; to give scope to our imaginations as well as to the sensations of our hearts.

At twenty the beauty of both sexes is equal; but man’s libertinism leads him to draw a distinction, and aging coquettes usually share his opinion; for when they can no longer inspire love, they pay for the vigour and vivacity of youth. The French, who allow more of the mind into their idea of beauty, prefer women of thirty. I mean that they consider women to be at their most perfect when vivacity gives way to reason and to that majestic seriousness of character which marks maturity, the resting point. In youth the body shoots up until twenty; until thirty the solid parts are gaining a degree of density, and the flexible muscles, growing more rigid every day, give character to the face; that is, they record the workings of the mind with the iron pen of fate, and tell us not only what powers lie within, but how they have been used.

It is worth observing that animals which mature slowly are the longest-lived and belong to the noblest species. Men cannot, however, claim any natural superiority on the strength of that grand mark, long life; for in this respect nature has not favoured the male.

Polygamy is another physical degradation; and a plausible argument for a custom that blights every domestic virtue is drawn from the well-attested fact that more females than males are born in the countries where it is established. This seems to be a sign from nature, and to nature apparently reasonable speculations must give way. A further conclusion obviously follows: if polygamy is necessary, woman must be inferior to man, and made for him.

We know very little about how the foetus is formed in the womb; but it seems probable to me that some accidental physical cause may account for this phenomenon and show that it is not a law of nature. I have come across some apt observations on the subject in Forster’s Account of the Isles of the South Sea which will explain what I mean. After remarking that, of the two sexes among animals, the one with the more vigorous and hotter constitution always prevails and produces its own kind, he adds: “If this be applied to the inhabitants of Africa, it is evident that the men there, accustomed to polygamy, are enervated by the use of so many women, and therefore less vigorous; the women on the contrary, are of a hotter constitution, not only on account of their more irritable nerves, more sensitive organization, and more lively fancy; but likewise because they are deprived in their matrimony of that share of physical love which in a monogamous condition, would all be theirs; and thus for the above reasons, the generality of children are born females.”

“In the greater part of Europe it has been proved by the most accurate lists of mortality, that the proportion of men to women is nearly equal, or, if any difference takes place, the males born are more numerous, in the proportion of 105 to 100.”

Polygamy, therefore, does not appear to be necessary; yet when a man seduces a woman, it ought, I think, to be called a LEFT-HANDED marriage, and the man should be LEGALLY obliged to support the woman and her children, unless adultery, a natural divorce, cancelled the law. And this law should stay in force as long as women’s weakness led the word seduction to be used as an excuse for their frailty and lack of principle; indeed, as long as they depend on man for their livelihood instead of earning it with their own hands or heads. But these women should not be called wives in the full meaning of that relationship, or the very purpose of marriage would be overturned, and all those endearing kindnesses that flow from personal fidelity, and give the tie its sanctity when neither love nor friendship unites the hearts, would dissolve into selfishness. The woman who is faithful to the father of her children deserves respect and should not be treated like a prostitute; though I readily grant that if a man and woman must live together to bring up their offspring, nature never intended a man to have more than one wife.

Still, though I respect marriage highly as the foundation of almost every social virtue, I cannot help feeling the most lively compassion for those unfortunate women who are severed from society and, through a single error, torn away from all the affections and relationships that develop the heart and mind. Often it does not even deserve to be called an error; for many innocent girls become the dupes of a sincere, affectionate heart, and still more are, as it may pointedly be put, RUINED before they know the difference between virtue and vice; and so, prepared for infamy by their education, they become infamous. Asylums and Magdalens are not the proper remedies for these abuses. What the world lacks is justice, not charity!

A woman who has lost her honour imagines that she cannot sink any lower; and as for regaining her former position, that is impossible: no effort can wash the stain away. Having thus lost every spur, and having no other means of support, she finds in prostitution her only refuge, and her character is quickly corrupted by circumstances over which the poor wretch has little control, unless she has an uncommon share of good sense and loftiness of spirit. Necessity never makes prostitution the business of men’s lives; yet countless women are made systematically vicious in this way. This, however, arises largely from the idleness in which women are brought up; they are always taught to look to man for their maintenance and to regard their persons as the proper return for his efforts to support them. Meretricious airs, and the whole science of wantonness, then have a more powerful stimulus than either appetite or vanity; and this observation lends force to the prevailing opinion that with chastity everything respectable in woman is lost. Her character depends on keeping one virtue, though the only passion fostered in her heart — is love. Indeed, a woman’s honour is not even made to depend on her own will.

When Richardson has Clarissa tell Lovelace that he had robbed her of her honour, his notions of honour and virtue must have been strange ones. For the condition of a being who could be degraded without its own consent is miserable beyond every name of misery! I have heard this excessive strictness defended as a salutary error. My answer is in the words of Leibnitz: “Errors are often useful; but it is commonly to remedy other errors.”

Most of the evils of life spring from a desire for present enjoyment that outruns itself. The obedience demanded of women in marriage falls under this description: the mind, naturally weakened by depending on authority, never exerts its own powers, and so the obedient wife becomes a weak, indolent mother. Or, supposing that this is not always the result, a future state of existence hardly enters the reckoning when only negative virtues are cultivated. For in discussing morals, especially where women are concerned, writers have too often taken virtue in a very narrow sense and based it SOLELY on worldly usefulness; indeed, this stupendous structure has been set on an even more fragile foundation, and the wayward, fluctuating feelings of men have been made the standard of virtue. Yes, virtue, like religion, has been made subject to the verdicts of taste.

If man’s vain absurdities did not strike us on every side, it would almost provoke a smile of contempt to see how eager men are to degrade the sex from whom they claim to receive the chief pleasure of life; and I have often, with full conviction, turned Pope’s sarcasm back on them; or, to put it plainly, it has seemed to me to apply to the whole human race. A love of pleasure or of power seems to divide mankind, and the husband who lords it in his little harem thinks only of his pleasure or his convenience. Indeed, an intemperate love of pleasure carries some prudent men, or worn-out libertines who marry to have a safe companion, so far that they seduce their own wives. Hymen banishes modesty, and chaste love takes flight.

Love, considered as an animal appetite, cannot feed on itself for long without dying out; and this extinction in its own flame may be called love’s violent death. But a wife who has been made licentious in this way will probably try to fill the emptiness left when her husband’s attentions cease; for after being treated like a goddess she cannot contentedly become a mere upper servant. She is still handsome, and rather than turning her fondness towards her children, she dreams only of basking in the sunshine of life. Besides, many husbands have so little sense and parental affection that, in the first ferment of voluptuous fondness, they will not allow their wives to nurse their own children. The wives are to dress and live only to please them; and love, even innocent love, soon sinks into lasciviousness when the performance of a duty is sacrificed to its indulgence.

Personal attachment is a very happy basis for friendship; yet even when two virtuous young people marry, it might perhaps be a blessing if some circumstance held their passion in check — if the memory of an earlier attachment, or of disappointed affection, made the match, on one side at least, one founded rather on esteem. They would then look beyond the present moment and try to make the whole of their life respectable, by forming a plan to govern a friendship that only death ought to end.

Friendship is a serious affection — the most sublime of all, because it rests on principle and is cemented by time. Exactly the reverse may be said of love. To a great extent, love and friendship cannot dwell together in one breast; even when different objects inspire them, each weakens or destroys the other, and towards the same object they can only be felt in turn. Vain fears and doting jealousies, the winds that fan love’s flame when judiciously or artfully tempered, are both incompatible with the tender trust and sincere respect of friendship.

Love as the glowing pen of genius has portrayed it does not exist on earth, or lives only in those exalted, fervent imaginations that have sketched such dangerous pictures. Dangerous, because they not only give a plausible excuse to the voluptuary, who disguises sheer sensuality under a sentimental veil, but also spread affectation and detract from the dignity of virtue. Virtue, as the very word implies, should look serious, if not austere; and to try to dress her up in the costume of pleasure, because the epithet has been used as another name for beauty, is to raise her up on a quicksand — a most insidious attempt to hasten her fall under a show of respect. In fact, virtue and pleasure are not so closely allied in this life as some eloquent writers have laboured to prove. Pleasure prepares the fading wreath and mixes the intoxicating cup; but the fruit that virtue yields is the reward of toil, and, seen gradually as it ripens, it gives only calm satisfaction; indeed, since it seems to be the result of the natural course of things, it is hardly noticed. Bread, the common food of life, seldom thought of as a blessing, sustains the constitution and preserves health; yet feasts delight the heart of man, though disease and even death lurk in the cup or delicacy that lifts the spirits or tickles the palate. In the same way, the lively, heated imagination paints love, as it paints every other picture, in those glowing colours which the daring hand will steal from the rainbow — a hand directed by a mind condemned, in a world like this, to prove its noble origin by panting after unattainable perfection, forever pursuing what it admits to be a fleeting dream. An imagination of this vigorous kind can give existence to insubstantial forms, and stability to the shadowy reveries into which the mind naturally falls when realities prove flat. It can then paint love with heavenly charms and dote on the grand ideal object; it can imagine a degree of mutual affection that will refine the soul and not expire once it has served as a “scale to heavenly”; and, like religious devotion, make it absorb every lesser affection and desire. In each other’s arms, as in a temple whose summit is lost in the clouds, the lovers are to shut out the world, and every thought and wish that does not nourish pure affection and permanent virtue. Permanent virtue! Alas, Rousseau, respectable visionary! Your paradise would soon be violated by the entrance of some unexpected guest. Like Milton’s, it would contain only angels, or men sunk below the dignity of rational creatures. Happiness is not material; it cannot be seen or felt! Yet the eager pursuit of the good which everyone shapes to his own fancy proclaims man the lord of this lower world, an intelligent creature who is not to receive happiness but to acquire it. Those who complain of the delusions of passion, therefore, forget that they are crying out against a strong proof of the immortality of the soul.

But leaving superior minds to correct themselves, and to pay dearly for their experience, I should point out that what I wish to guard the female heart against, by exercising the understanding, is not strong, persevering passions but romantic, wavering feelings; for these paradisal reveries come more often from idleness than from a lively imagination.

Women seldom have enough serious occupation to silence their feelings; and since a round of petty cares or vain pursuits fritters away all their strength of mind and body, they naturally become mere objects of sense. In short, the whole drift of female education (the education given by society) tends to make the best-disposed romantic and inconstant, and the rest vain and low. In the present state of society this evil can hardly be remedied in the slightest degree, I fear; but should a worthier ambition ever gain ground, women may be brought closer to nature and reason, and become more virtuous and useful as they become more respectable.

But I will venture to assert that their reason will never gain enough strength to govern their conduct while making a show in the world is the first wish of most of mankind. To this weak wish the natural affections and the most useful virtues are sacrificed. Girls marry merely to BETTER THEMSELVES, to borrow an expressive common phrase, and have such perfect command over their hearts that they do not allow themselves to FALL IN LOVE until a man of superior fortune proposes. I intend to enlarge on this subject in a later chapter; for now it is only necessary to drop a hint, because women are so often degraded by letting the selfish prudence of age chill the ardour of youth.

From the same source comes the opinion that young girls ought to devote a large part of their time to needlework; yet this occupation narrows their faculties more than any other that could have been chosen for them, by confining their thoughts to their own persons. Men order their clothes to be made and are done with the subject; women make their own clothes, whether necessary or ornamental, and are forever talking about them, and their thoughts follow their hands. Indeed, it is not making necessities that weakens the mind, but the frippery of dress. For when a woman of the lower ranks makes her husband’s and children’s clothes, she is doing her duty; this is part of her business. But when women sew only to dress better than they could otherwise afford, it is worse than a sheer waste of time. To make the poor virtuous, they must be given work; and women of the middle ranks, if they did not ape the fashions of the nobility without acquiring their ease, might employ them, while they themselves managed their families, taught their children and exercised their own minds. Gardening, experimental science and literature would give them subjects to think about, and material for conversation, that would to some degree exercise their understandings. The conversation of French women, who are not so rigidly nailed to their chairs twisting lappets and knotting ribbons, is often superficial; but I maintain that it is not half so insipid as that of those English women whose time is spent making caps, bonnets and the whole mischief of trimmings, not to mention shopping, bargain-hunting, etc., etc.; and it is the decent, prudent women who are most degraded by these practices, for their motive is simply vanity. The wanton, who exercises her taste to make her person alluring, has something more in view.

All these observations branch out of a general one which I have made before, and which cannot be insisted on too often: whether we speak of men, women or professions, it will be found that the way the thoughts are employed shapes the character, both generally and individually. Women’s thoughts always hover around their own persons; is it any wonder, then, that their persons are thought their most valuable part? Yet some degree of freedom of mind is necessary even to form the person; and this may be one reason why some gentle wives have so few attractions besides that of their sex. Add to this that sedentary occupations make most women sickly, and false notions of female excellence make them proud of this delicacy, though it is yet another fetter which, by constantly drawing attention to the body, cramps the activity of the mind.

Women of rank seldom do any of the manual work of their dress, so only their taste is exercised; and because they think less about the finery once the business of dressing is over, they acquire that ease which seldom appears in the bearing of women who dress merely for the sake of dressing. In fact, the observation about the middle rank, the one in which talents thrive best, does not hold for women; for those of the upper class, by picking up at least a smattering of literature and talking more with men on general subjects, gain more knowledge than the women who ape their fashions and faults without sharing their advantages. As for virtue, taking the word in a broad sense, I have seen the most of it among the lowly. Many poor women support their children by the sweat of their brow, and hold together families that the fathers’ vices would have scattered; but gentlewomen are too indolent to be actively virtuous, and are softened rather than refined by civilization. Indeed, the good sense I have found among poor women who have had few advantages of education, and yet have acted heroically, strongly confirmed me in the opinion that trifling occupations have made woman a trifler. Men, taking her (“I take her body,” says Ranger.) body, leave the mind to rust; so that while physical love enervates man, being his favourite recreation, he will try to enslave woman: and who can tell how many generations may be needed to give vigour to the virtue and talents of the freed descendants of abject slaves? (“Supposing that women are voluntary slaves — slavery of any kind is unfavourable to human happiness and improvement.” — Knox’s Essays.)

In tracing the causes that, in my opinion, have degraded woman, I have limited my observations to those that act universally on the morals and manners of the whole sex; and it seems clear to me that they all spring from a lack of understanding. Whether this arises from a physical or an accidental weakness of the faculties, only time can tell; for I shall not lay much stress on the example of a few women (Sappho, Eloisa, Mrs. Macaulay, the Empress of Russia, Madame d’Eon, etc. These, and many more, may be counted as exceptions; and are not all heroes, as well as heroines, exceptions to general rules? I wish to see women neither heroines nor brutes, but reasonable creatures.) who have acquired courage and resolution through having received a masculine education. I only maintain that men placed in similar situations have acquired a similar character — I speak of men taken as a body — and that men of genius and talent have sprung from a class in which women have never yet been placed.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Animadversions on Some of the Writers Who Have Rendered Women Objects of Pity, Bordering on Contempt
paragraphs: It now remains to examine the opinions that have been plausibly defended in some modern publications on the female character and on education, and that have set the tone for most of the more cursory remarks made about the sex.
SECTION 5.1.

Rousseau is where I shall start. I will outline his portrait of women in his own words, interspersing comments and reflections of my own. Admittedly, those comments all flow from a few simple principles, and a reader could have worked them out from what I have said already; but the artificial edifice has been put together so ingeniously that it seems I must attack it point by point and draw the application myself.
According to Rousseau, Sophia ought to be as perfect a woman as Emilius is a man, and making her so requires us to look into the character nature has given her sex.

Next he undertakes to prove that, since woman has less bodily strength than man, she ought to be weak and passive; from which he infers that she was made to please him and submit to him, and that her duty is to make herself AGREEABLE to her master — the great end of her existence.

Grant that women were made only to please men and to be subject to them, and the conclusion follows: a woman ought to sacrifice every other consideration to making herself agreeable to him. Let this brutal urge for self-preservation, then, drive all her actions, once it is proved to be the iron bed of fate — the bed to which her character must be stretched or cut down to fit, whatever the moral or physical distinctions. But if, as I think can be shown, practical rules erected on so ignoble a foundation defeat even the purposes of this present life, viewed as a whole, then I may be allowed to doubt that woman was created for man. Let them raise the cry of irreligion, or even of atheism, against me: I will simply declare that even if an angel from heaven told me that Moses’s beautiful, poetic cosmogony and his account of man’s fall were literally true, I could not believe something my reason told me was derogatory to the character of the Supreme Being. With no fear of the devil before my eyes, I dare to call this a prompting of reason, instead of laying my weakness on the broad shoulders of the first seducer of my frail sex.

“It being once demonstrated,” Rousseau continues, “that man and woman are not, nor ought to be, constituted alike in temperament and character, it follows of course, that they should not be educated in the same manner. In pursuing the directions of nature, they ought indeed to act in concert, but they should not be engaged in the same employments: the end of their pursuits should be the same, but the means they should take to accomplish them, and, of consequence, their tastes and inclinations should be different.” (Rousseau’s ‘Emilius’, Volume 3 page 176.)

“Girls are from their earliest infancy fond of dress. Not content with being pretty, they are desirous of being thought so; we see, by all their little airs, that this thought engages their attention; and they are hardly capable of understanding what is said to them, before they are to be governed by talking to them of what people will think of their behaviour. The same motive, however, indiscreetly made use of with boys, has not the same effect: provided they are let to pursue their amusements at pleasure, they care very little what people think of them. Time and pains are necessary to subject boys to this motive.

“Whencesoever girls derive this first lesson it is a very good one. As the body is born, in a manner before the soul, our first concern should be to cultivate the former; this order is common to both sexes, but the object of that cultivation is different. In the one sex it is the development of corporeal powers; in the other, that of personal charms: not that either the quality of strength or beauty ought to be confined exclusively to one sex; but only that the order of the cultivation of both is in that respect reversed. Women certainly require as much strength as to enable them to move and act gracefully, and men as much address as to qualify them to act with ease.”

“Children of both sexes have a great many amusements in common; and so they ought; have they not also many such when they are grown up? Each sex has also its peculiar taste to distinguish in this particular. Boys love sports of noise and activity; to beat the drum, to whip the top, and to drag about their little carts: girls, on the other hand, are fonder of things of show and ornament; such as mirrors, trinkets, and dolls; the doll is the peculiar amusement of the females; from whence we see their taste plainly adapted to their destination. The physical part of the art of pleasing lies in dress; and this is all which children are capacitated to cultivate of that art.”

“Here then we see a primary propensity firmly established, which you need only to pursue and regulate. The little creature will doubtless be very desirous to know how to dress up her doll, to make its sleeve knots, its flounces, its head dress, etc., she is obliged to have so much recourse to the people about her, for their assistance in these articles, that it would be much more agreeable to her to owe them all to her own industry. Hence we have a good reason for the first lessons which are usually taught these young females: in which we do not appear to be setting them a task, but obliging them, by instructing them in what is immediately useful to themselves. And, in fact, almost all of them learn with reluctance to read and write; but very readily apply themselves to the use of their needles. They imagine themselves already grown up, and think with pleasure that such qualifications will enable them to decorate themselves.”

Plainly this is nothing but an education of the body. Yet Rousseau is not alone among men in having hinted that a young woman’s mere person is very pleasing without any mind — unless we count high spirits as mind. To make the body weak, and what some would call beautiful, girls have their understanding neglected and are made to sit still, play with dolls and listen to silly talk; then the effect of habit is held up as an unmistakable sign of nature. I know Rousseau believed that the first years of youth should be spent forming the body, though he strays from this plan in educating Emilius; yet to strengthen the body, on which strength of mind largely depends, is a very different thing from merely teaching it to move with ease.

It should be noted that Rousseau formed his observations in a country where the art of pleasing had been refined only so as to take the coarseness out of vice. He did not return to nature — or else his dominant appetite interfered with his reasoning — for otherwise he would never have reached such crude conclusions.

In France, girls above all, but boys as well, are brought up only to please, to manage their persons and to control their outward conduct; and at a very early age their minds are corrupted by the worldly and pious cautions meant to guard them against immodesty. I speak of times now past. The very confessions required of mere children, and the questions the holy men put to them — I have these facts on good authority — were enough to impress a sexual character upon them, and what society taught them was a school of coquetry and artifice. By ten or eleven, and often much earlier, girls were already flirting, and spoke freely, with no one to rebuke them, of making their way in the world through marriage.

In short, they were turned into women almost from birth, and heard compliments where they should have received instruction. As these weakened the mind, it was assumed that Nature had behaved like a stepmother in forming this afterthought of creation.

Having denied them understanding, however, he was merely being consistent in subjecting them to an authority that owes nothing to reason; and to prepare them for that subjection he offers this advice:

“Girls ought to be active and diligent; nor is that all; they should also be early subjected to restraint. This misfortune, if it really be one, is inseparable from their sex; nor do they ever throw it off but to suffer more cruel evils. They must be subject, all their lives, to the most constant and severe restraint, which is that of decorum: it is, therefore, necessary to accustom them early to such confinement, that it may not afterward cost them too dear; and to the suppression of their caprices, that they may the more readily submit to the will of others. If, indeed, they are fond of being always at work, they should be sometimes compelled to lay it aside. Dissipation, levity, and inconstancy, are faults that readily spring up from their first propensities, when corrupted or perverted by too much indulgence. To prevent this abuse, we should learn them, above all things, to lay a due restraint on themselves. The life of a modest woman is reduced, by our absurd institutions, to a perpetual conflict with herself: not but it is just that this sex should partake of the sufferings which arise from those evils it hath caused us.”

Why is a modest woman’s life a perpetual conflict? My answer is that this very system of education makes it one. Modesty, temperance and self-denial are the sober children of reason; but when sensibility is fostered at the understanding’s expense, beings so weak have to be kept in check by arbitrary means and must live in constant conflict. Widen the field in which their minds can act, and their appetites and feelings will be governed by nobler passions and motives.

“The common attachment and regard of a mother, nay, mere habit, will make her beloved by her children, if she does nothing to incur their hate. Even the restraint she lays them under, if well directed, will increase their affection, instead of lessening it; because a state of dependence being natural to the sex, they perceive themselves formed for obedience.”

This begs the question; for servitude not only debases the one who serves, but its effects appear to be handed down to descendants. When we consider how long women have lived in dependence, should we be surprised that some of them hug their chains and fawn like spaniels? “These dogs,” observes a naturalist, “at first kept their ears erect; but custom has superseded nature, and a token of fear is become a beauty.”

“For the same reason,” Rousseau adds, “women have or ought to have, but little liberty; they are apt to indulge themselves excessively in what is allowed them. Addicted in everything to extremes, they are even more transported at their diversions than boys.”

The reply is very simple. Slaves and mobs, once they break loose from authority, have always run to the same excesses. When the hand that forcibly held a bent bow suddenly relaxes, the bow flies back with violence; and sensibility, which outward circumstances toy with, must be either held under authority or tempered by reason.

“There results,” he continues, “from this habitual restraint, a tractableness which the women have occasion for during their whole lives, as they constantly remain either under subjection to the men, or to the opinions of mankind; and are never permitted to set themselves above those opinions. The first and most important qualification in a woman is good-nature or sweetness of temper; formed to obey a being so imperfect as man, often full of vices, and always full of faults, she ought to learn betimes even to suffer injustice, and to bear the insults of a husband without complaint; it is not for his sake, but her own, that she should be of a mild disposition. The perverseness and ill-nature of the women only serve to aggravate their own misfortunes, and the misconduct of their husbands; they might plainly perceive that such are not the arms by which they gain the superiority.”

Since they are made to live with so imperfect a being as man, they ought to learn the necessity of forbearance through the exercise of their own faculties; but all the sacred rights of humanity are violated when blind obedience is insisted upon — or else the most sacred rights belong ONLY to man.

Whoever patiently endures injustice and bears insults in silence will soon become unjust, or lose the power of telling right from wrong. Moreover, I dispute the fact itself: this is not how a temper is formed or improved. Men, taken as a sex, have better tempers than women, because their occupations engage the head as well as the heart, and a steady head keeps the heart at a healthy heat. People of sensibility rarely have good tempers. A temper is formed by the cool labour of reason, as, with the advance of life, she skilfully harmonizes discordant elements. I have never known a weak or ignorant person with a good temper, though the name is often bestowed on mere constitutional good humour, and on the docility that fear imprints on behaviour. I say behaviour, because true meekness never touches the heart or mind unless it comes from reflection; and many sensible men who find some of these gentle, irritable creatures very tiresome companions will grant that simple restraint breeds a whole crop of unhealthy humours in domestic life.

“Each sex,” he argues further, “should preserve its peculiar tone and manner: a meek husband may make a wife impertinent; but mildness of disposition on the woman’s side will always bring a man back to reason, at least if he be not absolutely a brute, and will sooner or later triumph over him.” True, if it is the mildness of reason; but abject fear always breeds contempt, and tears speak eloquently only when they run down fair cheeks.

What can a heart be made of that melts when it is insulted and, instead of rebelling against injustice, kisses the rod? Is it unfair to infer that a woman who can caress a man with true feminine softness at the very moment he treats her tyrannically has a virtue built on narrow views and selfishness? Nature never dictated such insincerity; and though prudence of this kind is called a virtue, morality becomes vague when any part of it is supposed to rest on falsehood. These are mere expedients, and expedients are useful only for the moment.

Let the husband take care not to rely too implicitly on this servile obedience. If his wife can caress him with winning sweetness when he is angry — and when she ought to be angry herself, unless contempt has smothered a natural flash of indignation — she can do the same after taking leave of a lover. All of this prepares the way for adultery. Or suppose fear of the world, or of hell, holds back her wish to please other men once she can no longer please her husband: what substitute is left to a being whom nature and art formed only to please man? What will compensate her for this loss, and where is she to find a new occupation? Where will she find the strength of mind even to decide to begin looking, when her habits are set and vanity has long governed her chaotic mind?
Yet this biased moralist advocates cunning, and does so systematically and plausibly.

“Daughters should be always submissive; their mothers, however, should not be inexorable. To make a young person tractable, she ought not to be made unhappy; to make her modest she ought not to be rendered stupid. On the contrary, I should not be displeased at her being permitted to use some art, not to elude punishment in case of disobedience, but to exempt herself from the necessity of obeying. It is not necessary to make her dependence burdensome, but only to let her feel it. Subtlety is a talent natural to the sex; and as I am persuaded, all our natural inclinations are right and good in themselves, I am of opinion this should be cultivated as well as the others: it is requisite for us only to prevent its abuse.”

“Whatever is, is right,” he then triumphantly concludes. Granted; yet perhaps no maxim ever made a more paradoxical claim. As regards God, it is a solemn truth. He — and I say this with reverence — takes in the whole at a glance, and saw its due proportions while they still lay in the womb of time. But man, who can inspect only scattered fragments, finds much that is wrong; and it is part of the system, and so right, that he should strive to alter what seems wrong to him, even as he bows to his Creator’s wisdom and respects the darkness he labours to dispel.

Granting the principle, the inference that follows is valid: “The superiority of address, peculiar to the female sex, is a very equitable indemnification for their inferiority in point of strength: without this, woman would not be the companion of man; but his slave: it is by her superior art and ingenuity that she preserves her equality, and governs him while she affects to obey. Woman has everything against her, as well our faults as her own timidity and weakness: she has nothing in her favour, but her subtlety and her beauty. Is it not very reasonable, therefore, she should cultivate both?” Cunning and address can never live together with greatness of mind; for I will not split hairs over words whose plain meaning is insincerity and falsehood, but will simply observe that if any class of mankind is so made that it has to be educated by rules not strictly derived from truth, then virtue is a mere matter of convention. After giving this advice, how could Rousseau dare to claim that both sexes should aim at the same object in the great purpose of existence, when he knew very well that the mind is shaped by its pursuits — that it either grows larger as great views swallow up little ones, or else itself grows little?

Men are physically stronger; but if it were not for mistaken ideas of beauty, women would gain strength enough to support themselves — which is what independence truly means — and to endure the physical discomforts and exertions required to strengthen the mind.

Let us, then, be allowed to take the same exercise as boys, not only in infancy but in youth, so that we may reach bodily perfection and learn how far man’s natural superiority really extends. For what reason or virtue can be expected from a creature whose seed-time of life has been neglected? None — were it not that the winds of heaven scatter many useful seeds by chance in the fallow ground.

“Beauty cannot be acquired by dress, and coquetry is an art not so early and speedily attained. While girls are yet young, however, they are in a capacity to study agreeable gesture, a pleasing modulation of voice, an easy carriage and behaviour; as well as to take the advantage of gracefully adapting their looks and attitudes to time, place, and occasion. Their application, therefore, should not be solely confined to the arts of industry and the needle, when they come to display other talents, whose utility is already apparent.” “For my part I would have a young Englishwoman cultivate her agreeable talents, in order to please her future husband, with as much care and assiduity as a young Circassian cultivates hers, to fit her for the Haram of an Eastern bashaw.”

To make women utterly insignificant, he goes on: “The tongues of women are very voluble; they speak earlier, more readily, and more agreeably than the men; they are accused also of speaking much more: but so it ought to be, and I should be very ready to convert this reproach into a compliment; their lips and eyes have the same activity, and for the same reason. A man speaks of what he knows, a woman of what pleases her; the one requires knowledge, the other taste; the principal object of a man’s discourse should be what is useful, that of a woman’s what is agreeable. There ought to be nothing in common between their different conversation but truth.”

“We ought not, therefore, to restrain the prattle of girls, in the same manner as we should that of boys, with that severe question, ‘To what purpose are you talking?’ but by another, which is no less difficult to answer, ‘How will your discourse be received?’ In infancy, while they are as yet incapable to discern good from evil, they ought to observe it as a law, never to say anything disagreeable to those whom they are speaking to: what will render the practice of this rule also the more difficult, is, that it must ever be subordinate to the former, of never speaking falsely or telling an untruth.” Ruling the tongue like this must take great address indeed, and men and women alike practise it far too much. How few people speak out of the abundance of the heart! So few that I, a lover of simplicity, would happily trade politeness for a quarter of the virtue that has been sacrificed to a doubtful quality which should at best be merely virtue’s polish.

But let me finish the sketch. “It is easy to be conceived, that if male children be not in a capacity to form any true notions of religion, those ideas must be greatly above the conception of the females: it is for this very reason, I would begin to speak to them the earlier on this subject; for if we were to wait till they were in a capacity to discuss methodically such profound questions, we should run a risk of never speaking to them on this subject as long as they lived. Reason in women is a practical reason, capacitating them artfully to discover the means of attaining a known end, but which would never enable them to discover that end itself. The social relations of the sexes are indeed truly admirable: from their union there results a moral person, of which woman may be termed the eyes, and man the hand, with this dependence on each other, that it is from the man that the woman is to learn what she is to see, and it is of the woman that man is to learn what he ought to do. If woman could recur to the first principles of things as well as man, and man was capacitated to enter into their minutiae as well as woman, always independent of each other, they would live in perpetual discord, and their union could not subsist. But in the present harmony which naturally subsists between them, their different faculties tend to one common end; it is difficult to say which of them conduces the most to it: each follows the impulse of the other; each is obedient, and both are masters.”

“As the conduct of a woman is subservient to the public opinion, her faith in matters of religion, should for that very reason, be subject to authority. ‘Every daughter ought to be of the same religion as her mother, and every wife to be of the same religion as her husband: for, though such religion should be false, that docility which induces the mother and daughter to submit to the order of nature, takes away, in the sight of God, the criminality of their error’.* As they are not in a capacity to judge for themselves, they ought to abide by the decision of their fathers and husbands as confidently as by that of the church.”

(*Footnote. And what follows if the mother and the husband happen to disagree? An ignorant person cannot be argued out of an error; and when she is talked into exchanging one prejudice for another, her mind is left unsettled. Indeed, the husband may have no religion to teach her, although in that position she will sorely need something to support her virtue apart from worldly considerations.)

“As authority ought to regulate the religion of the women, it is not so needful to explain to them the reasons for their belief, as to lay down precisely the tenets they are to believe: for the creed, which presents only obscure ideas to the mind, is the source of fanaticism; and that which presents absurdities, leads to infidelity.”

Absolute and unquestioned authority must, it seems, reside somewhere; but is this not a direct and exclusive seizure of reason? Thus the RIGHTS of humanity have been restricted to the male line, from Adam down. Rousseau would push his male aristocracy further still. He hints that he would not fault those who want woman left in the deepest ignorance, if it were not necessary to give her some little knowledge of men, and of the customs that human passions give rise to, in order to protect her chastity and vindicate the man’s choice in the world’s eyes. Otherwise she could breed at home without the use of her understanding making her any less voluptuous and innocent — except, to be sure, in the first year of marriage, when she might use it to dress herself, as Sophia does. “Her dress is extremely modest in appearance, and yet very coquettish in fact: she does not make a display of her charms, she conceals them; but, in concealing them, she knows how to affect your imagination. Everyone who sees her, will say, There is a modest and discreet girl; but while you are near her, your eyes and affections wander all over her person, so that you cannot withdraw them; and you would conclude that every part of her dress, simple as it seems, was only put in its proper order to be taken to pieces by the imagination.” Is this modesty? Is this how one prepares for immortality? Once more: what are we to think of a system of education whose author says of his heroine “that with her, doing things well is but a SECONDARY concern; her principal concern is to do them NEATLY.”

Secondary, in fact, are all her virtues and qualities; for, with respect to religion, he has her parents address her, accustomed as she is to submission, in these words: “Your husband will instruct you in good time.”

Having cramped a woman’s mind in this way — if, to keep it fair, he has not wiped it entirely blank — he advises her to reflect, so that a man who reflects may not be bored in her company once he is tired of caressing her. But what can a woman who must obey have to reflect about? And would it not be a refinement of cruelty to open her mind merely to make the darkness and misery of her lot VISIBLE? Still, these are his sensible remarks; the reader can decide how well they agree with what I have had to quote already to present the subject fairly.

“They who pass their whole lives in working for their daily bread, have no ideas beyond their business or their interest, and all their understanding seems to lie in their fingers’ ends. This ignorance is neither prejudicial to their integrity nor their morals; it is often of service to them. Sometimes, by means of reflection, we are led to compound with our duty, and we conclude, by substituting a jargon of words, in the room of things. Our own conscience is the most enlightened philosopher. There is no need of being acquainted with Tully’s offices, to make a man of probity: and perhaps the most virtuous woman in the world is the least acquainted with the definition of virtue. But it is no less true, than an improved understanding only can render society agreeable; and it is a melancholy thing for a father of a family, who is fond of home, to be obliged to be always wrapped up in himself, and to have nobody about him to whom he can impart his sentiments.

“Besides, how should a woman void of reflection be capable of educating her children? How should she discern what is proper for them? How should she incline them to those virtues she is unacquainted with, or to that merit of which she has no idea? She can only soothe or chide them; render them insolent or timid; she will make them formal coxcombs, or ignorant blockheads; but will never make them sensible or amiable.” How indeed could she, when her husband is not always on hand to lend her his reason — when together they form only a single moral being? A blind will, “eyes without hands,” would not get far; and his abstract reason, which is supposed to focus the scattered rays of her practical reason, may perhaps be occupied in assessing the flavour of wines and holding forth on the sauces that best suit turtle; or, still more deeply engrossed at the card table, he may be generalizing his ideas while he bets away his fortune, and leaving all the minute details of education to his helpmate or to chance.

Yet suppose we grant that a woman should be beautiful, innocent and silly, so as to make her a more alluring and indulgent companion — to what end is her understanding sacrificed? And why, on Rousseau’s own showing, is all this preparation needed only to make her mistress of her husband for a very brief time? For no man ever stressed more than he did how quickly love passes. Here is the philosopher: “Sensual pleasures are transient. The habitual state of the affections always loses by their gratification. The imagination, which decks the object of our desires, is lost in fruition. Excepting the Supreme Being, who is self-existent, there is nothing beautiful but what is ideal.”

Yet he falls back on his unintelligible paradoxes when he speaks to Sophia like this: “Emilius, in becoming your husband, is become your master, and claims your obedience. Such is the order of nature. When a man is married, however, to such a wife as Sophia, it is proper he should be directed by her: this is also agreeable to the order of nature: it is, therefore, to give you as much authority over his heart as his sex gives him over your person, that I have made you the arbiter of his pleasures. It may cost you, perhaps, some disagreeable self-denial; but you will be certain of maintaining your empire over him, if you can preserve it over yourself; what I have already observed, also shows me, that this difficult attempt does not surpass your courage.

“Would you have your husband constantly at your feet? keep him at some distance from your person. You will long maintain the authority of love, if you know but how to render your favours rare and valuable. It is thus you may employ even the arts of coquetry in the service of virtue, and those of love in that of reason.”

Let me end these extracts with an apt portrait of a comfortable married couple. “And yet you must not imagine, that even such management will always suffice. Whatever precaution be taken, enjoyment will, by degrees, take off the edge of passion. But when love hath lasted as long as possible, a pleasing habitude supplies its place, and the attachment of a mutual confidence succeeds to the transports of passion. Children often form a more agreeable and permanent connexion between married people than even love itself. When you cease to be the mistress of Emilius, you will continue to be his wife and friend; you will be the mother of his children.” (Rousseau’s Emilius.)

Children, as he rightly says, bind married people together far more lastingly than love. Beauty, he declares, ceases to be valued, or even seen, after a couple have spent six months together, and artificial graces and coquetry will likewise grow stale to the senses. Why, then, does he say that a girl should be brought up for her husband as carefully as for an Eastern harem?

From the reveries of fancy and refined licentiousness I now appeal to the good sense of mankind. If education aims at preparing women to be chaste wives and sensible mothers, is the method so plausibly urged in the sketch above really the one best suited to that aim? Will anyone concede that the surest way to make a wife chaste is to train her in the wanton arts of a mistress — arts that the sensualist calls virtuous coquetry, because he can no longer relish the unaffected charms of sincerity, or enjoy the pleasure of a tender intimacy in which confidence is unchecked by suspicion and given interest by good sense?

A man who can be satisfied living with a pretty, useful companion without a mind has lost, through voluptuous indulgence, all taste for more refined pleasures; he has never known the calm contentment — refreshing to a parched heart like heaven’s silent dew — of being loved by someone capable of understanding him. With his wife he is still alone, except when the man sinks into the brute. “The charm of life,” says a grave philosophical reasoner, is “sympathy; nothing pleases us more than to observe in other men a fellow-feeling with all the emotions of our own breast.”

Yet by the logic that keeps women from the tree of knowledge, the precious years of youth, the usefulness of old age and the rational hopes of the hereafter must all be sacrificed so that woman may be an object of desire for a brief while. And how could Rousseau expect women to be virtuous and constant, when reason may not be the ground of their virtue, nor truth the aim of their inquiries?

Still, every one of Rousseau’s errors of reasoning sprang from sensibility — and sensibility to their charms is something women are only too ready to forgive! Where he ought to have reasoned, he grew impassioned; reflection set his imagination ablaze instead of enlightening his understanding. Even his virtues led him further astray. Born with a warm constitution and a lively fancy, he was drawn by nature to the other sex with such eager fondness that he soon became lascivious. Had he yielded to these desires, the fire would have died out of its own accord; but virtue, and a romantic sort of delicacy, made him deny himself. Yet whenever fear, delicacy or virtue restrained him, he debauched his imagination; brooding on the sensations that fancy intensified, he painted them in the most glowing colours and sank them deep into his soul.

He then sought solitude — not to sleep with the man of nature, or calmly to investigate the causes of things in the shade where Sir Isaac Newton gave himself up to contemplation, but merely to indulge his feelings. And he has painted what he felt so forcibly with such warmth that, by engaging the hearts and inflaming the imaginations of his readers, he leads them, in proportion to the strength of their fancy, to imagine that their understanding is convinced, when they are only sympathizing with a poetic writer who skilfully displays the objects of the senses, most voluptuously shaded or gracefully veiled. And so, as he makes us feel while we dream that we are reasoning, mistaken conclusions are left in the mind.

Why did Rousseau’s life swing between ecstasy and misery? What other answer can be given than that both were produced by the ferment of his imagination? Had his fancy been left to cool, he might possibly have gained greater strength of mind. Even so, if life’s purpose is to educate man’s intellectual part, all was right as far as he was concerned; yet, if death had not opened onto a nobler scene of action, he would probably have known a steadier happiness on earth and felt the calm sensations of the man of nature, instead of being readied for another stage of existence by feeding the passions that disturb civilized man.
But may his spirit rest in peace! My quarrel is not with his ashes but with his opinions. I quarrel only with the sensibility that led him to degrade woman by making her love’s slave.
....“Curs’d vassalage, First idoliz’d till love’s hot fire be o’er, Then slaves to those who courted us before.” Dryden.
The harmful tendency of those books in which the writers insidiously degrade the sex while they lie prostrate before women’s personal charms cannot be exposed too often or too severely.

Let us, my dear contemporaries, rise above prejudices so narrow! If wisdom is worth having for its own sake, and if virtue, to merit the name, must rest on knowledge, then let us labour to strengthen our minds through reflection until our heads can balance our hearts. Let us not limit all our thoughts to the trivial happenings of the day, or our knowledge to acquaintance with the hearts of our lovers or husbands; rather, let every other duty be subordinate to the great duty of improving our minds and preparing our affections for a higher state!
Beware, then, my friends, of letting the heart be moved by every trivial incident: the reed is shaken by a breeze and dies every year, but the oak stands firm and braves the storm for ages.

Were we truly created merely to flutter through our hour and then die — why, then, let us indulge our sensibility and laugh at reason’s severity. Yet, alas! even so we should lack strength of body and of mind, and life would be wasted in feverish pleasures or tedious languor.

But the system of education that I earnestly wish to see discredited seems to presuppose what ought never to be taken for granted: that virtue shields us from the accidents of life, and that fortune, slipping off her blindfold, will smile on a well-educated woman and bring her an Emilius or a Telemachus by the hand. On the contrary, the reward that virtue promises her devotees is clearly confined to their own hearts; and they must often struggle with the most vexing worldly cares and put up with the vices and moods of relations for whom they can never feel friendship.

Many women in the world, far from being upheld by the reason and virtue of their fathers and brothers, have strengthened their own minds by struggling against their vices and follies; and yet they have never met a hero in the form of a husband who, repaying the debt mankind owed them, might happen to return their reason to its natural state of dependence and give back to man his usurped privilege of rising above opinion.
SECTION 5.2.

Dr. Fordyce’s sermons have long formed part of a young woman’s library; indeed, girls at school are allowed to read them. But I would remove them at once from my pupil’s shelves if I wished to strengthen her understanding by leading her to form sound principles on a broad foundation, or even if I were only anxious to cultivate her taste — though it must be granted that they contain many sensible observations.

Dr. Fordyce may have had a very praiseworthy aim; but these discourses are written in so affected a style that, on that account alone, even if I had no other objection to his MELLIFLUOUS precepts, I would not let girls read them — unless I meant to hunt every spark of nature out of their make-up and melt every human quality into female weakness and artificial grace. I say artificial, for true grace springs from a certain independence of mind.

Children, who do not care about pleasing and want only to amuse themselves, are often very graceful; and the nobility, who have mostly lived among inferiors and have always had money at their command, acquire an easy, graceful bearing which ought rather to be called a habitual grace of the body than that higher gracefulness which is truly the expression of the mind. This mental grace, unnoticed by common eyes, often flashes across a rough face and, lighting up every feature, reveals simplicity and independence of mind. It is then that we read the marks of immortality in the eye and see the soul in every gesture, even though, at rest, neither the face nor the limbs may have much beauty to recommend them, nor the behaviour anything distinctive to draw general attention. The bulk of mankind, however, look for more TANGIBLE beauty; yet simplicity is generally admired when people do not stop to consider what they admire — and can there be simplicity without sincerity? But enough of remarks that are somewhat rambling, though the subject naturally prompted them.

In high-flown, declamatory sentences Dr. Fordyce spins out Rousseau’s eloquence, and in the most sentimental rant he sets out his opinions on the female character and on the behaviour a woman ought to adopt to make herself lovely.

Let him speak for himself, for this is how he makes nature address man: “Behold these smiling innocents, whom I have graced with my fairest gifts, and committed to your protection; behold them with love and respect; treat them with tenderness and honour. They are timid and want to be defended. They are frail; O do not take advantage of their weakness! Let their fears and blushes endear them. Let their confidence in you never be abused. But is it possible, that any of you can be such barbarians, so supremely wicked, as to abuse it? Can you find in your hearts* to despoil the gentle, trusting creatures of their treasure, or do anything to strip them of their native robe of virtue? Curst be the impious hand that would dare to violate the unblemished form of Chastity! Thou wretch! thou ruffian! forbear; nor venture to provoke heaven’s fiercest vengeance.” No serious comment on this curious passage occurs to me, though I could produce many like it — some so very sentimental that I have heard rational men apply the word indecent to them, speaking of them with disgust.
(*Footnote. “Can you? — Can you?” would be the most emphatic comment, if it were drawled out in a whining voice.)

All through, cold and artificial feelings are on display, together with that parade of sensibility which boys and girls ought to be taught to despise as the sure mark of a small, vain mind. Heaven is appealed to in florid terms, as are the BEAUTEOUS INNOCENTS, the fairest images of heaven here below, and sober sense is left far behind. Such language does not come from the heart and will never reach it, though it may tickle the ear.

Perhaps I shall be told that these volumes have pleased the public. So they have — and Hervey’s Meditations are still read, although their author offended just as much against good sense and good taste.

What I object to most is the lover-like language of pumped-up passion scattered all through the book. If women are ever to be allowed to walk without leading-strings, why must artful flattery and compliments to their sex be used to coax them into virtue? Speak to them the language of truth and soberness, and away with these lullabies of condescending endearment! Teach them to respect themselves as rational creatures, instead of leading them into a passion for their own insipid persons. It stirs my bile to hear a preacher hold forth on dress and needlework, and it galls me still more to hear him address the “British fair, the fairest of the fair,” as though feelings were all they had.

Even when recommending piety he uses the following argument: “Never, perhaps, does a fine woman strike more deeply, than when, composed into pious recollection, and possessed with the noblest considerations, she assumes, without knowing it, superior dignity and new graces; so that the beauties of holiness seem to radiate about her, and the by-standers are almost induced to fancy her already worshipping amongst her kindred angels!” Why must women be raised in this way to desire conquest? The very word, in this sense, turns my stomach! Have religion and virtue no stronger motives to offer, no brighter reward? Must they always be degraded by being made to keep in mind the sex of those around them? Must pleasing always be their lesson? And as they aim their little artillery at man’s heart, do they really need to be told that a little sense is enough to make their attention INCREDIBLY SOOTHING? “As a small degree of knowledge entertains in a woman, so from a woman, though for a different reason, a small expression of kindness delights, particularly if she have beauty!” I should have thought the reason was the same.

Why tell girls that they resemble angels, if not to sink them below women? Or tell them that no object comes nearer to the idea we have formed of angels than a gentle, innocent female? Yet in the same breath they learn that they resemble angels only while young and beautiful; it follows that this homage is paid to their persons, not to their virtues.

Idle, empty words! Where can such deceptive flattery lead, except to vanity and folly? A lover, admittedly, enjoys a poet’s licence to exalt his mistress; passion makes a dupe of his reason, and when he borrows the language of adoration he tells no lie. No one blames his imagination for raising the idol of his heart above humanity; and women would be fortunate if the only men who flattered them were those who loved them — I mean, who love the individual, not the sex. But ought a grave preacher to stuff his discourses with such foolishness?

In sermons and novels alike, however, voluptuousness always stays true to its text. Moralists allow men to cultivate, as nature directs, different qualities, and to take on the different characters that the same passions, varied almost infinitely, give to each individual. A virtuous man may have a choleric or a sanguine temperament, may be merry or serious, without reproach; he may be firm to the point of being almost overbearing, or so weakly submissive that he has no will or opinion of his own. But all women are to be levelled, by meekness and docility, into one single character of yielding softness and gentle compliance.

I will use the preacher’s own words: “Let it be observed, that in your sex manly exercises are never graceful; that in them a tone and figure, as well as an air and deportment, of the masculine kind, are always forbidding; and that men of sensibility desire in every woman soft features, and a flowing voice, a form not robust, and demeanour delicate and gentle.”

Is not the following portrait — the portrait of a house slave? “I am astonished at the folly of many women, who are still reproaching their husbands for leaving them alone, for preferring this or that company to theirs, for treating them with this and the other mark of disregard or indifference; when, to speak the truth, they have themselves in a great measure to blame. Not that I would justify the men in anything wrong on their part. But had you behaved to them with more RESPECTFUL OBSERVANCE, and a more EQUAL TENDERNESS; STUDYING THEIR HUMOURS, OVERLOOKING THEIR MISTAKES, SUBMITTING TO THEIR OPINIONS in matters indifferent, passing by little instances of unevenness, caprice, or passion, giving SOFT answers to hasty words, complaining as seldom as possible, and making it your daily care to relieve their anxieties and prevent their wishes, to enliven the hour of dullness, and call up the ideas of felicity: had you pursued this conduct, I doubt not but you would have maintained and even increased their esteem, so far as to have secured every degree of influence that could conduce to their virtue, or your mutual satisfaction; and your house might at this day have been the abode of domestic bliss.” Such a woman must be an angel — or else she is an ass — for I can see no trace of human character in this domestic drudge, neither reason nor passion; her whole being is absorbed in that of a tyrant.

Yet if Dr. Fordyce really believed that such conduct would win back a straying love rather than provoke contempt, he must have known very little of the human heart. No: a heart may be won by beauty, gentleness and so forth; but esteem, the only lasting affection, is won by nothing except virtue supported by reason. Tenderness for the person is kept alive by respect for the understanding.

Because these volumes are so often given to young people, I have noticed them more than, strictly speaking, they deserve; but since they have helped to corrupt the taste and weaken the understanding of many of my fellow creatures, I could not let them pass without comment.
SECTION 5.3.

Dr. Gregory’s Legacy to his daughters is so full of fatherly concern that I approach the task of criticizing it with affectionate respect. Yet this little volume has many attractions to recommend it to the most respectable part of my sex, and so I cannot keep silent about arguments that lend such plausible support to opinions which, in my view, have done the greatest harm to the morals and conduct of the female world.

His easy, familiar style particularly suits the tenor of his advice, and the melancholy tenderness that his respect for the memory of a beloved wife spreads through the whole work makes it very affecting. Yet in many passages there is a noticeable degree of concise elegance that disturbs this sympathy; we stumble upon the author when we expected to meet only the — father.

Besides, since he had two aims, he rarely held steadily to either. He wished to make his daughters amiable, yet he feared that the only result of instilling sentiments which might lead them off the beaten track of ordinary life, without equipping them to act with a matching independence and dignity, would be unhappiness; so he checks the natural flow of his thoughts, and his advice goes neither one way nor the other.
In the preface he tells them a sad truth, “that they will hear, at least once in their lives, the genuine sentiments of a man, who has no interest in deceiving them.”

Unhappy woman! What can be expected of you, when the beings on whom you are said by nature to depend for reason and support all have an interest in deceiving you! This is the root of the evil that has spread a corroding mildew over all your virtues and, blighting your opening faculties in the bud, has made you the weak thing you are! It is this separate interest — this insidious state of warfare — that undermines morality and divides mankind!

If love has made some women wretched — how many more has the cold, meaningless traffic of gallantry made vain and useless! Yet this heartless attention to the sex is thought so manly, so polite, that until society is organized very differently, I fear, this relic of gothic manners will not give way to a more reasonable and affectionate mode of conduct. Moreover, to strip it of its imaginary dignity, I must point out that in the most civilized states of Europe this lip-service is extremely widespread, and goes together with an extreme looseness of morals. In Portugal, the country I particularly have in mind, it takes precedence over the most serious moral obligations; for a man is seldom assassinated while he is in the company of a woman. The savage hand of violence is unnerved by this chivalrous spirit; and if the stroke of vengeance cannot be held back — the lady is begged to pardon the rudeness and to go in peace, though she may be spattered with her husband’s or her brother’s blood.
I shall not discuss his strictures on religion here, since I plan to treat that subject in a chapter of its own.

Many of his remarks on behaviour are very sensible, yet I disapprove of them entirely, because he seems to me to start, so to speak, at the wrong end. A cultivated understanding and an affectionate heart will never need starched rules of decorum; they will produce something more substantial than mere seemliness; while without understanding, the behaviour he recommends would be sheer affectation. Decorum, indeed, is the one thing needful! Nature is to be supplanted by decorum, and all simplicity and variety of character banished from the female world. Yet what good purpose can such superficial counsel serve? Admittedly, it is far easier to prescribe one way of behaving or another than to set the reason to work; but once the mind has been stocked with useful knowledge and strengthened by exercise, its guidance can safely be trusted to regulate behaviour.

Why, for example, give the following warning, when artifice of any kind must contaminate the mind? And why tangle the great motives of action, which reason and religion alike urge, with pitiful worldly dodges and sleight-of-hand tricks meant to earn the applause of gaping, tasteless fools? “Be even cautious in displaying your good sense.* It will be thought you assume a superiority over the rest of the company — But if you happen to have any learning keep it a profound secret, especially from the men, who generally look with a jealous and malignant eye on a woman of great parts, and a cultivated understanding.” If, as he later observes, men of real merit are above such baseness, why must the conduct of the entire sex be tuned to please fools — or men who, having little claim to respect as individuals, choose to close ranks in their phalanx? Men, indeed, whose only superiority is that of sex can certainly be excused for insisting on the superiority they all share.
(*Footnote. Let women once acquire good sense — and if it deserves the name, it will teach them how to use it; otherwise, what use will it be?)
If it were right always to adopt the tone of the company, rules of behaviour would be endless; for with the key changing constantly, a FLAT would often pass for a NATURAL note.

Surely the wiser advice would have been for women to improve themselves until they rose above the fumes of vanity, and then to leave public opinion to come round — for where are rules of accommodation to end? The narrow path of truth and virtue swerves neither right nor left; it runs straight ahead, and those who follow it in earnest may leap over many decorous prejudices without leaving modesty behind them. Purify the heart and give the head work to do, and I venture to predict that nothing in the behaviour will give offence.
