Whenever I see the fashionable air that so many young people are eager to acquire, it reminds me of the studied poses in certain modern prints, copied with tasteless servility from antique statues: the soul has been left out, and nothing that could properly be called character binds the parts together. This varnish of fashion, which rarely clings very closely to good sense, may dazzle the weak; but if nature is left to itself, it will seldom disgust the wise. Besides, if a woman has sense enough not to pretend to anything she does not in some measure understand, she has no need to resolve to hide her talents under a bushel. Let things take their natural course, and all will be well.

It is this system of dissimulation, running through the whole volume, that I despise. Women are always to SEEM to be this and that — yet virtue might address them in the words of Hamlet: “Seems! I know not seems! — Have that within that passeth show!”

The same tone recurs, for in another place, after recommending delicacy (without drawing sufficient distinctions), he adds, “The men will complain of your reserve. They will assure you that a franker behaviour would make you more amiable. But, trust me, they are not sincere when they tell you so. I acknowledge that on some occasions it might render you more agreeable as companions, but it would make you less amiable as women: an important distinction, which many of your sex are not aware of.”

This desire to be women at every moment is the very self-consciousness that degrades the sex. I must repeat, with emphasis, something I said before: except with a lover, it would be well if they were simply agreeable or rational companions. But on this point his advice even contradicts a passage which I intend to quote with the most marked approval.

“The sentiment, that a woman may allow all innocent freedoms, provided her virtue is secure, is both grossly indelicate and dangerous, and has proved fatal to many of your sex.” I agree with this opinion completely. Any man or woman of feeling must always want to assure the one they love that the caresses received and returned with pleasure are those of the individual, not of the sex, and that what is moved is the heart rather than the senses. Without this natural delicacy, love turns into a selfish personal gratification that soon degrades the character.

I carry this sentiment further still. Affection, when love is out of the question, justifies many personal endearments which, flowing naturally from an innocent heart, give life to behaviour; but physical familiarity prompted by appetite, gallantry or vanity is despicable. When a man squeezes the hand of a pretty woman he has never seen before as he hands her into a carriage, she will regard such an impertinent liberty as an insult, if she has any true delicacy, instead of being flattered by this meaningless homage to beauty. These are the privileges of friendship, or of the momentary homage the heart pays to virtue when it suddenly flashes into view — mere high spirits have no claim to the kindnesses of affection.

Since I wish the affections to be nourished by what now nourishes vanity, I would gladly persuade my sex to act on simpler principles. If they deserve love they will win it, even if no one ever tells them that “The power of a fine woman over the hearts of men, of men of the finest parts, is even beyond what she conceives.”

I have already remarked on his narrow cautions about duplicity, female softness and delicacy of constitution; he rings the changes on these without ceasing — more decorously than Rousseau, it is true, yet it all comes back to the same point, and whoever takes the trouble to analyze these sentiments will find that the first principles are not quite so delicate as the superstructure built on them.
The subject of amusements is treated too briefly, but in the same spirit.

When I come to treat friendship, love and marriage, it will be seen that we differ materially in opinion. I shall not, then, anticipate what I have to say on these important subjects, but will confine my remarks to their general tenor: to that cautious family prudence, to those narrow views of partial, unenlightened affection, which shut out pleasure and improvement by vainly trying to ward off sorrow and error — and which, by guarding the heart and mind in this way, destroy all their energy as well. It is far better to be often deceived than never to trust; to be disappointed in love than never to love; to lose a husband’s fondness than to forfeit his esteem.

How happy it would be for the world — and so, of course, for individuals — if all this fruitless anxiety to secure worldly happiness on a narrow plan were turned into an eager wish to improve the understanding. “Wisdom is the principal thing: THEREFORE get wisdom; and with all thy gettings get understanding.” “How long ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity, and hate knowledge?” So Wisdom says to the daughters of men!
SECTION 5.4.

I do not intend to discuss every writer who has taken up the subject of female manners — that would in fact merely mean treading old ground, since in general they have all written in the same strain. But in attacking man’s much-boasted prerogative — which may emphatically be called the iron sceptre of tyranny, the original sin of tyrants — I declare my opposition to all power that rests on prejudices, however ancient.

If the submission demanded rests on justice, no appeal to any higher power is possible — for God is justice itself. So let us, as children of the same parent (unless being the younger born makes us bastards), reason together, and learn to yield to reason’s authority whenever her voice can be distinctly heard. But suppose it is shown that this throne of prerogative stands merely on a chaotic heap of prejudices with no inherent principle of order binding them together, or on an elephant, a tortoise, or even the mighty shoulders of a son of the earth. Then whoever dares to face the consequences may break free without failing in any duty, and without sinning against the order of things.

While reason raises man above the brutish herd, and death is pregnant with promises, only those who have no confidence in their own strength are subject to blind authority. “They are free who will be free!”*
(*Footnote. “He is the free man, whom TRUTH makes free!” Cowper.)

The being who can govern itself has nothing to fear in life; but if anything is dearer to it than its own self-respect, the price must be paid to the last penny. Virtue, like everything of value, must be loved for her own sake alone, or she will not come to dwell with us. She will not grant that peace “which passeth understanding,” when she is merely used as stilts for reputation and observed with pharisaical exactness, because “honesty is the best policy.”

It cannot be denied that the plan of life which enables us to carry some knowledge and virtue into another world is the one best designed to secure contentment in this one; yet few people act on this principle, though everyone agrees that it is beyond dispute. Present pleasure, or present power, sweeps these sober convictions aside; and it is for the day, not for life, that man strikes his bargain with happiness. How few! how very few! have enough foresight or resolve to endure a small evil in the moment in order to avoid a greater one later.

Woman especially, whose virtue* rests on mutual prejudices, rarely reaches such greatness of mind; and so, enslaved to her own feelings, she is easily subdued by other people’s. Degraded like this, her reason — her misty reason! — serves to polish her chains rather than snap them.
(*Footnote. I mean to use a word that covers more than chastity, the sexual virtue.)
I have listened with indignation to women arguing along the same lines as men, and adopting the sentiments that brutalize them with all the stubbornness of ignorance.
Let me support what I say with a few examples. Mrs. Piozzi, who frequently repeated by rote things she did not understand, steps up with sentences rolled out in the style of Dr. Johnson.

“Seek not for happiness in singularity; and dread a refinement of wisdom as a deviation into folly.” So she dogmatically lectures a newly married man; and to explain this pompous opening, she adds, “I said that the person of your lady would not grow more pleasing to you, but pray let her never suspect that it grows less so: that a woman will pardon an affront to her understanding much sooner than one to her person, is well known; nor will any of us contradict the assertion. All our attainments, all our arts, are employed to gain and keep the heart of man; and what mortification can exceed the disappointment, if the end be not obtained: There is no reproof however pointed, no punishment however severe, that a woman of spirit will not prefer to neglect; and if she can endure it without complaint, it only proves that she means to make herself amends by the attention of others for the slights of her husband!”

Here are genuinely masculine sentiments. “All our ARTS are employed to gain and keep the heart of man:” — and what follows? — if her person should be neglected (and has any person, even one shaped with the proportions of the Medici Venus, ever escaped being slighted?), she will console herself by trying to please other men. Noble morality! Yet this is how the understanding of the entire sex is insulted, and how their virtue is stripped of the common foundation of all virtue. A woman ought to know that her husband cannot find her person as pleasing as her lover once did; and if she takes offence at him for being a human creature, she might as well whine over losing his heart as over any other foolish thing. Indeed, this very lack of discernment, or this unreasonable anger, shows that he was unable to turn his doting on her person into affection for her virtues or respect for her understanding.

As long as women profess such opinions and live by them, their understandings, at least, deserve the contempt and abuse which men — men WHO NEVER insult their persons — have pointedly directed at the female mind. And vain women thoughtlessly take up the sentiments of exactly these polite men, who have no wish to be encumbered with mind. They ought to realize, however, that only the reason they insult can throw around their persons that SACRED reserve which makes human affections (and human affections always carry some base alloy) as lasting as is consistent with the grand purpose of existence — namely, the attainment of virtue.

The Baroness de Stael speaks the same language as the lady I have just quoted, only with more enthusiasm. Her eulogy of Rousseau happened to fall into my hands, and her sentiments — which are shared by too many of my sex — may serve as the text for a few comments. “Though Rousseau,” she observes, “has endeavoured to prevent women from interfering in public affairs, and acting a brilliant part in the theatre of politics; yet, in speaking of them, how much has he done it to their satisfaction! If he wished to deprive them of some rights, foreign to their sex, how has he for ever restored to them all those to which it has a claim! And in attempting to diminish their influence over the deliberations of men, how sacredly has he established the empire they have over their happiness! In aiding them to descend from an usurped throne, he has firmly seated them upon that to which they were destined by nature; and though he be full of indignation against them when they endeavour to resemble men, yet when they come before him with all THE CHARMS WEAKNESSES, VIRTUES, and ERRORS, OF their sex, his respect for their PERSONS amounts almost to adoration.” Quite true! — for no sensualist ever worshipped more fervently at the shrine of beauty. His reverence for the person was so devout, in fact, that apart from the virtue of chastity, for obvious reasons, he wanted to see it decorated with nothing but charms, weaknesses and errors. He feared that the severity of reason might upset the soft playfulness of love. The master wanted a meretricious slave to caress, wholly dependent on his reason and his generosity; he had no wish for a companion whom he would be obliged to esteem, or for a friend to whom he could entrust his children’s education should death take their father from them before he had completed that sacred task. He denies woman reason, bars her from knowledge and steers her away from truth; yet he is forgiven, because “he admits the passion of love.” It would take some ingenuity to explain why women should feel so indebted to him for admitting love on these terms, when he plainly admits it only to give men relaxation and to continue the species; but he wrote with passion, and that powerful spell worked on the sensibility of a young admirer. “What signifies it,” this rhapsodist goes on, “to women, that his reason disputes with them the empire, when his heart is devotedly theirs.” What women ought to contend for is not empire but equality. Yet even if all they wanted was to prolong their reign, they should not rely wholly on their persons; for although beauty may win a heart, it cannot hold it — not even while the beauty is in full bloom — unless the mind contributes at least some graces.

Once women are enlightened enough to see where their real interest lies, on a grand scale, I am convinced they will readily give up every prerogative of love that is not mutual (speaking of these as lasting prerogatives) in return for the calm satisfaction of friendship and the tender trust that comes from habitual esteem. They will neither put on insolent airs before marriage nor grovel in submission afterwards; instead, trying to behave as reasonable creatures in both situations, they will avoid being tumbled from a throne onto a stool.

Madame Genlis has written several entertaining books for children, and her letters on education contain many useful suggestions which sensible parents will certainly make use of; but her outlook is narrow, and her prejudices are as unreasonable as they are strong.

I shall pass over her vehement argument that punishment in the next life is eternal, since I blush to think that any human being should argue vehemently for such a cause; I shall merely make a few remarks on the absurd way she lets parental authority take the place of reason. For everywhere she preaches not only BLIND submission to parents, but submission to the opinion of the world as well.*

(*Footnote. A person is not to act in this or that way, even when convinced that doing so is right, because some ambiguous circumstances might lead the world to SUSPECT different motives. This is sacrificing the substance for the shadow. If people will simply watch their own hearts and act rightly as far as they are able to judge, they can wait patiently for the world’s opinion to come round. It is best to be guided by a single motive — for justice has too often been sacrificed to propriety — which is just another word for convenience.)

She tells the story of a young man who, at his father’s express wish, becomes engaged to a girl with a fortune. Before the wedding can take place the girl loses her fortune and is cast friendless upon the world. The father resorts to the most infamous tricks to part his son from her; and when the son uncovers his villainy and, obeying the call of honour, marries the girl, nothing follows but misery — because, if you please, he married WITHOUT his father’s consent. What ground is left for religion or morality to stand on, when justice is flouted like this? In the same spirit she portrays an accomplished young woman as willing to marry anyone her MAMMA saw fit to recommend, and as actually marrying the young man of her own choice without any stirrings of passion, since a well-educated girl had no time to fall in love. Can anyone have much respect for a system of education that insults reason and nature in this way?

Her writings contain many similar opinions, mixed with sentiments that do credit to her head and heart. Yet her religion is so mingled with superstition, and her morality with worldly wisdom, that I would not let a young person read her books unless I could discuss the subjects with them afterwards and point out the contradictions.

Mrs. Chapone’s Letters show such good sense and unaffected humility, and offer so many useful observations, that I mention them only to pay their worthy author this tribute of respect. I cannot, admittedly, always share her opinions; but I always respect her.

The very word respect calls Mrs. Macaulay to mind — without doubt the most able woman this country has ever produced. And yet this woman was allowed to die without her memory receiving the respect it deserved.

Posterity, however, will do her more justice, and will remember that Catharine Macaulay was living proof of intellectual attainments thought to be incompatible with the weakness of her sex. In her style of writing, indeed, no sex is visible; like the sense it expresses, it is strong and clear.

I will not call hers a masculine understanding, because I refuse to allow so arrogant a claim to reason; but I maintain that it was a sound one, and that her judgment, the ripened fruit of deep thought, proved that a woman can acquire judgment in the fullest sense of the word. Having more penetration than shrewdness, and more understanding than imagination, she writes with sober energy and closely reasoned argument; yet sympathy and benevolence lend her sentiments interest, and give her arguments that living warmth which compels the reader to weigh them.*
(*Footnote. Since I share Mrs. Macaulay’s opinions on many branches of education, I refer the reader to her valuable work rather than quote her views in support of mine.)

When I first thought of writing these criticisms, I looked forward to Mrs. Macaulay’s approval with a little of that hopeful eagerness which it has been the business of my life to repress; but I soon learned — with the sick pang of disappointed hope, and the still seriousness of regret — that she was no more!
SECTION 5.5.

In reviewing the various works written on education, I cannot pass over Lord Chesterfield’s Letters in silence. Not that I intend to analyse his unmanly, immoral system, or even to gather any of the useful, shrewd remarks scattered through his frivolous correspondence — no, I only mean to reflect briefly on what they openly aim at: the art of gaining an early knowledge of the world. It is an art, I will venture to assert, that feeds in secret, like the worm in the bud, on the unfolding powers, and turns to poison the generous sap which ought to rise vigorously through the young frame, inspiring warm affections and great resolutions.

There is a reason for everything, says the wise man; and who would look for the fruits of autumn in the mild months of spring? But this is mere rhetoric, and I intend to reason with those worldly-wise instructors who, instead of training the judgment, implant prejudices, and harden a heart that gradual experience would merely have cooled. To my mind, an early acquaintance with human failings — or what is called knowledge of the world — is the surest way to shrink the heart and dampen that natural ardour of youth which gives rise not only to great talents but to great virtues. For the vain attempt to produce the fruit of experience before the sapling has put out its leaves only drains its strength and stops it from growing into a natural shape; just as the shape and strength of metals as they settle are damaged when the attraction of cohesion is disturbed. Tell me, you who have studied the human mind, is it not an odd way to fix principles, to show young people that principles are rarely stable? And how can habits fortify them, when example proves those habits to be deceptive? Why must the ardour of youth be damped like this, and the richness of imagination cut to the quick? Such dry caution may, admittedly, shield a character from worldly mishaps; but it will certainly rule out excellence in either virtue or knowledge. The stumbling-block that suspicion lays across every path will prevent any vigorous effort of genius or benevolence, and life will be robbed of its most alluring charm long before its calm evening, when man ought to withdraw into contemplation for comfort and support.

A young man who has been raised among friends at home, and encouraged to fill his mind with as much speculative knowledge as can be gained from reading and from the natural reflections prompted by youthful bursts of high spirits and by instinctive feelings, will go out into the world with warm and mistaken expectations. But this seems to be the course of nature; and in morals, as in matters of taste, we should heed her sacred signs, and not presume to lead where we ought humbly to follow.

In the world, few people act on principle; present feelings and early habits are the chief motives. But how deadened the former would be, and how the latter would turn into corroding iron fetters, if young people were shown the world exactly as it is, before any knowledge of mankind or of their own hearts, slowly gained through experience, had taught them forbearance! Their fellow creatures would then not be seen as frail beings like themselves, condemned to struggle with human failings, showing now the bright and now the dark side of their characters, and drawing from us love and disgust by turns; instead, they would be guarded against like beasts of prey, until every broad social feeling — in a word, humanity — was rooted out.

In life, by contrast, as we gradually discover the imperfections of our nature, we discover virtues as well; and when we mix with our fellow creatures and look at the same things they do, all sorts of circumstances bind us to them which are never considered by those who acquire a hasty, unnatural knowledge of the world. We watch a folly swell into a vice by almost imperceptible degrees, and we pity even as we blame; but if the hideous monster burst upon our sight all at once, fear and disgust, making us harsher than man ought to be, might lead us in blind zeal to usurp the role of the Almighty and condemn our fellow mortals to damnation — forgetting that we cannot read the heart, and that the seeds of the same vices lie hidden in our own.

I have already remarked that we expect more from instruction than instruction alone can achieve: for instead of preparing young people to meet the evils of life with dignity, and to gain wisdom and virtue by using their own faculties, we pile precept upon precept and demand blind obedience, when conviction ought to be brought home to their reason.

Suppose, for example, that a young person in the first ardour of friendship idolizes the beloved one — what harm can this mistaken, enthusiastic attachment do? Perhaps virtue must first appear in human form in order to impress young hearts; the ideal model, which a more mature and elevated mind looks up to and fashions for itself, would be beyond their sight. How can a man who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, love God? asked the wisest of men.

It is natural for the young to credit the first object of their affection with every good quality; and the emulation born of ignorance — or, more properly, of inexperience — draws out the mind that is capable of such an affection. Then, as time passes and perfection proves to be beyond mortal reach, virtue in the abstract comes to seem beautiful, and wisdom sublime. Admiration then yields to friendship in the true sense, because it is bound together by esteem; and the person walks alone, relying on heaven alone for that eager, emulous longing for perfection which always glows in a noble mind. But a man must gain this knowledge by exerting his own faculties; and this is surely the blessed fruit of disappointed hope! For He who delights in spreading happiness and showing mercy to the weak creatures who are learning to know him never planted a good inclination in us to be a tormenting will-o’-the-wisp.

We now let our trees spread with wild luxuriance, and do not expect to force the majestic marks of age upon youthful graces; we wait patiently until they have sent their roots deep and weathered many a storm. Is the mind, then, which advances towards perfection more slowly the greater its dignity, to be treated with less respect? To argue by analogy, everything around us is in a state of progress; and when an unwelcome knowledge of life brings something close to weariness of it, and the natural course of things shows us that all that is done under the sun is vanity, we are approaching the solemn close of the drama. The days of activity and hope are past, and the opportunities the first stage of existence has offered for rising in the scale of intelligence must soon be added up. A knowledge of the futility of life at this stage — or earlier, if experience has taught it — is very useful, because it is natural; but when a frail being is shown the follies and vices of man so that he may learn to guard prudently against the ordinary accidents of life by sacrificing his heart, it is surely not too harsh to call this the wisdom of this world, as opposed to the nobler fruit of piety and experience.

I will venture a paradox and state my opinion without reserve: if men were born only to complete a circle of life and death, it would be wise to take every step foresight could suggest to make life happy. Moderation in every pursuit would then be the highest wisdom; and the prudent pleasure-seeker might enjoy a fair measure of contentment, even though he neither cultivated his understanding nor kept his heart pure. If we were merely mortal, prudence would be true wisdom — or, more precisely, it would secure the greatest share of happiness over the whole of life; but any knowledge beyond the conveniences of life would be a curse.

Why should we ruin our health with close study? The exalted pleasure that intellectual pursuits give would hardly make up for the hours of lethargy that follow — especially if we must also count the doubts and disappointments that cloud our inquiries. Every inquiry ends in vanity and vexation: for the cause we most wanted to discover retreats before us like the horizon as we advance. The ignorant, on the other hand, are like children, who suppose that if they could only walk straight ahead they would eventually reach the place where the earth meets the clouds. Yet, disappointed as we are in our inquiries, the mind grows stronger through the exercise — strong enough, perhaps, to grasp the answers it may receive, at another stage of existence, to the anxious questions it asked when the understanding, on feeble wings, was fluttering around visible effects in the hope of plunging into the hidden cause.

The passions too, the winds of life, would be useless, if not harmful, if the matter that makes up our thinking being, once we had thought in vain, merely went to sustain plant life — to nourish a cabbage, or to blush in a rose. The appetites would then serve every earthly purpose, and yield a more moderate and lasting happiness. But the powers of the soul, which are of little use here and probably disturb our animal pleasures even while a sense of our own dignity makes us glory in them, prove that life is merely an education, a state of infancy, and that its only hopes worth cherishing must not be sacrificed. My conclusion, therefore, is that we ought to know precisely what we want education to achieve; for the immortality of the soul is contradicted by the conduct of many people who firmly profess to believe in it.

If your first concern is to secure comfort and prosperity on earth, leaving the future to take care of itself, you are acting prudently when you give your child an early insight into the weaknesses of his nature. You may not, admittedly, turn him into an Inkle; but do not imagine that someone who absorbed a low opinion of human nature very early will keep to more than the letter of the law, or will feel any need to rise much above the common standard. He may avoid gross vices, since honesty is the best policy; but he will never aim at great virtues. The example of writers and artists will illustrate this point.

I must therefore venture to doubt whether what has passed for an axiom in morals may not be a dogmatic assertion made by men who have coolly observed mankind through the medium of books; and I say, in flat contradiction to them, that regulating the passions is not always wisdom. On the contrary, it would appear that one reason why men have better judgment and more fortitude than women is undoubtedly this: that they give freer rein to the grand passions, and, by going astray more often, broaden their minds. If, then, by using their own reason, they settle on some stable principle, they probably owe it to the force of their passions — passions fed by FALSE views of life and allowed to leap the boundary that secures contentment. But if at the dawn of life we could soberly survey the scenes ahead as though in perspective, and see everything in its true colours, how could the passions ever grow strong enough to unfold the faculties?

Let me now, as if from a height, look out over the world stripped of all its false and deceptive charms. The clear air lets me see each object as it truly is, while my heart is still. I am as calm as the landscape on a morning when the mists, slowly lifting, silently reveal the beauties of nature, refreshed by rest.
How will the world look now? I rub my eyes and wonder whether, perhaps, I am only just waking from a vivid dream.

I see the sons and daughters of men chasing shadows, and anxiously squandering their powers to feed passions that have no adequate object — were it not that the very excess of these blind impulses, pampered by that lying yet ever-trusted guide, the imagination, prepares them for some other state and so makes short-sighted mortals wiser without their own consent; or, what amounts to the same thing, while they were pursuing some imaginary present good.

After looking at things in this light, it would not be too fanciful to imagine that this world is a stage on which a pantomime is performed every day for the entertainment of superior beings. How amused they would be to watch the ambitious man wearing himself out in the chase after a phantom, pursuing the bubble fame into “the cannon’s mouth” that was to blow him to nothing: for once consciousness is gone, it makes no difference whether we rise in a whirlwind or fall as rain. And if they took pity on him and sharpened his sight, and showed him the thorny path that led to eminence — a path that sinks like quicksand as he climbs, cheating his hopes just when they are almost within his grasp — would he not leave to others the honour of amusing them, and strive to make sure of the present moment, even though the constitution of his nature would make it far from easy to catch the flying stream? Such slaves are we to hope and fear!

But, futile as the ambitious man’s pursuit would be, he is often striving for something more substantial than fame — which would indeed be the most fleeting of meteors, the wildest will-o’-the-wisp that ever lured a man to ruin. What! give up the smallest gratification in order to be applauded after he is gone! Why this struggle, whether man is mortal or immortal, if that noble passion did not truly raise the being above his fellows?

And love! What comic scenes it would provide — Pantaloon’s tricks would have to give way to more outrageous folly. To watch a mortal deck out an object with imaginary charms, and then fall down and worship the idol he himself had set up — how ridiculous! But what serious consequences follow, robbing man of that share of happiness which the Deity, in calling him into existence, has undoubtedly promised him (or else on what can his attributes rest?); would not all the purposes of life have been far better served if he had felt only what has been called physical love? And would not the sight of the object, when not seen through the medium of the imagination, soon reduce the passion to an appetite — if reflection, man’s noble distinction, did not give it force and make it a means of raising him above this earthly dross, by teaching him to love the centre of all perfection! whose wisdom shows more and more clearly in the works of nature as reason is enlightened and exalted by contemplation, and by gaining that love of order which the struggles of passion produce?

It could be shown that the habit of reflection, and the knowledge gained by nurturing any passion, are equally useful, even though the object proves equally illusory; for all objects would look alike if they were not magnified by the ruling passion which the Author of all good has planted in us, in order to call out and strengthen the faculties of each individual, and to let it gain all the experience that an infant can gain who does certain things without knowing why.

I come down from my height and, mingling with my fellow creatures, feel myself swept along by the common current; ambition, love, hope and fear exert their usual power, even though reason convinces us that their present and most attractive promises are only lying dreams. But if the cold hand of caution had damped each generous feeling before it had left any lasting mark on the character, or formed some habit, what could we expect but selfish prudence, and a reason barely rising above instinct? Who that has read with a philosophical eye Dean Swift’s disgusting description of the Yahoos, and his insipid one of the Houyhnhnm, can fail to see how futile it is to degrade the passions, or to make man rest content?

The young man should ACT; for if he had the experience of a grey head, he would be fitter for death than for life. His virtues, living in his head rather than his heart, could produce nothing great, and his understanding, trained for this world, would not show by any noble flights that it had a claim to a better one.

Besides, it is impossible to give a young person a true view of life; he must have wrestled with his own passions before he can gauge the strength of the temptation that led his brother into vice. Those who are setting out in life and those who are leaving it look at the world from such very different standpoints that they can rarely think alike — unless the unfledged reason of the young has never attempted a flight of its own.

When we hear of some daring crime, it strikes us full on, in the deepest shade of wickedness, and stirs our indignation; but the eye that watched the darkness gradually deepen must regard it with more compassionate forbearance. No unmoved spectator can see the world; we must mix in the crowd and feel as men feel before we can judge their feelings. In short, if we mean to live in the world so as to grow wiser and better, and not merely to enjoy life’s good things, we must come to know others at the same time as we come to know ourselves — knowledge gained in any other way only hardens the heart and confuses the understanding.

I may be told that knowledge gained in this way is sometimes bought too dearly. I can only reply that I very much doubt whether any knowledge can be acquired without labour and sorrow; and those who want to spare their children both should not complain if their children turn out neither wise nor virtuous. Their only aim was to make them prudent; and prudence, early in life, is nothing more than the wary craft of ignorant self-love. I have noticed that young people whose education received special attention have generally been very shallow and conceited, and not at all pleasing in any respect, because they had neither the trusting warmth of youth nor the cool depth of age. I cannot help blaming this unnatural character chiefly on that hasty, premature instruction which leads them to parrot, presumptuously, all the crude notions they have taken on trust; so that the careful education they received makes them lifelong slaves to prejudice.

Mental exertion, like physical exertion, is irksome at first — so much so that most people would gladly let others do both their working and their thinking for them. An observation I have often made will make my meaning clear. When, in a gathering of strangers or acquaintances, a person of moderate abilities asserts an opinion heatedly, I will venture to say — for I have very often traced the fact to its source — that it is a prejudice. These echoes hold the understanding of some relative or friend in high regard, and, without fully grasping the opinions they are so eager to peddle, they defend them with a stubbornness that would astonish even the person who first devised them.

I know that a certain fashion for respecting prejudices now prevails; and when anyone dares to confront them, though moved by humanity and armed with reason, he is asked with disdain whether his ancestors were fools. No, I would answer; opinions of every kind were probably all considered at first, and were therefore founded on some reason; yet, naturally enough, that reason was quite often a local expedient rather than a fundamental principle that would hold good at all times. But moss-covered opinions take on the misshapen form of prejudices when they are lazily adopted merely because age has given them a venerable look, even though the reason on which they were built has ceased to be a reason, or can no longer be traced. Why should we love prejudices simply because they are prejudices? A prejudice is a doting, obstinate conviction for which we can give no reason; for the moment a reason can be given for an opinion, it stops being a prejudice, though it may still be an error of judgment. Are we then advised to cherish opinions only in order to defy reason? This way of arguing, if it deserves to be called arguing, reminds me of what is commonly called a woman’s reason. For women sometimes declare that they love or believe certain things BECAUSE they love or believe them.

It is impossible to have a useful conversation with people who, in this manner, only ever say yes or no. Before you can bring them to a point from which you can fairly begin, you have to go back to the simple principles that existed before power spread its prejudices abroad; and it is ten to one that you will be halted by the philosophical claim that certain principles are as false in practice as they are true in the abstract. Indeed, one may infer that reason has whispered some doubts; for people generally assert their opinions most heatedly just when they begin to waver: trying to drive out their own doubts by convincing their opponent, they grow angry when those gnawing doubts are flung back to prey upon them.

The truth is that men expect from education what education cannot give. A wise parent or tutor can strengthen the body and sharpen the tools with which the child is to gather knowledge; but the honey must be the reward of the individual’s own industry. It is almost as absurd to try to make a youth wise through another person’s experience as to expect the body to grow strong through exercise that is only talked about or watched.

Many of the children whose conduct has been most closely watched grow into the weakest men, because their instructors merely instil certain notions into their minds that rest on nothing but the instructors’ authority; and if the children love or respect them, the mind is cramped in its efforts and hesitant in its progress. In this case the business of education is only to guide the shooting tendrils to a proper pole; yet after heaping precept upon precept, without letting a child form any judgment of its own, parents expect their children to act by this borrowed, deceptive light just as if they had kindled it themselves, and to be, when they enter life, what their parents are at its close. They forget that a tree, and even the human body, does not strengthen its fibres until it has reached its full growth.

Something similar seems to hold for the mind. During childhood and youth, the senses and the imagination shape the character; and as life goes on, the understanding lends firmness to the first fair intentions of sensibility — until, with virtue springing from the clear conviction of reason rather than from the impulse of the heart, morality comes to rest on a rock against which the storms of passion beat in vain.

I hope I shall not be misunderstood when I say that religion will not have this consolidating force unless it is grounded in reason. If it is merely a refuge for weakness or for wild fanaticism, and not a governing principle of conduct drawn from self-knowledge and a rational understanding of God’s attributes, what can we expect it to produce? The religion that consists in warming the feelings and exalting the imagination is only its poetic part, and may give the individual pleasure without making it a more moral being. It may replace worldly pursuits, yet narrow the heart rather than enlarge it: but virtue must be loved as sublime and excellent in itself, and not for the benefits it brings or the evils it wards off, if any high degree of excellence is to be expected. Men will not become moral while they merely build castles in the air in a future world to make up for the disappointments they meet in this one — if they turn their thoughts away from their duties to one another towards religious reveries.

Most prospects in life are spoiled by the shuffling worldly wisdom of men who, forgetting that they cannot serve God and mammon, try to combine things that contradict each other. If you want to make your son rich, take one course — if your only concern is to make him virtuous, you must take another; but do not imagine that you can jump from one road to the other without losing your way.*
(*Footnote. See an excellent essay on this subject by Mrs. Barbauld, in Miscellaneous pieces in Prose.)

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Effect Which an Early Association of Ideas Has Upon the Character
paragraphs: Given that women are educated in the enervating manner recommended by the writers I have been criticizing, and that their subordinate place in society gives them no chance to recover the ground they have lost, is it any wonder that everywhere they appear to be a defect in nature? When we consider how decisively an early association of ideas shapes the character, is it any wonder that they neglect their understandings and give all their attention to their persons?

The great advantages that naturally follow from stocking the mind with knowledge are obvious from the following considerations. The association of our ideas is either habitual or instantaneous, and the latter kind seems to depend on the original temperament of the mind rather than on the will. Once ideas and matters of fact have been taken in, they lie in reserve until some chance circumstance makes information received at very different periods of our lives dart into the mind with illuminating force. Many recollections are like a flash of lightning, one idea assimilating and explaining another with astonishing speed. I am not now referring to that quick perception of truth which is so intuitive that it defies investigation, and leaves us at a loss to decide whether it is memory or reasoning, lost to sight in its swiftness, that opens the dark cloud. Over those instantaneous associations we have little power; for once the mind has been enlarged by wide-ranging flights or deep reflection, the raw materials will, to some degree, arrange themselves of their own accord. The understanding, it is true, may keep us from drawing out of proportion when we group our thoughts, or when we copy the warm sketches of fancy from the imagination; but the animal spirits, the individual character, supply the colouring. Over this subtle electric fluid,* how little power we have, and how little power reason can gain over it! These fine, intractable spirits seem to be the essence of genius, and, beaming in its eagle eye, they produce in the highest degree that happy energy of associating thoughts which surprises, delights and instructs. These are the glowing minds that concentrate pictures for their fellow creatures, forcing them to view with interest objects, reflected from the impassioned imagination, which they had passed over in nature.

(*Footnote. Sometimes, when in the mood to laugh at materialists, I have asked whether — since the most powerful effects in nature seem to be produced by fluids, the magnetic, etc. — the passions might not be fine volatile fluids enveloping humanity and holding its more refractory elementary parts together, or whether they were simply a liquid fire running through the more sluggish materials and giving them life and heat?)

Let me explain myself. Most people are unable to see or feel poetically; lacking imagination, they run from solitude in search of things their senses can grasp. But once an author lends them his eyes, they can see as he saw and take pleasure in images that lay before them but that they could not have singled out.

Education, then, only supplies the man of genius with knowledge that gives variety and contrast to his associations. But there is a habitual association of ideas, which grows “with our growth,” that has a great effect on the moral character of mankind, and which gives the mind a bent that usually remains throughout life. The understanding is so pliable, and yet so stubborn, that associations formed by chance circumstances during the years in which the body grows to maturity can seldom be disentangled by reason. One idea calls up another, its old associate, and memory, faithful to first impressions, especially when the intellectual powers are not employed to cool our sensations, retraces them with mechanical exactness.

Such habitual slavery to first impressions does more harm to the female character than to the male, since business and other dry work of the understanding tends to deaden the feelings and to break up associations that do violence to reason. Females, however, are made women while still mere children, and then brought back to childhood just when they ought to leave the baby-walker behind for good; so they lack the strength of mind to wipe away the artificial layers under which nature has been smothered.

Whatever they see or hear serves to fix impressions, stir emotions and link ideas in ways that give their minds a sexual character. Mistaken notions of beauty and delicacy stunt the growth of their limbs, producing a sickly tenderness instead of fineness of organs. Weakened like this, because they spend their energy unfolding the first associations that everything around them forces on them rather than examining them, how are they to gain the vigour required to throw off their artificial character? — where will they find the strength to turn back to reason and rise above a system of oppression that blights the fair promise of spring? This cruel association of ideas, which every influence conspires to weave into all their habits of thought — or, more precisely, of feeling — grows stronger once they begin to act a little on their own; for they then discover that pleasure and power are to be had only through their skill in arousing emotions in men. Moreover, every book written expressly to instruct them, making the first impression on their minds, instils the same opinions. Since they are educated in a bondage worse than Egypt’s, to reproach them for faults they can scarcely avoid is as unreasonable as it is cruel — unless we assume in them a native vigour that falls to the lot of very few among mankind.

The harshest sarcasms, for instance, have been directed at the sex, and women have been mocked for repeating “a set of phrases learnt by rote,” though nothing could be more natural, considering how they are educated, and that their “highest praise is to obey, unargued” — the will of man. If they are not granted reason enough to govern their own conduct — why, then everything they learn has to be learned by rote! And since all their ingenuity is spent on arranging their dress, “a passion for a scarlet coat” is so natural that it has never surprised me. And if we grant that Pope’s summary of their character is just, “that every woman is at heart a rake,” why should they be harshly condemned for looking for a kindred mind and preferring a rake to a man of sense?

Rakes know how to play on their sensibility, whereas the modest merit of reasonable men naturally affects their feelings less; such men cannot reach women’s hearts through the understanding, since the two have few sentiments in common.

To expect women to be more reasonable than men in their LIKINGS, while still denying them the free use of reason, seems a little absurd. When do men FALL IN LOVE with good sense? When do they, with all their superior powers and advantages, turn from the person to the mind? How can they then expect women — taught only to watch behaviour and to acquire manners rather than morals — to despise what they have toiled all their lives to attain? Where are women suddenly to find the judgment to weigh patiently the good sense of an awkward but virtuous man, whose manners, which they have been trained to judge critically, repel them, and whose conversation seems cold and dull because it is not made up of pretty repartees and well-turned compliments? If we are to admire or esteem anything for long, our curiosity must at least be roused by some knowledge of what we admire; we cannot judge the worth of qualities and virtues that lie beyond our comprehension. Such respect, where it is felt, may be very sublime, and the confused awareness of her own humility may, from some points of view, make the dependent creature an interesting object; but human love needs coarser ingredients, and the person will quite naturally claim its share — and it mostly claims an ample one!

Love is largely an arbitrary passion; like certain other stalking mischiefs, it rules by its own authority and does not deign to reason. It is also easily told apart from esteem, the foundation of friendship, because fleeting beauties and graces often arouse it — although, to give the feeling energy, something more solid must deepen their impression and set the imagination working, to make the fairest — the first good.

Ordinary qualities arouse ordinary passions. What men look for is beauty and the simper of good-humoured docility; what captivates women is an easy manner. A gentlemanly man seldom fails to please them; their thirsty ears eagerly drink in the insinuating nothings of politeness, while they turn from the unintelligible sounds of the charmer — reason, charm he never so wisely. In superficial accomplishments the rake certainly has the advantage, and of these women are able to judge, for this is their own ground. Since the whole tenor of their lives has made them gay and giddy, the mere look of wisdom, or the severe graces of virtue, must seem gloomy to them and impose a kind of restraint against which they — and love, that playful child — naturally rebel. Lacking taste, except of the lighter sort — for taste is born of judgment — how are they to discover that true beauty and grace must spring from the play of the mind? And how can anyone expect them to value in a lover what they themselves lack, or have only very imperfectly? In them the sympathy that joins hearts and invites confidence is so faint that it cannot catch fire and rise into passion. No, I say it again: the love such minds cherish must feed on coarser fuel!

The conclusion is plain. Until women are led to use their understandings, they should not be mocked for being attached to rakes, or even for being rakes at heart, since this seems the inevitable result of their education. Those whose life is to please must find their enjoyment, their happiness, in pleasure! It is a trite remark, but a true one, that we never do anything well unless we love it for its own sake.

Suppose for a moment, however, that at some future turn of time women were to become what I sincerely wish them to be: even love would then gain a more serious dignity and be refined in its own fires, and, as virtue lent true delicacy to their affections, they would turn from a rake in disgust. Reasoning as well as feeling — for feeling is at present woman’s only province — they could then easily guard themselves against outward graces, and they would soon learn to despise a sensibility that had been aroused, and made stale, among women whose trade was vice and by the wanton airs of allurement. They would bear in mind that the flame (one has to use the proper expressions) which they hoped to kindle had been burned out by lust, and that the sated appetite, having lost its taste for pure and simple pleasures, could be stirred only by the licentious arts of variety. What satisfaction could a woman of delicacy expect from a union with such a man, when the very guilelessness of her affection might strike him as insipid? Dryden describes the situation thus:
“Where love is duty on the female side, On theirs mere sensual gust, and sought with surly pride.”

But there is one great truth that women have yet to learn, though it matters greatly to them that they act on it. In choosing a husband they should not be led astray by the qualities of a lover — for a husband, even supposing him to be wise and virtuous, cannot long remain a lover.

If women were educated more rationally, and could take a more comprehensive view of things, they would be content to love only once in their lives, and after marriage calmly let passion subside into friendship — into that tender intimacy which is the best refuge from care, yet which is built on such pure, still affections that idle jealousies would not be allowed to disturb the discharge of the sober duties of life, nor to take up thoughts that ought to be employed otherwise. This is a state in which many men live, but few, very few, women. And the difference can easily be accounted for without resorting to a character peculiar to their sex. Men, for whom, we are told, women were made, have occupied women’s thoughts too much; and this association has so entangled love with all their motives of action that — to harp a little on an old string — having been employed solely either in preparing themselves to excite love or in actually putting their lessons into practice, they cannot live without love. But when a sense of duty, or fear of shame, obliges them to restrain this pampered desire to please beyond certain lengths — too far for delicacy, it is true, though far from criminality — they obstinately resolve to love their husbands (I speak of their passion) to the end of the chapter; and then, acting the part which they foolishly demanded of their lovers, they become abject wooers and doting slaves.

Men of wit and fancy are often rakes, and fancy is what love feeds on. Such men will inspire passion. In its present childish state, half the sex would pine for a Lovelace — so witty, so graceful, so brave a man; and do they DESERVE blame for acting on principles that are drummed into them so constantly? They want a lover and a protector — and there he kneels before them: bravery prostrate before beauty! So love pushes a husband’s virtues into the background, and bright hopes or lively emotions keep reflection at bay until the day of reckoning — which will surely come, turning the sprightly lover into a surly, suspicious tyrant who treats with contempt the very weakness he encouraged. Or suppose the rake reformed: old habits are not quickly shed. When a man of ability is first swept away by his passions, sentiment and taste are needed to varnish the enormities of vice and give zest to brutal indulgences; but once the gloss of novelty wears off and pleasure palls upon the senses, lasciviousness shows its bare face, and enjoyment is reduced to the desperate effort of weakness fleeing from reflection as from a legion of devils. Oh, virtue, you are no empty name! All that life can give — you give!

If much comfort cannot be expected from the friendship of a reformed rake of superior abilities, what follows when he lacks sense as well as principles? Truly, misery in its most hideous form. When the habits of weak people have been hardened by time, reform is barely possible, and it actually makes those beings miserable who have not mind enough to be amused by innocent pleasure. Like the tradesman who retires from the bustle of business, they find that nature presents them with nothing but a universal blank, and their restless thoughts prey on their dampened spirits. Their reformation, like his retirement, actually makes them wretched, because it deprives them of all employment by quenching the hopes and fears that set their sluggish minds in motion.

If habit has such force, if folly holds us in such bondage, then how carefully we should guard the mind from storing up vicious associations! And we should take equal care to cultivate the understanding, to rescue the poor creature from the weak, dependent condition of even harmless ignorance. For only the right use of reason makes us independent of everything — except the unclouded Reason, “Whose service is perfect freedom.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Modesty. Comprehensively Considered, and Not as a Sexual Virtue
paragraphs: Modesty! Sacred child of sensibility and reason! True delicacy of mind! May I presume, without blame, to inquire into your nature, and to trace to its hidden source the gentle charm that softens every harsh feature of a character and makes lovely what would otherwise inspire only cold admiration? You who smooth the wrinkles of wisdom, and soften the tone of the loftier virtues until they all melt into humanity! You who spread the airy cloud around love, heightening every beauty it half conceals, and breathing out those shy sweetnesses that steal into the heart and charm the senses — shape for me the language of persuasive reason, until I rouse my sex from the bed of flowers on which they lie idly sleeping their lives away!

When discussing the association of our ideas, I pointed out two distinct ways in which it works; and in defining modesty, it seems to me just as proper to separate two things. One is the purity of mind that chastity produces. The other is a simplicity of character that leads us to judge ourselves fairly, as far from vanity as from presumption, though by no means at odds with a lofty sense of our own dignity. Taken in this second meaning, modesty is that sobriety of mind which teaches a man not to think more highly of himself than he ought to think. It should be kept distinct from humility, since humility is a kind of self-abasement. A modest man often conceives a great plan and clings to it tenaciously, aware of his own strength, until success confers a sanction on it that settles its character. Milton was not arrogant when he let slip a judgment of his own that later proved a prophecy; nor was General Washington when he accepted command of the American forces. Washington has always been described as a modest man; yet had he been merely humble, he would probably have shrunk back irresolute, afraid to entrust himself with the direction of an enterprise on which so much depended.

A modest man is steady, a humble man timid, and a vain one presumptuous: this is the judgment that observing many characters has led me to form. Jesus Christ was modest, Moses was humble, and Peter vain.

Having thus distinguished modesty from humility on the one side, I do not mean to confuse it with bashfulness on the other. Bashfulness is in fact so distinct from modesty that the most bashful girl, or the rawest country lout, often becomes the most impudent; for their bashfulness is merely the instinctive timidity of ignorance, and habit soon turns it into brazen self-assurance.*

(*Footnote. “Such is the country-maiden’s fright, When first a red-coat is in sight; Behind the door she hides her face, Next time at distance eyes the lace: She now can all his terrors stand, Nor from his squeeze withdraws her hand, She plays familiar in his arms, And every soldier hath his charms; From tent to tent she spreads her flame; For custom conquers fear and shame.”)

The shameless behaviour of the prostitutes who crowd the streets of London, stirring pity and disgust by turns, may serve to illustrate this remark. They trample on maidenly bashfulness with a kind of bravado and, glorying in their shame, become more boldly lewd than men ever appear to be, however depraved — men to whom this sexual quality has not been gratuitously assigned. But these poor ignorant wretches never had any modesty to lose when they gave themselves up to infamy; for modesty is a virtue, not a quality. No, they were only bashful, shamefaced innocents; and when they lost their innocence, their shamefacedness was roughly rubbed away. A virtue, had it been sacrificed to passion, would have left some traces in the mind, making us respect the grand ruin.

Purity of mind, or that genuine delicacy which is the only virtuous support of chastity, is closely related to that refinement of humanity which is never found except in cultivated minds. It is something nobler than innocence: it is the delicacy of reflection, not the coyness of ignorance. The reserve of reason, which, like habitual cleanliness, is seldom seen in any great degree unless the soul is active, can easily be told apart from rustic shyness or wanton skittishness; and far from being incompatible with knowledge, it is knowledge’s fairest fruit. What a gross idea of modesty the writer of the following remark had! “‘The lady who asked the question whether women may be instructed in the modern system of botany, consistently with female delicacy?’ was accused of ridiculous prudery: nevertheless, if she had proposed the question to me, I should certainly have answered — They cannot.” So the fair book of knowledge is to be shut with an everlasting seal! On reading similar passages I have reverently lifted up my eyes and heart to Him who lives for ever and ever, and said: O my Father, have You, by the very constitution of her nature, forbidden Your child to seek You in the fair forms of truth? And can her soul be sullied by the knowledge that solemnly calls her to You?

I have then pursued these reflections philosophically until I concluded that the women who have most developed their reason must have the most modesty — though a dignified composure of bearing may have replaced the playful, bewitching bashfulness of youth.*
(*Footnote. Modesty is the graceful, calm virtue of maturity; bashfulness, the charm of lively youth.)

This, then, is how I have argued. If chastity is to be the virtue from which unaffected modesty naturally flows, attention must be drawn away from occupations that exercise nothing but the sensibility, and the heart must be taught to beat in time with humanity instead of throbbing with love. A woman who has given a large share of her time to purely intellectual pursuits, and whose affections have been exercised by humane and useful plans, must, as a natural consequence, possess more purity of mind than those ignorant beings whose hours and thoughts are filled with gay pleasures or schemes for conquering hearts. Regulating outward behaviour is not modesty, though those who study the rules of decorum are, in general, called modest women. Make the heart clean; let it open out and feel for everything human, instead of being narrowed by selfish passions; let the mind often turn to subjects that exercise the understanding without inflaming the imagination — and unaffected modesty will put the finishing touches to the picture.

She who can make out the dawn of immortality in the streaks of light that shoot across the misty night of ignorance, promising a clearer day, will respect as a sacred temple the body that houses a soul capable of such improvement. True love, too, spreads this kind of mysterious sanctity around the beloved, making the lover most modest in her presence. Affection is so reserved that, in receiving or returning physical endearments, it wishes not only to avoid the human eye, as a kind of profanation, but to spread around itself a cloudy obscurity that shuts out even the impudent, sparkling sunbeams. Yet an affection does not deserve to be called chaste unless it takes on a sublime shade of tender melancholy, which lets the mind stand still for a moment and enjoy the present satisfaction, when a sense of the Divine presence is felt — for this must always be the food of joy!

As I have always liked to trace any prevailing custom back to its source in nature, I have often thought that the respect for relics, so much abused by selfish priests, was born of a feeling of affection for whatever had touched the person of an absent or lost friend. Devotion, or love, may be allowed to make the garments sacred as well as the person; for a lover must lack imagination who does not feel a sort of sacred respect for his mistress’s glove or slipper. He could not confuse them with ordinary things of the same kind.

This fine feeling, perhaps, would not bear analysis by the experimental philosopher — but of such stuff is human rapture made! A shadowy phantom glides before us, hiding every other object; yet when the soft cloud is grasped, the form melts into common air, leaving a lonely emptiness, or a sweet perfume stolen from the violet, which memory holds dear for a long time. But I have stumbled unawares onto fairy ground, feeling the mild breeze of spring stealing over me, though November frowns.

As a sex, women are more chaste than men; and since modesty is the effect of chastity, they may deserve to have this virtue attributed to them in a rather special sense. Yet I must be allowed to add a hesitant “if”: for I doubt whether chastity will produce modesty — though it may produce propriety of conduct — when it is merely a respect for the world’s opinion, and when flirtation and the lovesick tales of novelists occupy the thoughts. Indeed, experience and reason would lead me to expect more modesty among men than among women, simply because men exercise their understandings more than women do.

But as regards propriety of behaviour, women, with the exception of one class, clearly have the advantage. What can be more disgusting than that impudent dross of gallantry, thought so manly, which makes many men stare insultingly at every woman they meet? Is this respect for the sex? Such loose behaviour shows so much habitual depravity and such weakness of mind that it is useless to expect much public or private virtue until both men and women grow more modest — until men, curbing a sensual fondness for the sex, or an affectation of manly assurance (more properly, impudence), treat one another with respect, unless appetite or passion gives their behaviour its own particular tone. I mean even respect for the person — the modest respect of humanity and fellow-feeling; not the lustful mockery of gallantry, nor the insolent condescension of the protector.

To carry the observation further still, modesty must wholeheartedly disown, and refuse to live alongside, that debauchery of mind which leads a man coolly and without a blush to bring out indecent allusions or obscene witticisms in the presence of a fellow creature. Women are now out of the question, for in their presence it is brutality. Respect for man as man is the foundation of every noble sentiment. How much more modest is the libertine who obeys the call of appetite or fancy than the lewd joker who sets the table roaring with laughter!

This is one of the many cases in which the sexual distinction regarding modesty has proved fatal to virtue and happiness. It is, however, carried further still: woman, weak woman, made the slave of sensibility by her education, is required to resist that sensibility on the most trying occasions. “Can any thing,” says Knox, “be more absurd than keeping women in a state of ignorance, and yet so vehemently to insist on their resisting temptation?” Thus, when virtue or honour makes it proper to check a passion, the burden is thrown onto the weaker shoulders, contrary to reason and true modesty, which ought at least to make the self-denial mutual — to say nothing of the generosity of courage, supposed to be a manly virtue.

Rousseau’s and Dr. Gregory’s advice about modesty — strangely misnamed! — runs in the same vein; for they both want a wife to leave it in doubt whether sensibility or weakness led her into her husband’s arms. The woman who can let the shadow of such a doubt rest on her husband’s mind for a moment is immodest.

But let me put the subject in a different light. The lack of modesty, which I chiefly deplore as destructive of morality, arises from the state of warfare between the sexes that voluptuous men so strenuously uphold as the very essence of modesty, though it is in fact its bane. For this warfare is a refinement of sensual desire into which men fall who have not virtue enough to enjoy the innocent pleasures of love. A man of delicacy carries his notions of modesty further still, for neither weakness nor sensibility will satisfy him — he looks for affection.

Again: men boast of their triumphs over women. What do they boast of? Truly, that the creature of sensibility was surprised by her sensibility into folly — into vice;* and the dreadful reckoning falls heavily on her own weak head when reason wakes. For where are you to find comfort, forlorn and disconsolate one? He who ought to have guided your reason and supported your weakness has betrayed you! In a dream of passion you consented to wander through flowery meadows, and, heedlessly stepping over the precipice to which your guide lured you instead of guarding you from it, you start out of your dream only to face a sneering, frowning world, and to find yourself alone in a wilderness; for he who triumphed in your weakness is now pursuing new conquests. But for you — there is no redemption this side of the grave! And what resource do you have in an enfeebled mind to raise a sinking heart?
(*Footnote. The poor moth, fluttering round a candle, burns its wings.)

But if the sexes really are to live in a state of warfare, if nature has marked it out for them, let men at least act nobly, or let pride whisper to them that the victory is base when all they overcome is sensibility. The real conquest is over affection that has not been taken by surprise — as when a woman, like Heloisa, deliberately gives up the whole world for love. I am not now weighing the wisdom or virtue of such a sacrifice; I only maintain that it was a sacrifice to affection, and not merely to sensibility, though sensibility had its share. And I must be allowed to call her a modest woman, before I leave this part of the subject with the remark that until men are more chaste, women will be immodest. Where, indeed, could modest women find husbands from whom they would not constantly turn away in disgust? Modesty must be cultivated equally by both sexes, or it will always remain a sickly hothouse plant, while the affectation of it — the fig leaf borrowed by wantonness — may add relish to voluptuous enjoyments.

Men will probably still insist that woman ought to have more modesty than man; but it is not dispassionate reasoners who will most eagerly oppose my opinion. No, it will be the men of fancy, the favourites of the sex, who outwardly respect and inwardly despise the weak creatures they toy with in this way. They cannot bring themselves to give up the highest sensual gratification, or even to acquire a taste for the refined pleasure of virtue — self-denial.
To look at the subject from another angle, I will confine my remarks to women.

The absurd falsehoods told to children out of mistaken notions of modesty tend very early to inflame their imaginations and set their little minds working on subjects that nature never meant them to think about until the body had reached some degree of maturity. At that stage the passions naturally begin to take over from the senses as the instruments that unfold the understanding and form the moral character.

It is in nurseries and boarding schools, I fear, that girls are first spoiled, and particularly in the latter. A number of girls sleep in the same room and wash together. Now, though I would be sorry to taint an innocent creature’s mind by instilling false delicacy, or those indecent prudish notions that early warnings about the other sex naturally breed, I would be very anxious to prevent their acquiring indelicate or immodest habits; and since many girls have learned very indelicate tricks from ignorant servants, mixing them together in this indiscriminate way is highly improper.

To tell the truth, women are in general too familiar with one another, and this leads to the gross degree of familiarity that so often makes married life unhappy. Why, in the name of decency, should sisters, close female friends, or ladies and their maids be so grossly familiar as to forget the respect that one human creature owes another? That squeamish delicacy which shrinks from the most disgusting tasks when affection or humanity leads us to watch at a sickbed is contemptible. But why women in good health should be more familiar with one another than men are, when they boast of their superior delicacy, is an inconsistency in manners that I have never been able to explain.

To preserve health and beauty, I would earnestly recommend frequent ablutions — to give my advice a dignified word so that it does not offend the fastidious ear. Girls ought to be taught, by example, to wash and dress alone, whatever their rank; and if habit should make them need a little help, let them not ask for it until that part of the business is over which ought never to be done in front of a fellow creature, because it is an insult to the majesty of human nature. I say this not on grounds of modesty but of decency; for the care some modest women take not to let their legs be seen, while making a display of that very care, is as childish as it is immodest.*

(*Footnote. I remember coming across a sentence in a book on education that made me smile. “It would be needless to caution you against putting your hand, by chance, under your neck-handkerchief; for a modest woman never did so!”)

I could go further still, and comment on some even more indelicate customs into which men never fall. Secrets are told where silence ought to reign; and that regard for cleanliness which some religious sects have perhaps carried too far — especially the Essenes among the Jews, who made an insult to God of what is only an insult to humanity — is violated in a brutal manner. How can DELICATE women force on others’ notice that part of our animal functions which is so very disgusting? And is it not quite rational to conclude that women who have not been taught to respect the human nature of their own sex in these particulars will not long respect the mere difference of sex in their husbands? Once their maidenly bashfulness is lost, I have in fact generally observed that women fall back into their old habits and treat their husbands as they treated their sisters or female acquaintances.

Besides, because their minds are not cultivated, women are very often driven by necessity to what I call, in plain terms, bodily wit; and their intimacies are of the same kind. In short, in both mind and body they are too intimate. The decent personal reserve that is the foundation of dignity of character must be kept up between women, or their minds will never gain strength or modesty.

For this reason, too, I object to shutting up many females together in nurseries, schools or convents. I cannot remember without indignation the jokes and tomboyish pranks that groups of young women indulged in when, in my youth, chance threw me, an awkward country girl, into their company. They were almost on a level with the double meanings that shake the dinner table when the wine has gone round freely. But it is useless to try to keep the heart pure unless the head is stocked with ideas and set to work comparing them, so as to acquire judgment by generalizing simple ideas, and modesty by letting the understanding dampen the sensibility.

It may be thought that I lay too much stress on personal reserve; but it is always the handmaid of modesty. So much so that if I were to name the graces that ought to adorn beauty, I would at once exclaim: cleanliness, neatness and personal reserve. It is obvious, I suppose, that the reserve I mean has nothing sexual in it, and that I think it EQUALLY necessary in both sexes. Indeed, that reserve and cleanliness which lazy women too often neglect are so necessary that I will venture to affirm this: when two or three women live in the same house, the one who pays this kind of habitual respect to her own person will be the most respected by the men of the family who live with them, leaving love entirely out of the question.

When members of a household meet in the morning, an affectionate seriousness will naturally prevail, especially if each is looking forward to carrying out the day’s duties. It may be thought fanciful, but this feeling has often risen spontaneously in my mind. After breathing the sweet, bracing morning air, I have been pleased to see the same kind of freshness in the faces I particularly loved; I was glad to see them braced, as it were, for the day, and ready to run their course with the sun. In this way the greetings of affection in the morning are more respectful than the familiar tenderness that often draws out the evening’s talk. Indeed, I have often felt hurt, not to say disgusted, when a friend whom I had left fully dressed the evening before appeared with her clothes thrown on anyhow, because she chose to indulge herself in bed until the last moment.

Domestic affection can be kept alive only by these neglected attentions. Yet if men and women took half as much trouble to be habitually neat in their dress as they take to ornament, or rather to disfigure, their persons, much would be done towards achieving purity of mind. But women dress only to gratify men of gallantry; for the lover is always best pleased with simple clothing that fits close to the figure. There is an impertinence in ornaments that repels affection, because love always clings to the idea of home.

As a sex, women are habitually indolent, and everything tends to make them so. I do not forget the bursts of activity that sensibility produces; but since these flights of feeling only make the evil worse, they are not to be confused with the slow, orderly walk of reason. In reality, their mental and bodily indolence is so great that until their bodies are strengthened and their understandings enlarged by active exertion, there is little reason to expect modesty to take the place of bashfulness. They may find it prudent to put on its appearance; but that fair veil will be worn only on holidays.

Perhaps there is no virtue that blends so kindly with every other as modesty does. It is the pale moonbeam that makes every virtue it softens more appealing, lending a mild grandeur to the narrowed horizon. Nothing can be more beautiful than the poetic fiction that makes Diana, with her silver crescent, the goddess of chastity. I have sometimes thought that a modest lady of antiquity, wandering with measured step in some lonely retreat, must have felt a glow of conscious dignity when, after gazing on the soft, shadowy landscape, she calmly and fervently invited the gentle reflection of her sister’s beams to turn to her chaste bosom.
