A Christian has still nobler motives to urge her to preserve her chastity and acquire modesty, for her body has been called the Temple of the living God — of that God who requires more than a modest demeanour. His eye searches the heart. Let her remember, then, that if she hopes to find favour in the sight of purity itself, her chastity must be founded on modesty and not on worldly prudence; otherwise, truly, a good reputation will be her only reward. For that solemn intercourse, that sacred communion, which virtue establishes between man and his Maker must give rise to the wish to be pure as he is pure!

After the foregoing remarks it is almost superfluous to add that I consider immodest all those feminine airs of maturity which follow bashfulness and to which truth is sacrificed in order to secure a husband’s heart — or rather to force him to remain a lover when nature, had her workings not been interrupted, would have made love give way to friendship. The tenderness a man feels for the mother of his children is an excellent substitute for the ardour of unsatisfied passion; but for women to feign an unnatural coldness of constitution in order to prolong that ardour is indelicate, not to say immodest. Women as well as men ought to have the common appetites and passions of their nature; these are brutal only when reason does not check them. But the obligation to check them is the duty of mankind, not a sexual duty. In these respects nature may safely be left to herself; let women only acquire knowledge and humanity, and love will teach them modesty. There is no need for falsehoods, as disgusting as they are futile; for studied rules of behaviour deceive only shallow observers, and a man of sense soon sees through the affectation and despises it.

How young people behave towards each other as men and women is the last thing that should be thought of in education. In fact, behaviour in most circumstances is now given so much thought that simplicity of character is rarely seen. Yet if men were anxious only to cultivate each virtue and let it take firm root in the mind, the grace that results from it — its natural outward mark — would soon strip affectation of its showy plumes; for conduct not founded on truth is as deceptive as it is unstable!

(Footnote. I have often been disgusted by the way many newly married women behave. They seem anxious that their husbands should never forget the privilege of marriage, and they appear to take no pleasure in his company unless he is acting the lover. Love’s reign must indeed be short when its flame is perpetually fanned like this without ever being fed any solid fuel.)

If you really wish to possess modesty, my sisters, you must remember that possessing virtue of any kind is incompatible with ignorance and vanity! You must acquire that sobriety of mind which only the performance of duties and the pursuit of knowledge can inspire, or you will still remain in a doubtful, dependent situation, and be loved only while you are beautiful! The downcast eye, the rosy blush, the retiring grace are all proper in their season; but modesty, being the child of reason, cannot long survive alongside a sensibility that reflection has not tempered. Besides, when love, even innocent love, is the whole business of your lives, your hearts will be too soft to give modesty that quiet retreat where she delights to live, in close union with humanity.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Morality Undermined by Sexual Notions of the Importance of a Good Reputation
paragraphs: It struck me long ago that the advice on conduct, and all the many ways of keeping a good reputation, which have been pressed so insistently upon women, were poisons in attractive disguise, which put a crust over morality while they ate away its substance. It struck me, too, that this measuring of shadows yielded a false reckoning, since their length depends so much on the height of the sun and on other chance circumstances.

What is the source of a courtier’s smooth, deceitful manner? Without doubt, his situation: because he needs people to depend on him, he must learn the art of refusing without causing offence, and of evasively nourishing hope on the chameleon’s food of air. In this way politeness makes a game of truth, and, by eating away the sincerity and humanity natural to man, turns out the fine gentleman.

In the same way, women acquire, out of a supposed necessity, an equally artificial manner of behaving. Yet no one can trifle with truth and go unpunished, for the practised deceiver ends by being taken in by his own tricks, and loses the shrewdness that has rightly been called common sense — that is, a quick grasp of common truths, which the unsophisticated mind always accepts as truths, even though it might not have had the energy to discover them for itself when local prejudices obscured them. Most people take their opinions on trust to spare themselves the trouble of using their own minds, and such lazy beings naturally cling to the letter rather than the spirit of a law, whether divine or human. “Women,” says some author whose name I cannot remember, “mind not what only heaven sees.” And why, indeed, should they? It is the eye of man that they have been taught to fear — and if they can lull their Argus to sleep, they seldom give a thought to heaven or to themselves, because their reputation is safe; and it is reputation, not chastity and all its fair train, that they are busy keeping free of stains, not as a virtue but in order to hold on to their place in the world.

To prove this remark true, I need only point to the love affairs of married women, especially in high society, and in countries where parents marry their daughters off suitably, according to their rank. If an innocent girl falls a victim to love, she is disgraced for ever, although her mind has not been corrupted by the arts that married women practise under the convenient cover of marriage; nor has she broken any duty except the duty of respecting herself. The married woman, by contrast, breaks a most sacred commitment, and turns into a cruel mother when she becomes a false and faithless wife. If her husband still loves her, the tricks she has to use to deceive him will make her the most contemptible of human beings; and in any case the schemes needed to keep up appearances will hold her mind in that childish or vicious agitation which destroys all its energy. Moreover, in time, like people who habitually take cordials to lift their spirits, she will need an intrigue to put life into her thoughts, having lost all taste for pleasures that are not strongly spiced with hope or fear.
Married women sometimes behave even more brazenly; I will give one example.

A woman of rank, notorious for her love affairs — though, since she still lived with her husband, nobody chose to put her in the class where she belonged — made a point of treating with the most insulting contempt a poor timid creature, still ashamed of her earlier weakness, whom a gentleman of the neighbourhood had seduced and later married. This woman had actually mistaken reputation for virtue; and I truly believe she prided herself on how properly she had behaved before her marriage, although once she was settled to her family’s satisfaction, she and her lord were as unfaithful as each other — so that the half-alive heir to a vast estate came from heaven knows where!
Let me look at this subject from another side.

I have known many women who, if they did not love their husbands, loved no one else, yet gave themselves over wholly to vanity and dissipation and neglected every household duty — indeed, even wasted all the money that ought to have been put aside for their helpless younger children — and who still preened themselves on their spotless reputation, as though the entire scope of their duty as wives and mothers were simply to keep it intact. Other idle women, meanwhile, neglecting every duty they personally owed, have supposed that they earned their husbands’ affection because they behaved properly in this one respect.

Weak minds always like to rest in the ceremonies of duty, but morality offers far simpler motives; and one could wish that shallow moralists had said less about behaviour and outward observances, for unless virtue of any kind is founded on knowledge, it will produce nothing but a sort of insipid decency. Nevertheless, respect for the world’s opinion has been called, in the plainest terms, woman’s chief duty, for Rousseau declares, “that reputation is no less indispensable than chastity.” “A man,” he adds, “secure in his own good conduct, depends only on himself, and may brave the public opinion; but a woman, in behaving well, performs but half her duty; as what is thought of her, is as important to her as what she really is. It follows hence, that the system of a woman’s education should, in this respect, be directly contrary to that of ours. Opinion is the grave of virtue among the men; but its throne among women.” It is strictly logical to conclude that a virtue resting on opinion is purely worldly, and that it is the virtue of a being who has been denied reason. But even as regards the world’s opinion, I am convinced that reasoners of this kind are wrong.

This concern for reputation, however — quite apart from its being one of the natural rewards of virtue — arose from a cause I have already lamented as the chief source of female depravity: the impossibility of recovering respectability by returning to virtue, although men keep theirs while they indulge in vice. It was natural, then, for women to try to hold on to what, once lost, was lost for ever, until this concern swallowed up every other, and a reputation for chastity became the one thing needful to the sex. But the anxious scruples of ignorance are futile, for neither religion nor virtue, when they dwell in the heart, demands such childish attention to mere ceremonies, since conduct must on the whole be right when the motive is pure.

In support of my opinion I can cite very respectable authority; and the authority of a cool reasoner ought to carry enough weight to compel consideration, though not to settle an opinion. Speaking of the general laws of morality, Dr. Smith observes — “That by some very extraordinary and unlucky circumstance, a good man may come to be suspected of a crime of which he was altogether incapable, and upon that account be most unjustly exposed for the remaining part of his life to the horror and aversion of mankind. By an accident of this kind he may be said to lose his all, notwithstanding his integrity and justice, in the same manner as a cautious man, notwithstanding his utmost circumspection, may be ruined by an earthquake or an inundation. Accidents of the first kind, however, are perhaps still more rare, and still more contrary to the common course of things than those of the second; and it still remains true, that the practice of truth, justice and humanity, is a certain and almost infallible method of acquiring what those virtues chiefly aim at, the confidence and love of those we live with. A person may be easily misrepresented with regard to a particular action; but it is scarcely possible that he should be so with regard to the general tenor of his conduct. An innocent man may be believed to have done wrong: this, however, will rarely happen. On the contrary, the established opinion of the innocence of his manners will often lead us to absolve him where he has really been in the fault, notwithstanding very strong presumptions.”

I entirely share this writer’s opinion, for I truly believe that few people of either sex have ever been despised for certain vices without deserving it. I am not speaking of the passing slander that hangs over a character like one of the thick November fogs over this capital, until it slowly lifts before the ordinary light of day; I only maintain that the daily conduct of most people prevails in stamping their character with the mark of truth. Quietly, day after day, the clear light shines and disproves the ignorant guess or the malicious story that has thrown mud on a pure character. For a short time a false light distorted its shadow — reputation; but that shadow seldom fails to become accurate once the cloud that caused the error of vision has dispersed.

Many people, no doubt, in several respects win a better reputation than, strictly speaking, they deserve, for untiring effort will usually reach its goal in every race. Those who strive only for this paltry prize, like the Pharisees who prayed at the street corners to be seen of men, truly obtain the reward they are after; for the heart of man cannot be read by man! Still, the good name that good actions naturally reflect, when a man is concerned only to walk rightly, without regard to the onlookers, is generally not only truer but also more secure.

There are, admittedly, ordeals in which the good man must appeal from the injustice of man to God, and, amid the whining of candour or the hissing of envy, set up a pavilion in his own mind to withdraw into until the rumour has passed; indeed, the darts of undeserved blame may pierce an innocent, tender heart through with many sorrows. But all these are exceptions to general rules, and it is by these common laws that human conduct should be governed. The eccentric orbit of a comet never affects astronomers’ calculations of the unchanging order established in the movement of the main bodies of the solar system.

I will therefore venture to state that, once a man has reached maturity, the general outline of his character as the world sees it is accurate, allowing for the exceptions to the rule mentioned above. I do not claim that a prudent, worldly-wise man, with only negative virtues and qualities, may not sometimes gain a smoother reputation than a wiser or better man. Far from it: experience inclines me to conclude that where two people are almost equal in virtue, the world at large will like the more negative character better, while the other may have more friends in private life. But the hills and valleys, the clouds and sunshine, so visible in the virtues of great men, set one another off; and although they give envious weakness a better target, the real character will still make its way into the light, however much it is spattered by weak affection or clever malice.*
(*Footnote. I am alluding to various biographical writings, but above all to Boswell’s Life of Johnson.)

As for that anxiety to protect a reputation hardly won, which leads shrewd people to analyse it, I will not make the obvious comment; but I fear that morality is being very insidiously undermined among women by turning their attention to the show rather than the substance. In this way a simple thing becomes strangely complicated; indeed, virtue and its shadow are sometimes set against each other. We should perhaps never have heard of Lucretia if she had died to preserve her chastity rather than her reputation. If we truly deserve our own good opinion, the world will usually respect us; but if we long for higher improvement and higher attainments, it is not enough to look at ourselves as we imagine others look at us, although this has been ingeniously put forward as the basis of our moral sentiments. (Smith.) For every bystander may have his own prejudices, in addition to those of his age or country. We should rather try to see ourselves as we imagine that Being sees us who watches each thought ripen into action, and whose judgment never departs from the eternal rule of right. Righteous are all his judgments — just, as merciful!

The humble mind that seeks to find favour in His sight, and calmly examines its own conduct when it feels only His presence, will seldom form a badly mistaken view of its own virtues. In the still hour of self-recollection, it will either pray in fear to be spared the angry brow of offended justice, or it will recognize the bond that draws man to the Deity in the pure feeling of reverent adoration, which fills the heart without stirring any turbulent emotions. In these solemn moments a man discovers the seeds of those vices which, like the Java tree, give off a poisonous vapour all around them — death is in the shade! — and he sees them without loathing, because he feels himself drawn by some cord of love to all his fellow creatures, for whose follies he is eager to find every excuse in their nature — that is, in himself. He may reason like this: If I, who exercise my own mind and have been refined by suffering, find the serpent’s egg in some fold of my heart and crush it only with difficulty, shall I not pity those who are made with less vigour, or who have carelessly nursed the insidious reptile until it poisoned the lifeblood it fed on? Can I, aware of my own secret sins, cast off my fellow creatures and calmly watch them fall into the chasm of perdition that gapes to receive them? No! no! The agonized heart will cry out in choking impatience — I too am a man! and I have vices, hidden perhaps from human eyes, which bow me to the dust before God and, when all is silent, tell me loudly that we are made of the same earth and breathe the same air. So humanity grows naturally out of humility, and twists the cords of love that wind about the heart in many coils.

This sympathy extends further still, until a man is glad to see force in arguments that do not convince him, and willingly presents to himself in the best light the semblances of reason that have misled others, delighted to find some reason in all the errors of man, though already convinced that he who rules the day makes his sun shine on all. Yet while he thus, as it were, shakes hands with corruption, one foot stays on earth while the other climbs with bold strides to heaven and claims kinship with higher natures. Virtues unseen by men let fall their healing fragrance in this cool hour, and the thirsty land, refreshed by the pure streams of comfort that suddenly pour forth, is crowned with smiling green; this is the living green on which that eye may look with pleasure which is too pure to behold iniquity! But my spirits are flagging, and I must quietly give myself up to the reverie these reflections lead to, unable to describe the feelings that calmed my soul when, as I watched the sun rise, a soft shower drizzling through the leaves of the nearby trees seemed to fall on my weary yet tranquil spirits, cooling a heart heated by passions that reason was struggling to tame.

The main principles running through all my discussions would make it unnecessary to dwell on this subject, if constant care to keep the varnish of the character fresh and in good repair were not often preached as the whole of female duty; and if rules for governing behaviour and preserving reputation did not too often take the place of moral obligations. But where reputation is concerned, attention is confined to a single virtue — chastity. If a woman’s honour, as it is absurdly called, is safe, she may neglect every social duty, and even ruin her family through gambling and extravagance, yet still show a shameless face to the world — for truly she is an honourable woman!

Mrs. Macaulay has rightly observed that “there is but one fault which a woman of honour may not commit with impunity.” She then adds, with justice and humanity — “This has given rise to the trite and foolish observation, that the first fault against chastity in woman has a radical power to deprave the character. But no such frail beings come out of the hands of nature. The human mind is built of nobler materials than to be so easily corrupted; and with all their disadvantages of situation and education, women seldom become entirely abandoned till they are thrown into a state of desperation, by the venomous rancour of their own sex.”
But the more women prize this regard for a reputation for chastity, the more men despise it; and the two extremes are equally destructive of morality.

Men are certainly more governed by their appetites than women, and their appetites are more corrupted by unrestrained indulgence and by the fastidious devices of satiety. Luxury has brought in a refinement in eating that ruins the constitution, and a degree of gluttony so bestial that all sense of seemly behaviour must be worn away before one person could eat to excess in front of another and afterwards complain of the discomfort his intemperance naturally caused. Some women, especially Frenchwomen, have also lost their sense of decency in this respect, for they will talk quite calmly about an indigestion. One could wish that idleness were not allowed to breed, on the rank soil of wealth, those swarms of summer insects that feed on rottenness; we would not then be disgusted by the sight of such brutish excesses.

There is one rule of behaviour which, I think, ought to govern all the others: simply to cherish so habitual a respect for mankind as may keep us from disgusting a fellow creature for the sake of a momentary indulgence. The shameful laziness of many married women, and of others somewhat advanced in years, often leads them to offend against delicacy. For although they are convinced that the person, the body, is the bond that unites the sexes, how often, out of sheer laziness or to enjoy some trifling indulgence, do they disgust?

The corruption of the appetite that brings the sexes together has had a still more fatal effect. Nature must always be the standard of taste and the measure of appetite — yet how grossly the voluptuary insults nature! Setting aside the refinements of love, nature, by making the gratification of this appetite, as of every other, a natural and commanding law for preserving the species, raises the appetite and mingles a little mind and affection with a sensual relish. A parent’s feelings, blending with a merely animal instinct, give it dignity; and as the man and woman often come together because of the child, a mutual interest and affection is awakened through the exercise of a shared sympathy. Women, then, necessarily having some duty to fulfil nobler than adorning their persons, would not be content to be the slaves of casual appetite, which is now the condition of a very considerable number who are, literally speaking, standing dishes to which every glutton may help himself.

I may be told that, great as this enormity is, it affects only a sacrificed portion of the sex — sacrificed for the salvation of the rest. But, although every argument that recommends sanctioning a small evil to produce a greater good could easily be proved false, the harm does not stop there; for the moral character and peace of mind of the chaster part of the sex are undermined by the conduct of the very women to whom they allow no refuge from guilt — women whom they relentlessly condemn to practise the arts that lure their husbands away from them and debauch their sons, and that force the chaste themselves — let modest women not start in alarm — to take on, to some extent, the same character. For I will venture to assert that all the causes of female weakness, as well as of depravity, which I have already dealt with at length, branch out from one great cause — the lack of chastity in men.

This intemperance, so widespread, corrupts the appetite to such a degree that a wanton stimulus is needed to arouse it; but nature’s parental purpose is forgotten, and the mere person — and that only for a moment — takes up all the thoughts. Indeed, the lustful prowler often grows so voluptuous that he cultivates an ever more refined taste for female softness.

To satisfy this bent in men, women are made systematically voluptuous; and although they may not all carry their libertinism to the same lengths, this heartless intercourse with the sex, which they allow themselves, depraves both sexes, because men’s taste is corrupted, and women of all classes naturally shape their behaviour to gratify the taste through which they gain pleasure and power. As a result, women become weaker in mind and body than they ought to be if one of the great purposes of their existence — bearing and nursing children — were taken into account, and they lack the strength to carry out the first duty of a mother; and, sacrificing to lust the parental affection that ennobles instinct, they either destroy the embryo in the womb or abandon the child once it is born. Nature demands respect in everything, and those who break her laws seldom break them unpunished. The weak, enervated women who particularly catch the eye of libertines are unfit to be mothers, though they may conceive; so that the rich sensualist who has run riot among women, spreading depravity and misery, receives from his wife, when he wishes to carry on his name, only a half-formed being that inherits the weakness of both its father and its mother.

In contrasting the humanity of the present age with the barbarism of antiquity, much has been made of the savage custom of exposing children whom their parents could not support; while the man of sensibility who perhaps makes this complaint produces, through his promiscuous love affairs, a most destructive barrenness and a contagious wickedness of morals. Surely nature never meant that women, in satisfying an appetite, should defeat the very purpose for which it was implanted?

I have observed before that men ought to support the women they have seduced; this would be one way of reforming female manners and of stopping an abuse that is equally fatal to population and to morals. Another way, no less obvious, would be to direct women’s attention to the real virtue of chastity; for a woman who smiles on the libertine while she spurns the victims of his lawless appetites and of their own folly has little claim to respect on grounds of modesty, though her reputation may be as white as the driven snow.

Besides, pure as she thinks herself, she shares a taint of the same folly when she carefully adorns her person only to be seen by men, to draw respectful sighs and all the idle homage of what is called innocent gallantry. If women truly respected virtue for its own sake, they would not look to vanity to compensate them for the self-denial they must practise to keep their reputation, nor would they keep company with men who openly defy reputation.

The two sexes corrupt and improve each other in turn. This I believe to be an indisputable truth, and I extend it to every virtue. Chastity, modesty, public spirit and the whole noble train of virtues on which social virtue and happiness rest should be understood and cultivated by all mankind, or they will be cultivated to little purpose. And instead of handing the vicious or the idle an excuse for breaking some sacred duty by calling it a sexual one, it would be wiser to show that nature has made no difference here, since the unchaste man doubly defeats nature’s purpose, by making women barren and by ruining his own constitution, even though he escapes the shame that pursues the same offence in the other sex. These are the physical consequences; the moral ones are more alarming still, for virtue is merely a name when the duties of citizens, husbands, wives, fathers, mothers and heads of families become nothing more than the selfish ties of convenience.

Why, then, do philosophers look for public spirit? Public spirit must be nourished by private virtue, or it will resemble the artificial sentiment that makes women careful of their reputation and men of their honour — a sentiment that often exists without the support of virtue, without the support of that sublime morality which makes the habitual breach of one duty a breach of the whole moral law.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Of the Pernicious Effects Which Arise from the Unnatural Distinctions Established in Society
paragraphs: Most of the evils and vices that make this world so dreary a scene to the reflective mind flow from the respect paid to property, as from a poisoned fountain. For it is in the most polished society that loathsome reptiles and venomous serpents lurk beneath the rank undergrowth; and there, too, is a sensuality pampered by the still, sultry air, which saps every good disposition before it can ripen into virtue.

One class presses upon another, for all are trying to win respect on account of their property; and property, once gained, will win the respect that is due only to talents and virtue. Men neglect the duties that fall upon them as men, yet are treated like demigods. Religion, too, is separated from morality by a ceremonial veil, and yet men wonder that the world is almost, quite literally, a den of swindlers or oppressors.

A homely proverb speaks a shrewd truth: the devil will find work for anyone he finds idle. And what can hereditary wealth and titles produce except habitual idleness? For man is so made that he can learn the proper use of his faculties only by exercising them, and he will not exercise them unless necessity of some kind first sets the wheels in motion. Likewise, virtue can be acquired only by carrying out our duties to one another; but a being who is coaxed out of his humanity by the flattery of hangers-on will scarcely feel the importance of these sacred duties. Society must establish more equality, or morality will never gain ground; and this virtuous equality will not stand firm even if it is founded on a rock, so long as one half of mankind is chained by fate to its base, for they will keep undermining it through ignorance or pride. It is useless to expect virtue from women until they are, to some degree, independent of men; indeed, it is useless to expect even that strength of natural affection which would make them good wives and good mothers. While they are wholly dependent on their husbands they will be cunning, base and selfish; and the men who can be gratified by the fawning, doting devotion of a spaniel have little delicacy. For love cannot be bought, in any sense of the word: its silken wings shrivel at once when anything other than a return in kind is sought. Yet while wealth makes men feeble, and women live, as it were, by their personal charms, how can we expect them to carry out those ennobling duties which demand both effort and self-denial? Hereditary property corrupts the mind with false refinement. Its unfortunate victims, swaddled from birth, if I may put it so, seldom use the power of moving either body or mind; and so, seeing everything through a single medium, and a false one, they cannot discern what true merit and happiness consist in. False indeed must that light be when the trappings of rank hide the man and make him stalk about in masquerade, dragging from one scene of dissipation to the next his nerveless limbs, which hang in stupid listlessness, and rolling about that vacant eye which tells us plainly that there is no mind at home.

What I mean to conclude, therefore, is that a society is not properly organized if it does not compel men and women to carry out their respective duties by making that the only way to earn the approval of their fellow creatures, which every human being wishes to gain somehow. It follows that the respect paid to wealth and to mere personal charms is a true north-east wind, which withers the tender blossoms of affection and virtue. Nature has wisely attached affections to duties, to sweeten toil and to give the efforts of reason that vigour which only the heart can give. But affection that is merely put on, because it is the badge assigned to a certain role, while the duties of that role go unfulfilled, is one of the empty compliments that vice and folly are obliged to pay to virtue and to the real nature of things.

To illustrate my opinion, I need only point out this: when a woman is admired for her beauty and lets herself become so intoxicated by the admiration she receives that she neglects the indispensable duty of a mother, she sins against herself, by failing to cultivate an affection that would make her both useful and happy. True happiness, by which I mean all the contentment and virtuous satisfaction that can be snatched in this imperfect state, must arise from well-regulated affections; and every affection includes a duty. Men do not see the misery they cause, and the vicious weakness they foster, by urging women only to make themselves pleasing. They do not consider that in this way they set natural and artificial duties in conflict, sacrificing the comfort and respectability of a woman’s life to sensual notions of beauty, when in nature all these things are in harmony.

Cold would be the heart of a husband, unless early debauchery had made him unnatural, who did not feel more delight at seeing his child nursed at its mother’s breast than the most artful wanton tricks could ever arouse. Yet wealth leads women to scorn this natural way of strengthening the marriage bond and of entwining esteem with more tender memories. To keep their beauty, and to wear the flowery crown of the day that gives them a kind of right to reign for a short while over the sex, they neglect to stamp impressions on their husbands’ hearts that would be remembered with more tenderness than even their maiden charms, when the snow on the head began to chill the breast. The maternal care of a reasonable, affectionate woman is deeply moving; and the chastened dignity with which a mother returns the caresses that she and her child receive from a father who has been carrying out the serious duties of his position is not only a respectable sight but a beautiful one. Indeed, so peculiar are my feelings (and I have tried not to catch artificial ones) that, after being wearied by the sight of insipid grandeur and of the slavish ceremonies that, with cumbersome pomp, took the place of domestic affection, I have turned to some other scene to relieve my eye by resting it on the refreshing green that nature scatters everywhere. I have then watched with pleasure a woman nursing her children and carrying out the duties of her position with, perhaps, only one servant to take the menial part of the housework off her hands. I have seen her make herself and her children ready, with no luxury but cleanliness, to receive her husband, who, coming home weary in the evening, found smiling babies and a clean hearth. My heart has lingered in the midst of that group, and has even throbbed with shared emotion when the scrape of the well-known footstep raised a pleasant stir.

While my benevolence has been gratified by contemplating this unaffected picture, I have thought that a couple of this kind, equally necessary to each other and equally independent, because each carried out the duties belonging to their station, possessed everything that life could give. They were raised far enough above abject poverty not to have to weigh the importance of every farthing they spent, and they had enough to spare them from a chilly system of economy that narrows both heart and mind. I declare, so common are my notions, that I do not know what else would be needed to make this the happiest as well as the most respectable situation in the world, except a taste for literature, to bring a little variety and interest into conversation, and some spare money to give to the needy and to buy books. For when the heart is opened by compassion, and the head is busy arranging useful plans, it is not pleasant to have a prim little imp constantly tugging back one’s elbow to stop the hand from drawing out an almost empty purse, while whispering some prudent maxim about justice coming first.

Yet destructive as riches and inherited honours are to human character, they debase and cramp women, if possible, even more than men, because men may still to some degree develop their faculties by becoming soldiers and statesmen.

As soldiers, I grant, they can now for the most part gather only vainglorious laurels, while they adjust the European balance of power to a hair, taking particular care that no bleak northern nook or strait should tip the scale. But the days of true heroism are over, when a citizen fought for his country like a Fabricius or a Washington and then went back to his farm, to let his virtuous ardour flow in a calmer but no less wholesome stream. No, our British heroes are more often sent from the gaming table than from the plough; and their passions have been inflamed by hanging in speechless suspense on the throw of a die rather than refined by longing after the adventurous march of virtue in the pages of history.

The statesman, it is true, might with more propriety leave the faro bank or the card table to take the helm, for he still has only to shuffle and play tricks. The whole system of British politics, if it may courteously be called a system, consists in multiplying dependents and devising taxes that grind the poor to pamper the rich. So a war, or any wild-goose chase, is, as common people say, a lucky turn-up of patronage for the minister, whose chief merit is the art of keeping himself in office.

It is not necessary, then, that he should have any compassion for the poor, so long as he can secure the odd trick for his family. Or if some show of respect for what is called, with ignorant ostentation, an Englishman’s birthright should be useful for cheating the gruff mastiff that he has to lead by the nose, he can make an empty show quite safely by giving his own single vote and letting his light squadron of followers file off to the other side. And when a question of humanity is debated, he may dip a sop in the milk of human kindness to silence Cerberus, and talk of the interest his heart takes in an attempt to stop the earth crying for vengeance as it drinks in its children’s blood, even though his cold hand may at that very moment be riveting their chains by sanctioning the abominable slave trade. A minister remains a minister only so long as he can carry any point he is determined to carry. Yet it is not necessary for a minister to feel like a man, when a bold push might shake his seat.
But, to finish with these digressions, let me return to the more plausible slavery that chains the very soul of woman and keeps her forever in the bondage of ignorance.

The absurd distinctions of rank, which make civilization a curse by dividing the world between sensual tyrants and cunning, envious dependents, corrupt almost every class of people to the same degree. They do so because respectability is attached not to the carrying out of our duties to one another but to rank; and when the duties are not fulfilled, the affections cannot grow strong enough to fortify the virtue of which they are the natural reward. Still, there are some loopholes through which a man may creep out and dare to think and act for himself; but for a woman this is a Herculean task, because she has difficulties peculiar to her sex to overcome, which call for almost superhuman powers.

A truly benevolent legislator always tries to make it in each individual’s interest to be virtuous; and so, as private virtue becomes the cement of public happiness, an orderly whole is bound together by the tendency of all its parts toward a common centre. But the private or public virtue of women is highly doubtful; for Rousseau and a long list of male writers insist that a woman should be subjected all her life to a severe restraint, that of propriety. Why subject her to propriety — blind propriety — if she is capable of acting from a nobler motive, if she is an heir of immortality? Must sugar always be produced with living blood? Is one half of the human species, like the poor African slaves, to be subjected to prejudices that brutalize them, when principles would be a surer safeguard, merely to sweeten man’s cup? Is this not indirectly denying women reason? For a gift is a mockery if it is unfit for use.

Like men, women are made weak and self-indulgent by the enervating pleasures that wealth provides; but on top of this they are made slaves to their bodies, and must make them alluring, so that man may lend them his reason to guide their tottering steps aright. Or, if they are ambitious, they must govern their tyrants by underhand tricks, for without rights there can be no binding duties. The laws concerning woman, which I intend to discuss in a later part, make an absurd unit of a man and his wife; and then, by the easy step of regarding only him as responsible, she is reduced to a mere cipher.

The being who carries out the duties of its station is independent; and, speaking of women in general, their first duty is to themselves as rational creatures, and the next in importance, as citizens, is that of a mother, which includes so many others. The rank in life that excuses them from fulfilling this duty necessarily degrades them by making them mere dolls. Or, if they turn to something more important than simply fitting clothes onto a smooth block, their minds are occupied only by some soft platonic attachment, or the actual conduct of an intrigue may keep their thoughts in motion. For when they neglect their domestic duties, it is not in their power to take the field and march and counter-march like soldiers, or to wrangle in the senate, to keep their faculties from rusting.

I know that, as proof of the inferiority of the sex, Rousseau has triumphantly exclaimed, How can they leave the nursery for the camp! And some moralists have called the camp the school of the most heroic virtues; though I think it would puzzle a sharp casuist to prove that most of the wars that have dubbed men heroes were reasonable. I do not intend to examine this question critically, because I have often regarded these freaks of ambition as the first natural stage of civilization, when the ground must be torn up and the woods cleared by fire and sword, and so I do not choose to call them plagues. But surely the present system of war has little connection with virtue of any kind, being a school of FINESSE and effeminacy rather than of fortitude.

Yet suppose that defensive war, which is the only justifiable war in the present advanced state of society, a state in which virtue can show its face and ripen amid the hardships that purify the air on a mountain top, were alone accepted as just and glorious: then the true heroism of the ancients might once again stir the hearts of women. But gently and softly, dear reader, male or female, do not be alarmed. Although I have set the character of a modern soldier beside that of a civilized woman, I am not going to advise women to turn their distaffs into muskets, though I sincerely wish to see the bayonet beaten into a pruning hook. I was only refreshing an imagination wearied by dwelling on the vices and follies which all spring from a foul stream of wealth that has muddied the clear brooks of natural affection. I did so by supposing that society will one day be so constituted that man must fulfil the duties of a citizen or be despised, and that while he was employed in any branch of civil life, his wife, also an active citizen, would be just as intent on managing her household, educating her children and helping her neighbours.

But to make her truly virtuous and useful, she must not, if she carries out her civil duties, lack the protection of civil laws in her own right. She must not depend on her husband’s bounty for her living during his life, or for her support after his death — for how can a being be generous who has nothing of its own? Or virtuous, who is not free? As things now stand, the wife who is faithful to her husband but neither nurses nor educates her children scarcely deserves the name of a wife, and has no right to that of a citizen. But take away natural rights, and of course duties come to an end.

So women inevitably become nothing more than the wanton amusement of men, when they are so weak in mind and body that they cannot exert themselves except to pursue some frothy pleasure or invent some frivolous fashion. What sight could be more melancholy to a thinking mind than to look into the many carriages that drive helter-skelter about this city in the morning, full of pale-faced creatures who are running away from themselves? I have often wished, with Dr. Johnson, to put some of them in a little shop, with half a dozen children looking up to their languid faces for support. I am much mistaken if some hidden vigour would not soon bring health and spirit to their eyes; and some lines, drawn by the exercise of reason on those blank cheeks, which before had been rippled only by dimples, might restore lost dignity to their character, or rather enable it to reach the true dignity of its nature. Virtue cannot be acquired even by speculation, and still less by the passive idleness that wealth naturally breeds.

Besides, when poverty is more disgraceful than even vice, is morality not cut to the quick? Still, to avoid being misunderstood: although I consider that women in the ordinary walks of life are called by religion and reason to fulfil the duties of wives and mothers, I cannot help lamenting that women of a higher class have no road open by which they can pursue wider plans of usefulness and independence. I may provoke laughter by dropping a hint, which I intend to follow up at some future time; for I really think that women ought to have representatives, instead of being governed arbitrarily without being allowed any direct share in the deliberations of government.

But since the entire system of representation in this country is at present merely a convenient handle for despotism, women need not complain; they are as well represented as a large class of hard-working artisans, who pay for the upkeep of royalty when they can barely stop their children’s mouths with bread. In what sense are those people represented whose very sweat keeps up the splendid stables of an heir apparent, or varnishes the carriage of some royal mistress who looks down on shame? Taxes on the barest necessities of life allow an endless tribe of idle princes and princesses to parade in stupid pomp before a gaping crowd, who almost worship the very show that costs them so dear. This is mere Gothic grandeur, rather like the barbarous and useless display of mounted sentries at Whitehall, which I have never been able to see without a mixture of contempt and indignation.

How strangely corrupted the mind must be when it is impressed by this sort of pomp! But until these monuments of folly are levelled by virtue, similar follies will leaven the whole mass. For the same character will, to some degree, prevail throughout society as a whole; and the refinements of luxury, or the vicious grumbling of envious poverty, will alike banish virtue from society as its defining characteristic, or allow it to appear only as one of the stripes in the harlequin coat worn by civilized man.

In the upper ranks of life every duty is performed by deputies, as though duties could ever be waived; and the empty pleasures which the resulting idleness drives the rich to pursue look so tempting to the rank below that the crowds scrambling for wealth sacrifice everything to tread on their heels. The most sacred trusts are then treated as sinecures, because they were obtained through influence and sought only to let a man keep GOOD COMPANY. Women in particular all want to be ladies, which simply means having nothing to do but drift listlessly about, they hardly care where, for a purpose they cannot name.

But what, I may be asked, have women to do in society except to idle with an easy grace? Surely you would not condemn them all to suckle fools, and chronicle small beer! No. Women might certainly study the art of healing and be physicians as well as nurses. And decency seems to assign midwifery to them, though I am afraid that the word midwife in our dictionaries will soon give way to accoucheur, and that one proof of the sex’s former delicacy will be erased from the language.

They might also study politics, and ground their benevolence on the broadest foundation. For reading history will hardly be more useful than reading romances if it is read as mere biography, without noticing the character of the times, political improvements, the arts and so on; in short, if it is not regarded as the history of man, rather than of particular men who filled a niche in the temple of fame and then dropped into the black, rolling stream of time, which silently sweeps everything before it into the shapeless void called eternity. For can it be called a shape, “that shape hath none?”

They might likewise pursue business of various kinds, if they were educated in a more orderly way, and this might save many from common and legal prostitution. Women would not then marry for a living, as men accept government posts and neglect the duties those posts imply; nor would an attempt to earn their own living, a most praiseworthy attempt, sink them almost to the level of those poor abandoned creatures who live by prostitution. For are not milliners and dressmakers counted as the next class down? The few occupations open to women are far from liberal; they are menial. And when a better education enables them to take charge of children’s education as governesses, they are not treated like the tutors of sons; though even clergymen who serve as tutors are not always treated in a way likely to make them respected in the eyes of their pupils, to say nothing of their own private comfort. But since women educated as gentlewomen are never intended for the humiliating positions that necessity sometimes forces them to fill, these positions are regarded as a degradation; and anyone who needs to be told that nothing sharpens sensibility so painfully as such a fall in life knows little of the human heart.

Some of these women might be held back from marrying by a proper pride or delicacy, and others may not have been able to escape from servitude in this pitiful way. Is not that government, then, gravely defective, and heedless of the happiness of half its members, if it makes no provision for honest, independent women by encouraging them to fill respectable positions? But if their private virtue is to become a public benefit, they must have a civil existence in the state, whether married or single; otherwise we shall constantly see some worthy woman, whose sensibility has been made painfully acute by undeserved contempt, droop like “the lily broken down by a plough share.”

It is a sad truth; yet such are the blessed effects of civilization! The most respectable women are the most oppressed; and unless their understandings are far above the common run of understanding in both sexes, they must, from being treated as contemptible beings, become contemptible. How many women waste their lives away like this, a prey to discontent, who might have practised as physicians, run a farm, managed a shop and stood upright, supported by their own work, instead of hanging their heads, weighed down with the dew of sensibility that consumes the very beauty it at first gave lustre to! Indeed, I doubt whether pity and love are as closely related as poets pretend; for I have seldom seen much compassion aroused by the helplessness of women unless they were beautiful. Then, perhaps, pity was the gentle handmaid of love, or the forerunner of lust.

How much more respectable is the woman who earns her own bread by fulfilling any duty than the most accomplished beauty! Beauty, did I say? I am so conscious of the beauty of moral loveliness, or of that harmonious propriety which brings the passions of a well-regulated mind into tune, that I blush to make the comparison. Yet I sigh to think how few women try to attain this respectability by withdrawing from the giddy whirl of pleasure, or from the idle calm that stupefies the good sort of women it draws in.

Proud of their weakness, however, they must always be protected, shielded from care and from all the hard labour that dignifies the mind. If this is the decree of fate, if they choose to make themselves insignificant and contemptible, to sweetly waste “life away,” then let them not expect to be valued when their beauty fades; for it is the fate of the fairest flowers to be admired and then pulled to pieces by the careless hand that plucked them. In how many ways, out of the purest benevolence, do I wish to press this truth upon my sex! Yet I fear they will not listen to a truth that hard-won experience has brought home to many a troubled heart, nor willingly give up the privileges of rank and sex for the privileges of humanity, to which those who do not carry out its duties have no claim.

In my opinion, those writers are especially useful who make man feel for man, regardless of the station he fills or the trappings of artificial sentiment. So I would gladly convince reasonable men of the importance of some of my remarks, and persuade them to weigh the whole drift of my observations without passion. I appeal to their understanding; and, as a fellow creature, I claim in the name of my sex some place in their hearts. I beg them to help set their companion free, to make her a help meet for them!

If men would only generously snap our chains, and be content with rational companionship instead of slavish obedience, they would find us more attentive daughters, more affectionate sisters, more faithful wives, more reasonable mothers — in a word, better citizens. We should then love them with true affection, because we should learn to respect ourselves; and the peace of mind of a worthy man would not be disturbed by his wife’s idle vanity, nor would his babies be sent to nestle at a stranger’s breast, never having found a home at their mother’s.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Parental Affection
paragraphs: Parental affection is perhaps the blindest form of perverse self-love; for, unlike the French, we do not have two terms (L’amour propre, L’amour de soi meme) to distinguish the pursuit of a natural and reasonable desire from the ignorant calculations of weakness. Parents often love their children in the most brutish way, and sacrifice every duty they owe to others in order to push them forward in the world — to promote, such is the perversity of unprincipled prejudices, the future welfare of the very beings whose present existence they embitter by the most despotic exercise of power. Power, indeed, is always true to its vital principle, for in every shape it wants to reign without check or question. Its throne is built over a dark abyss that no eye may dare to explore, lest the baseless structure should totter under investigation. Obedience, unconditional obedience, is the watchword of tyrants of every kind, and to make “assurance doubly sure,” one kind of despotism props up another. Tyrants would have cause to tremble if reason became the rule of duty in any of the relations of life, for the light might spread until full day appeared. And when it did, how men would smile at the sight of the bugbears that startled them during the night of ignorance or the twilight of timid inquiry!

Indeed, in many minds parental affection is merely an excuse to tyrannize wherever that can be done without penalty; for only good and wise men are satisfied with a respect that can bear discussion. Sure that they have a right to what they demand, they neither fear reason nor dread a searching examination of questions that turn on natural justice, since they firmly believe that the more enlightened the human mind grows, the deeper just and simple principles will strike root. They do not rest content with expedients, nor admit that what is true in theory can be false in practice; scorning the shifts of the moment, they wait calmly until time, by sanctioning innovation, silences the hiss of selfishness or envy.

If the power to reflect on the past and to dart the keen eye of contemplation into the future is the great privilege of man, it must be granted that some people enjoy this prerogative only to a very limited degree. Everything now looks wrong to them; and, unable to tell the possible from the monstrous, they fear where fear has no place, running from the light of reason as if it were a firebrand; yet the limits of the possible have never been defined so as to stop the hand of the bold innovator.

Woman, however, being everywhere a slave to prejudice, rarely shows an enlightened maternal love; she either neglects her children or spoils them by indulging them unwisely. Moreover, the love some women bear their children is, as I have already called it, often very brutish, for it destroys every spark of humanity. These Rebekahs sacrifice justice, truth, everything, and for their own children’s sake they break the most sacred duties, forgetting the common kinship that binds together the whole family on earth. Yet reason seems to tell us that whoever lets one duty or affection swallow up all the others has not heart or mind enough to fulfil even that one conscientiously. It then loses the venerable look of a duty and takes on the fantastic form of a whim.

Since the care of children in infancy is one of the great duties that nature has attached to the female character, this duty, properly considered, would supply many strong arguments for strengthening the female understanding.

The shaping of the mind must start very early, and the temper above all calls for the most careful attention — attention that women cannot give if they love their children merely because they are theirs, and seek the foundation of their duty no further than in the feelings of the moment. This lack of reason in their affections is what so often drives women to extremes, making them either the most doting or the most careless and unnatural of mothers.

A good mother needs good sense, and the independence of mind that few women have when they are taught to rely entirely on their husbands. Meek wives generally make foolish mothers: they want their children to love them best and to take their side secretly against the father, who is held up as a bogeyman. When the children must be punished, even for offending the mother, it is the father who must punish them; he must settle every dispute. But I shall discuss this subject more fully when I deal with private education; for now I only mean to insist that unless woman’s understanding is enlarged, and her character made firmer by letting her govern her own conduct, she will never have enough sense or self-control to manage her children properly. Indeed, her parental affection scarcely deserves the name if it does not lead her to breastfeed her children, since performing this duty is equally fitted to inspire maternal and filial affection; and men and women are bound, as an indispensable duty, to fulfil those duties that give rise to affections, for such affections are the surest safeguards against vice. What is called natural affection is, I believe, a very weak tie; affections must grow out of the habitual exercise of mutual sympathy; and what sympathy does a mother exercise who sends her baby off to a wet nurse, and takes it back from the nurse only to send it away to school?

Providence, through women’s natural feelings, has supplied them with a natural substitute for love once the lover has become merely a friend and mutual trust has taken the place of overstrained admiration: a child then gently tightens the loosening cord, and caring for it together creates a fresh mutual sympathy. Yet a child, though a pledge of affection, will not revive that affection if father and mother are both content to hand over its care to hirelings; for those who do their duty by proxy should not grumble if they miss duty’s reward — it is parental affection that produces filial duty.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. Duty to Parents
paragraphs: Man seems to have a lazy inclination to let long-established custom always take the place of reason, and to rest every duty on an arbitrary foundation. The rights of kings are traced in a direct line from the King of kings, and those of parents from our first parent.

Why do we reach so far back for principles that ought always to rest on the same foundation and carry the same weight today as they did a thousand years ago, and not one jot more? If parents do their duty, they have a strong hold on their children’s gratitude and a sacred claim to it; but few parents are willing to accept the respectful affection of their offspring on such terms. They demand blind obedience because they do not deserve a reasonable service; and to make these demands of weakness and ignorance more binding, a mysterious sanctity is cast around the most arbitrary of principles. For what else can we call the blind duty of obeying vicious or weak beings merely because they obeyed a powerful instinct? The reciprocal duty that naturally exists between parent and child can be defined simply, in a few words: the parent who gives proper care to a helpless infant has the right to demand the same care when the feebleness of old age comes upon him. But to subject a rational being to the mere will of another, once he is old enough to answer to society for his own conduct, is a most cruel and unwarranted stretch of power; and it is perhaps as harmful to morality as those religious systems which allow right and wrong no existence except in the will of God.

I have never known a parent who paid more than ordinary attention to his children to be disregarded by them (Dr. Johnson makes the same observation). On the contrary, the early habit of relying almost unquestioningly on the opinion of a respected parent is not easily shaken, even when mature reason has convinced the child that his father is not the wisest man in the world. A reasonable man must harden himself against this weakness, for it is a weakness, though the epithet AMIABLE may be attached to it. The absurd duty, too often instilled, of obeying a parent simply because he is a parent fetters the mind and prepares it to submit slavishly to any power except reason.
I distinguish between the natural duty owed to parents and the incidental one.

The parent who diligently tries to form his child’s heart and enlarge its understanding has given to the performance of a duty shared by the whole animal world a dignity that only reason can give. This is humane parental affection, and it leaves instinctive natural affection far behind. Such a parent acquires all the rights of the most sacred friendship, and his advice, even when his child is well on in life, deserves serious consideration.

As for marriage, although after the age of twenty-one a parent seems to have no right to withhold his consent for any reason, twenty years of anxious care still call for some return; and if the son’s choice does not fully win the approval of his first friend, the son ought at least to promise not to marry for two or three years.

But respect for parents is, generally speaking, a far more degrading principle; it is merely a selfish respect for property. The father who is obeyed blindly is obeyed out of sheer weakness, or from motives that debase human character.

It is generally admitted that a great share of the misery that roams the world in hideous forms arises from the negligence of parents; and yet these are the very people who cling most stubbornly to what they call a natural right, though it overturns the birthright of man, the right to act as his own reason directs.

I have already had frequent occasion to observe that vicious or lazy people are always eager to profit by enforcing arbitrary privileges, and generally in the same proportion as they neglect to carry out the duties that alone make those privileges reasonable. At bottom this is a dictate of common sense, or the instinct of self-defence peculiar to ignorant weakness. It resembles the instinct that makes a fish muddy the water it swims in to escape its enemy, instead of boldly facing it in the clear stream.

From the clear stream of argument, indeed, the defenders of established custom of every kind take flight; and, sheltering in the darkness that sublime poetry has imagined surrounding the throne of the Almighty, they dare to demand the unquestioning respect that is owed only to His unsearchable ways. But let me not be thought presumptuous. The darkness that hides our God from us concerns only speculative truths; it never obscures moral ones. Those shine clearly, for God is light, and by the constitution of our nature He never requires us to perform a duty whose reasonableness does not shine upon us when we open our eyes.

It is true that an idle parent of high rank may extort a show of respect from his child; and women on the Continent are especially subject to the designs of their families, who never think of consulting their wishes or of providing for the comfort of the poor victims of their pride. The result is well known: these dutiful daughters become adulteresses and neglect the education of their own children, from whom they in turn demand the same kind of obedience.

Women, it is true, are too much under the dominion of their parents in every country; and few parents think of speaking to their children in the following way, though it is in this reasonable manner that Heaven seems to command the whole human race. It is in your interest to obey me until you can judge for yourself; and the Almighty Father of all has planted an affection in me to protect you while your reason is developing. But when your mind reaches maturity, you must obey me, or rather respect my opinions, only so far as they agree with the light that is dawning in your own mind.

A slavish subjection to parents cramps every faculty of the mind; and Mr. Locke very wisely observes that “if the mind be curbed and humbled too much in children; if their spirits be abased and broken much by too strict an hand over them; they lose all their vigour and industry.” This strict hand may partly account for the weakness of women; for girls, for various reasons, are kept down by their parents more than boys are, in every sense of the word. The duty expected of them, like all the duties arbitrarily imposed on women, springs more from a sense of propriety and a regard for decorum than from reason; and, taught in this way to submit slavishly to their parents, they are prepared for the slavery of marriage. I may be told that many women are not slaves in the married state. True; but then they become tyrants, for what they gain by degrading means is not rational freedom but a lawless kind of power, like the authority wielded by the favourites of absolute monarchs. Nor do I dream of suggesting that either boys or girls are always slaves. I insist only that when they are forced to submit blindly to authority, their faculties are weakened and their tempers made either domineering or servile. I also regret that parents, lazily taking advantage of a supposed privilege, dampen the first faint glimmer of reason, and at the same time make the very duty they are so anxious to enforce an empty name, because they will not let it rest on the only basis on which a duty can securely rest. For unless it is founded on knowledge, it cannot gain enough strength to withstand the squalls of passion or the silent undermining of self-love. But it is not the parents who have given the surest proof of their affection for their children (or, more properly, who have fulfilled their duty and so allowed a natural parental affection to take root in their hearts, an affection born of practised sympathy and reason, not the presumptuous offspring of selfish pride) who most vehemently insist that their children submit to their will merely because it is their will. On the contrary, the parent who sets a good example patiently lets that example do its work, and it seldom fails to produce its natural effect: filial respect.

Children cannot be taught too early to submit to reason, which is the true definition of that necessity Rousseau insisted on without ever defining it; for to submit to reason is to submit to the nature of things, and to the God who made them so in order to promote our real interest.

Why should children’s minds be bent out of shape just as they begin to open, merely to indulge the laziness of parents who insist on a privilege without being willing to pay the price nature has set on it? I have had occasion before to observe that a right always includes a duty; and I think it may also fairly be inferred that those who do not fulfil the duty forfeit the right.

It is easier, I grant, to command than to reason; but it does not follow that children cannot understand why they are made to do certain things by habit. For the wholesome power that a sensible parent gradually gains over a child’s mind flows from steady adherence to a few simple principles of conduct. And this power becomes strong indeed if it is tempered by a consistent show of affection that reaches the child’s heart. For I believe it must be granted, as a general rule, that the affection we inspire always resembles the affection we cultivate; so that the natural affections, which have been thought almost separate from reason, may turn out to be more closely connected with judgment than is commonly admitted. Indeed, as a further proof that the female understanding needs to be cultivated, it is only fair to observe that the affections seem to have a kind of animal capriciousness when they live only in the heart.

It is the erratic exercise of parental authority that first damages the mind, and girls are more exposed to this erratic treatment than boys. The will of those who never allow their will to be questioned, except when they happen to be in a good mood and relax in proportion, is almost always unreasonable. To evade this arbitrary authority, girls learn very early the lessons they later practise on their husbands. I have often seen a sharp-faced little miss rule a whole family, except that every now and then Mamma’s anger bursts out of some chance cloud: either her hair was badly dressed,* or she had lost more money at cards the night before than she cared to admit to her husband, or some other such moral cause of anger.

(*Footnote. I once heard a little girl say to a servant, “My mamma has been scolding me finely this morning, because her hair was not dressed to please her.” The remark was pert, but it was true. And what respect could a girl come to feel for such a parent without doing violence to reason?)

Having watched outbursts of this kind, I have been led into a melancholy train of thought about women, and have concluded that when their first affection must lead them astray, or set their duties in conflict until those duties rest on nothing but whims and customs, little can be expected of them as they grow older. How, indeed, can a teacher remedy this evil? For to teach them virtue on any solid principle is to teach them to despise their parents. Children cannot, and ought not to, be taught to make allowances for their parents’ faults, because every such allowance weakens the force of reason in their minds and makes them still more indulgent toward their own faults. It is one of the most sublime virtues of maturity that leads us to be severe with ourselves and forbearing toward others; but children should be taught only the simple virtues. For if they begin too early to make allowances for human passions and manners, they blunt the fine edge of the standard by which they should regulate their own, and they become unjust in the same proportion as they grow indulgent.

The affections of children and of weak people are always selfish: they love others because others love them, not because of their virtues. Yet until esteem and love are blended together in the first affection, and reason is made the foundation of the first duty, morality will stumble on the threshold. But until society is constituted very differently, parents, I fear, will go on insisting on being obeyed because they will be obeyed, and will keep trying to rest that power on a divine right that cannot withstand the scrutiny of reason.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. On National Education
paragraphs: The benefits that come from attending to private education will always be very limited, and the parent who truly sets his own hand to the plough will always be disappointed to some degree, until education becomes a great national concern. A man cannot withdraw into a wilderness with his child; and even if he did, he could not carry himself back into childhood and become the fitting friend and playmate of an infant or a youth. And when children are restricted to the company of men and women, they very quickly acquire that sort of premature adulthood which halts the growth of every vigorous power of mind or body. To open their faculties, they should be stimulated to think for themselves; and this can be done only by bringing a number of children together and having them pursue the same aims jointly.

A child very soon falls into a numbing laziness of mind, which he seldom has vigour enough to throw off, when he merely asks a question instead of searching for information, and then trusts the answer he is given without question. Among equals in age this could never happen; and the subjects of their inquiry, though they might be influenced, would not be wholly under the direction of men, who often dampen, if they do not destroy, abilities by pushing them forward too quickly. And too quickly they will certainly be pushed forward, if the child could be confined to the company of a man, however shrewd that man may be.

Besides, the seeds of every affection should be sown in youth; and the respectful regard that one feels for a parent is very different from the social affections that are to make up the happiness of life as it goes on. The basis of these is equality, and an exchange of feelings not weighed down by that watchful gravity which discourages argument, even if it does not compel submission. However great a child’s affection for his parent may be, he will always long to play and chatter with other children. And the very respect he feels — for filial esteem always has a touch of fear mixed into it — will, if it does not teach him cunning, at least stop him from pouring out the little secrets that first open the heart to friendship and trust, and lead it by degrees to a wider benevolence. On top of this, he will never acquire that frank openness of behaviour which young people can gain only by being often in company where they dare to say what they think, neither afraid of being rebuked for their presumption nor laughed at for their foolishness.

Struck forcibly by the reflections that the sight of schools, as they are now run, naturally prompted, I once gave my opinion rather warmly in favour of a private education; but further experience has led me to see the subject in a different light. Nevertheless, I still think schools, as they are now regulated, the hotbeds of vice and folly, and I think the knowledge of human nature that is supposed to be gained there is nothing but cunning selfishness.

At school, boys become gluttons and slovens; and instead of developing the domestic affections, they rush very early into the dissipation that ruins the constitution before it is fully formed, hardening the heart as it weakens the understanding.

In fact, I would object to boarding schools if only because of the unsettled state of mind that the expectation of the holidays produces. On these the children’s thoughts are fixed with eager hopes for, to speak moderately, at least half of the time; and when the holidays come, they are spent in utter dissipation and bestial indulgence.

On the other hand, when boys are brought up at home, they may follow a plan of study in a more orderly way than is possible when nearly a quarter of the year is actually spent in idleness, and as much again in regret and anticipation. Yet at home they acquire too high an opinion of their own importance, from being allowed to tyrannize over the servants, and from the anxiety that most mothers show about manners; for these mothers, eager to teach the accomplishments of a gentleman, smother the virtues of a man at birth. So, taken into society when they ought to be seriously occupied, and treated as men while they are still boys, they grow vain and effeminate.

The only way to avoid two extremes that are equally harmful to morality would be to find some means of combining a public and a private education. In this way, to make men citizens, two natural steps might be taken which seem to lead directly to the goal we want. For the domestic affections, which first open the heart to the various forms of human feeling, would be cultivated, while the children would still be allowed to spend a large part of their time with other children on terms of equality.

I still remember with pleasure the country day school, to which a boy trudged in the morning, wet or dry, carrying his books, and his dinner too if it was a good distance away. In those days a servant did not lead the young master by the hand; for once he had put on coat and breeches, he was left to fend for himself and to come home alone in the evening, to tell the exploits of the day at his parents’ knee. His father’s house was his home, and was fondly remembered ever afterwards. Indeed, I appeal to some superior men who were educated in this way: has not the memory of some shady lane where they learned their lesson, or of some stile where they sat making a kite or mending a bat, made their country dear to them?

But what boy ever remembered with pleasure the years he spent in close confinement at an academy near London? Unless, indeed, he happens to recall the poor scarecrow of an assistant master whom he tormented, or the tart-seller from whom he snatched a cake, to devour it with the catlike appetite of selfishness. At boarding schools of every kind, the recreation of the younger boys is mischief, and that of the older boys is vice. Besides, in the great schools, what can be more damaging to moral character than the system of tyranny and abject slavery that is established among the boys, to say nothing of the slavery to forms which makes religion worse than a farce? For what good can be expected from the youth who takes the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper to avoid forfeiting half a guinea, which he will probably spend afterwards on some sensual pleasure? Half the boys’ effort goes into escaping the obligation to attend public worship; and well it may, for such constant repetition of the same thing must be a very tiresome restraint on their natural liveliness. Since these ceremonies have the most fatal effect on their morals, and since a ritual performed by the lips while the heart and mind are far away is no longer stored up by our church as a bank to draw on for the fees of the poor souls in purgatory, why should they not be abolished?

But in this country the fear of innovation extends to everything. It is only a disguised fear, the anxious timidity of lazy slugs who guard, by sliming it over, the snug position that they regard as a hereditary estate, and who eat, drink and enjoy themselves instead of fulfilling the duties, apart from a few empty forms, for which it was endowed. These are the people who insist most strenuously that the founder’s will be observed, crying out against all reform as if it were a violation of justice. I am alluding here especially to the relics of popery retained in our colleges, where the Protestant members seem such sticklers for the established church; yet their zeal never makes them lose sight of the spoils of ignorance which grasping priests of superstitious memory scraped together.
