No; wise in their generation, they revere the prescriptive right of possession as a stronghold, and still let the sluggish bell tinkle for prayers, as in the days when the elevation of the host was thought to atone for the sins of the people, for fear that one reformation should lead to another, and the spirit kill the letter. These Roman Catholic customs have the most damaging effect on the morals of our clergy. For the idle vermin who, two or three times a day, perform in the most slovenly manner a service they think useless, but call their duty, soon lose all sense of duty. At college, compelled either to attend public worship or to evade it, they acquire a habitual contempt for the very service whose performance is to enable them to live in idleness. It is mumbled through as a matter of business, as a dull boy recites his lesson; and often the college slang slips out of the preacher the moment he has left the pulpit, and even while he is eating the dinner he earned in so dishonest a way.

Nothing, indeed, can be more irreverent than the cathedral service as it is now performed in this country; nor does the country contain a set of weaker men than those who are the slaves of this childish routine. A disgusting skeleton of its former state is still on show; but all the solemnity that engaged the imagination, even if it did not purify the heart, has been stripped away. The performance of high mass on the Continent must impress every mind in which a spark of imagination glows with that awe-filled melancholy, that sublime tenderness, so closely akin to devotion. I do not say that these devotional feelings are of more use, morally speaking, than any other emotion of taste; but I maintain that the theatrical pomp which gratifies our senses is preferable to the cold parade that insults the understanding without reaching the heart.

Among remarks on national education, such observations cannot be out of place, especially as the supporters of these institutions, which have sunk into childishness, pose as the champions of religion. Religion, pure source of comfort in this vale of tears! how your clear stream has been muddied by the dabblers who have presumed to confine in one narrow channel the living waters that flow for ever towards God — the sublime ocean of existence! What would life be without that peace which only the love of God, when built on humanity, can give? Every earthly affection turns back at times to prey upon the heart that feeds it; and the purest outpourings of benevolence, often rudely dampened by men, must rise as a free-will offering to Him who gave them birth, whose bright image they faintly reflect.

In public schools, however, religion, confused with tiresome ceremonies and unreasonable restraints, takes on the most unattractive appearance: not the sober, austere one that commands respect while it inspires fear, but a ridiculous cast that serves as the point of a pun. For in fact most of the good stories and smart sayings that enliven minds which have been concentrating on whist are fashioned out of those very incidents; and the men who labour to give them a comic twist are the very men who countenance the abuse in order to live on its spoils.

There is not, perhaps, a more dogmatic or self-indulgent set of men in the kingdom than the pedantic tyrants who live in colleges and preside over public schools. The holidays are as harmful to the morals of the masters as to those of the pupils; and the contact the masters keep up with the nobility brings into their own families the same vanity and extravagance that drive domestic duties and comforts out of the lordly mansion, whose grandeur they clumsily imitate on a smaller scale. The boys, who board at great expense with the masters and their assistants, are never made part of the household, though they are placed there for that purpose. For after a silent dinner they gulp down a hasty glass of wine and withdraw to plan some mischievous prank, or to mock the looks or the manners of the very people they have just been fawning on, and whom they ought to regard as standing in for their parents.

Can it be surprising, then, that boys who are thus shut out from social conversation become selfish and vicious? Or that a bishop’s mitre often crowns the brow of one of these diligent pastors? The wish to live in the same style as the rank just above them infects every individual and every class of people, and baseness goes hand in hand with this ignoble ambition. But the most degrading professions are those in which patronage is the ladder; and yet the tutors of youth are generally chosen from one of these professions. Can men whose conduct must be governed by the cautious prudence that is always on the lookout for promotion be expected to inspire independent feelings?

Far from giving any thought to the morals of boys, however, I have heard several schoolmasters argue that they had undertaken only to teach Latin and Greek, and that they had done their duty by sending some good scholars to university.
A few good scholars, I admit, may have been produced by rivalry and discipline; but to bring these clever boys forward, the health and morals of a great many have been sacrificed.

The sons of our gentry and of wealthy commoners are mostly educated at these institutions; and will anyone claim that the majority of them, making every allowance, can be described as passable scholars?

It does not benefit society to bring forward a few brilliant men at the cost of the multitude. It is true that great men seem to spring up at the right moments, as great revolutions occur, to restore order and to blow away the clouds that gather over the face of truth; but let more reason and virtue prevail in society, and these strong winds would not be needed. Public education of every kind should aim at forming citizens; but if you wish to make good citizens, you must first exercise the affections of a son and a brother. This is the only way to enlarge the heart; for public affections, like public virtues, must always grow out of private character, or else they are mere meteors that streak across a dark sky and vanish even as they are gazed at and admired.

Few, I believe, have felt much affection for mankind who did not first love their parents, their brothers and sisters, and even the household animals they first played with. The exercise of youthful sympathies shapes the moral temperament; and it is the memory of these first affections and pursuits that gives life to those which later come more under the direction of reason. The warmest friendships are formed in youth, when the vital spirits, rising at the same time, blend kindly together; or rather, when the heart, prepared to receive friendship, grows used to seeking pleasure in something nobler than the surly gratification of appetite.

So, to inspire a love of home and of domestic pleasures, children ought to be educated at home; for riotous holidays only make them fond of home for their own selfish sakes. Yet the holidays, which do not nourish the domestic affections, constantly interrupt the course of study and defeat any plan of improvement that includes self-restraint. Still, if they were abolished, children would be completely separated from their parents; and I doubt whether they would become better citizens by sacrificing the affections that prepare them for citizenship, and by destroying the force of the family ties that make the married state as necessary as it is respectable. But if a private education breeds self-importance, or isolates a man within his family, the evil is merely moved elsewhere, not cured.
This line of reasoning brings me back to a subject I intend to dwell on: the need to establish proper day schools.

But these should be national institutions; for as long as schoolmasters depend on the whims of parents, little effort can be expected from them beyond what is needed to please ignorant people. Indeed, the master’s need to give the parents some sample of the boy’s abilities, which is shown to every visitor during the holidays, does more harm than one might at first suppose. For such samples are seldom, to put it moderately, entirely the child’s own work; and so the master either countenances falsehood or winds up the poor machine to some extraordinary effort that damages the wheels and halts the progress of gradual improvement. The memory is loaded with words it does not understand, to be shown off, while the understanding acquires no clear ideas. Yet only that education which teaches young people how to begin to think deserves, in the full sense, to be called cultivation of the mind. The imagination should not be allowed to corrupt the understanding before the understanding has gained strength, or vanity will become the forerunner of vice; for every way of displaying a child’s attainments harms its moral character.

How much time is wasted teaching children to recite what they do not understand! Meanwhile, seated on benches in all their finery, the mammas listen in amazement to the parrot-like chatter, delivered in solemn cadences with all the pomp of ignorance and folly. Such displays serve only to drive the spreading roots of vanity through the whole mind; for they teach children neither to speak fluently nor to behave gracefully. Quite the opposite: these frivolous exercises might, in a word, be called the study of affectation. For we now rarely see a simple, bashful boy, though few people of taste were ever put off by that awkward sheepishness so natural to the age, which schools and an early entry into society have turned into impudence and apish grimacing.

Yet how can these things be remedied as long as schoolmasters depend wholly on parents for a living, and while so many rival schools hang out their bait to catch the attention of vain fathers and mothers, whose parental affection leads them only to wish that their children should outshine their neighbours’?
Without great good luck, a sensible, conscientious man would starve before he could build up a school, if he scorned to dupe foolish parents by practising the secret tricks of the trade.

Even in the best-regulated schools, however, where crowds are not crammed together, many bad habits must be acquired. But at ordinary schools the body, the heart and the understanding are all equally stunted; for parents are often looking only for the cheapest school, and the master could not make a living unless he took far more pupils than he could manage by himself. Nor will the meagre sum paid for each child allow him to hire enough assistants to help with the mechanical part of the work. Besides, whatever show the house and garden may make, the children enjoy the comforts of neither; for they are continually reminded, by tiresome restrictions, that they are not at home, and the best rooms, the garden, etc., must be kept in order for the entertainment of the parents, who visit the school on a Sunday and are impressed by the very display that makes their children’s situation uncomfortable.

With what disgust have I heard sensible women — for girls are more restrained and intimidated than boys — describe the wearisome confinement they endured at school! Perhaps they were not allowed to step off one broad path in a magnificent garden, and were made to march stupidly back and forth with a steady bearing, heads held up, toes turned out and shoulders braced back, instead of bounding about, as nature directs in order to complete her own design, in the varied postures that do so much for health. The pure high spirits that make both mind and body shoot up, and that open the tender blossoms of hope, turn sour and are vented in idle wishes or pert complaints, which narrow the faculties and spoil the temper. Or else they rise to the brain and, sharpening the understanding before it has gained a matching strength, produce that pitiful cunning which is the disgraceful mark of the female mind — and which, I fear, will always mark it as long as women remain the slaves of power!

The little respect that the male world pays to chastity is, I am convinced, the chief source of many of the physical and moral evils that torment mankind, as well as of the vices and follies that degrade and destroy women. Yet at school boys unfailingly lose that decent bashfulness which might have ripened into modesty at home.

I have already criticized the bad habits that females acquire when they are shut up together; and I think the observation may fairly be extended to the other sex, until we reach the natural conclusion I have had in view throughout: that, to improve both sexes, they ought to be educated together, not only in private families but in public schools. If marriage is the cement of society, all mankind should be educated on the same model; otherwise relations between the sexes will never deserve the name of fellowship. Nor will women ever fulfil the particular duties of their sex until they become enlightened citizens, until they become free by being enabled to earn their own living, independent of men — in the same way, I mean, to prevent any misunderstanding, as one man is independent of another. Indeed, marriage will never be held sacred until women, by being brought up with men, are prepared to be their companions rather than their mistresses; for the base twists and turns of cunning will always make them contemptible, while oppression makes them timid. So convinced am I of this truth that I will venture to predict that virtue will never prevail in society until the virtues of both sexes are founded on reason, and until the affections common to both are allowed to gain their proper strength through the performance of mutual duties.

If boys and girls were allowed to pursue the same studies together, those graceful proprieties which produce modesty might be instilled early, without the sexual distinctions that taint the mind. Lessons in politeness, and that rulebook of decorum which follows close on the heels of falsehood, would be made useless by habitually correct behaviour — not, indeed, put on for visitors like the courtly robe of politeness, but the sober result of a clean mind. Would not this simple elegance of sincerity be a chaste tribute paid to the domestic affections, far surpassing the tawdry compliments that shine with a false lustre in the heartless dealings of fashionable life? But until more understanding holds sway in society, there will always be a lack of heart and taste, and the harlot’s rouge will take the place of that heavenly blush which only virtuous affections can bring to the face. Gallantry, and what is called love, may exist without simplicity of character; but the main pillars of friendship are respect and trust — esteem is never founded on it knows not what.

A taste for the fine arts requires much cultivation; but no more than a taste for the virtuous affections does; and both presuppose that enlargement of mind which opens so many sources of mental pleasure. Why do people rush to noisy scenes and crowded gatherings? I would answer: because they lack activity of mind, because they have not cherished the virtues of the heart. They therefore see and feel only coarsely, and constantly pine for variety, finding everything simple insipid.

This argument may be carried further than philosophers realize; for if nature destined woman in particular to perform domestic duties, she made her highly susceptible to the affections of attachment. Now women are notoriously devoted to pleasure; and, by my definition, they must naturally be so, because they cannot enter into the fine details of domestic taste, lacking judgment, which is the foundation of all taste. For the understanding, whatever sensual quibblers may say, keeps for itself the privilege of bringing pure joy to the heart.

With what a languid yawn have I seen an admirable poem tossed aside, one that a man of true taste returns to again and again with rapture! And while melody has almost stopped my breath, a lady has asked me where I bought my gown. I have also seen an eye that glanced coldly over a most exquisite painting come to rest, sparkling with pleasure, on a crudely sketched caricature; and while some awe-inspiring feature of nature has spread a sublime stillness through my soul, I have been asked to watch the pretty tricks of a lapdog with which my perverse fate forced me to travel. Is it surprising that such a tasteless creature would sooner caress this dog than her children? Or that she would prefer the ranting of flattery to the simple tones of sincerity?

To illustrate this remark, I must be permitted to point out that men of the highest genius and the most cultivated minds have seemed to take the keenest delight in the simple beauties of nature; and they must have felt strongly what they have described so well: the charm that natural affections and unaffected feelings spread around the human character. It is this power of looking into the heart, and of vibrating in response to each emotion, that enables the poet to personify every passion and the painter to sketch with a brush of fire.

True taste is always the work of the understanding engaged in observing natural effects; and until women have more understanding, it is pointless to expect them to have domestic taste. Their lively senses will always be at work hardening their hearts, and the emotions struck from them will go on being vivid and fleeting, unless a proper education fills their minds with knowledge.

It is the lack of domestic taste, and not the acquisition of knowledge, that draws women away from their families and tears the smiling baby from the breast that ought to feed it. Women have been left in ignorance and slavish dependence for many, very many years, and still we hear of nothing but their love of pleasure and of power, their preference for rakes and soldiers, their childish attachment to trinkets, and the vanity that makes them value accomplishments above virtues.

History presents a fearful catalogue of the crimes their cunning has produced, whenever the weak slaves have had skill enough to outwit their masters. In France, and in how many other countries, have men been the self-indulgent despots and women the crafty ministers? Does this prove that ignorance and dependence make them domestic? Is not their folly a byword among the libertines who unwind in their company? And do not men of sense constantly lament that an immoderate love of dress and dissipation keeps the mother of a family for ever away from home? Their hearts have not been corrupted by knowledge, nor their minds led astray by scientific pursuits; yet they do not fulfil the particular duties that nature calls on them, as women, to fulfil. On the contrary, the state of war that exists between the sexes makes them use those wiles which frustrate the more open schemes of force.
When, therefore, I call women slaves, I mean it in a political and civil sense; for indirectly they gain too much power, and are degraded by their efforts to gain illegitimate influence.

Let an enlightened nation, then, try what effect reason would have in bringing them back to nature and to their duty; and, allowing them to share the advantages of education and government with man, let it see whether they become better as they grow wiser and become free. They cannot be harmed by the experiment; for it is not in man’s power to make them more insignificant than they are now.

To make this practicable, the government should establish day schools for particular ages, in which boys and girls might be educated together. The school for the younger children, from five to nine years old, ought to be completely free and open to all classes.* A sufficient number of masters should also be chosen by a select committee in each parish, to which any complaint of negligence, etc., might be brought, if signed by six of the children’s parents.
(*Footnote. In treating this part of the subject I have borrowed some ideas from a very sensible pamphlet on public education written by the late Bishop of Autun.)

Assistant masters, or ushers, would then be unnecessary; for experience, I believe, will always show that this kind of subordinate authority does particular harm to the morals of the young. What, indeed, is more likely to corrupt the character than outward submission combined with inward contempt? Yet how can boys be expected to respect an usher when the master seems to regard him as a servant, and almost to encourage the ridicule that becomes the boys’ chief amusement in their play hours?

But nothing of this kind could happen in an elementary day school where boys and girls, rich and poor, would meet together. And to prevent any distinctions based on vanity, they should all be dressed alike and all be obliged to submit to the same discipline, or else leave the school. The schoolroom ought to be surrounded by a large plot of ground where the children could take useful exercise, for at this age they should not be kept at any sedentary task for more than an hour at a time. Yet these breaks could all be made part of elementary education, since many things that would fall on deaf ears if their principles were laid down dryly will both develop and delight the senses when they are introduced as a kind of show: botany, mechanics and astronomy, for instance. Reading, writing, arithmetic, natural history and some simple experiments in natural philosophy might fill the day; but these studies should never cut into games and exercise in the open air. The elements of religion, history, the history of man and politics might also be taught through conversation, in the Socratic manner.

After the age of nine, girls and boys who are intended for domestic service or for mechanical trades ought to be moved to other schools and given instruction suited, to some degree, to the future occupation of each individual. The two sexes would still be taught together in the morning; but in the afternoon the girls should attend a school where their work would be plain sewing, dressmaking, millinery and the like.

Young people of superior ability or fortune might now be taught, in another school, the dead and living languages and the elements of science, and might continue the study of history and politics on a broader scale, which would not exclude polite literature. Girls and boys still together? I hear some readers ask. Yes. And I should fear no other consequence than that some early attachment might form, which, while it had the best effect on the moral character of the young people, might not entirely suit the plans of their parents. For it will be a long time, I fear, before the world is so enlightened that parents whose only concern is to make their children virtuous will let them choose their own companions for life.

Besides, this would be a sure way to encourage early marriages, and the most beneficial physical and moral effects naturally follow from early marriage. How different is the character of a married citizen from that of the selfish fop who lives only for himself, and who is often afraid to marry in case he cannot keep up a certain style of living! Apart from great emergencies, which would seldom arise in a society founded on equality, a man can be prepared to carry out the duties of public life only by the habitual practice of those lesser duties that form the man.

Under this plan of education, boys’ health would not be ruined by the early debauchery that now makes men so selfish, nor would girls be made weak and vain by idleness and frivolous occupations. I am assuming, however, that such a degree of equality would be established between the sexes as would shut out gallantry and coquetry, while still allowing friendship and love to temper the heart for the performance of higher duties.

These would be schools of morality — and if man’s happiness were allowed to flow from the pure springs of duty and affection, what progress might the human mind not make? A society can be happy and free only to the degree that it is virtuous; yet the distinctions now established in society eat away all private virtue and blight all public virtue.

I have already protested against the custom of confining girls to their needlework and shutting them out of all political and civil occupations; for by narrowing their minds in this way we make them unfit to perform the particular duties that nature has assigned to them.

Occupied only with the little incidents of the day, they inevitably grow up cunning. My very soul has often been sickened to watch the sly tricks women use to obtain some foolish thing on which their silly hearts are set. Since they are not allowed to manage money or to call anything their own, they learn to make a penny on the housekeeping; or, if a husband gives offence by staying away from home, or arouses some feelings of jealousy, a new gown or some pretty trinket smooths Juno’s angry brow.

But these LITTLENESSES would not degrade their character if women were led to respect themselves and if political and moral subjects were opened to them; and I will venture to say that this is the only way to make them properly attentive to their domestic duties. An active mind takes in the whole range of its duties and finds time enough for all of them. It is not, I insist, a bold attempt to rival masculine virtues, nor the charm of literary studies, nor the steady investigation of scientific subjects, that leads women away from duty. No, it is idleness and vanity — the love of pleasure and the love of power — that will rule supreme in an empty mind. I say empty, and I say it emphatically, because the education women now receive hardly deserves the name. The little knowledge they are encouraged to acquire during the important years of youth relates merely to accomplishments, and to accomplishments with no foundation beneath them; for unless the understanding is cultivated, every grace is superficial and monotonous. Like the charms of a made-up face, they strike the senses only in a crowd; at home, lacking mind, they lack variety. The result is obvious. In the lively scenes of dissipation we meet the artificial mind along with the artificial face, for those who flee from solitude dread the domestic circle next to solitude itself. Having no power to amuse or interest others, they feel their own insignificance, or they find nothing there to amuse or interest themselves.

Besides, what could be more indelicate than a girl’s coming out into the fashionable world? In other words, it means bringing a marriageable young miss to market, her person carried richly decked out from one public place to another. Yet as they mix in this giddy circle under restraint, these butterflies long to flutter about freely, for the first affection of their souls is for their own persons, to which their attention has been directed with the most painstaking care while they were being prepared for the moment that decides their fate for life. Instead of following this idle routine and sighing after tasteless show and heartless ceremony, with what dignity the young people of both sexes would form attachments in the schools I have briefly outlined! In these schools, as the pupils grew older, dancing, music and drawing might be admitted as recreations, for young people of fortune ought to remain at them, more or less, until they came of age. Those who were intended for particular professions might attend, three or four mornings a week, the schools set aside for their specific training.

For the present I offer these observations only as hints — or rather, indeed, as an outline of the plan I have in mind, not a fully worked-out one. But I must add that I strongly approve of one rule mentioned in the pamphlet I referred to earlier (the Bishop of Autun’s): that of making children and young people independent of their masters in the matter of punishment. They should be tried by their peers. This would be an admirable way of fixing sound principles of justice in the mind, and might have the happiest effect on the temper, which is soured or irritated very early by tyranny until it becomes peevishly cunning or fiercely overbearing.

My imagination leaps ahead with benevolent warmth to greet these amiable and admirable groups, in spite of the sneers of cold hearts, who are free to pronounce, with frigid self-importance, the damning word — romantic. I shall try to blunt its force by repeating the words of an eloquent moralist: “I know not whether the allusions of a truly humane heart, whose zeal renders everything easy, is not preferable to that rough and repulsing reason, which always finds in indifference for the public good, the first obstacle to whatever would promote it.”

I know that libertines will also cry out that woman would be unsexed by acquiring strength of body and mind, and that beauty, soft bewitching beauty! would no longer adorn the daughters of men. I hold a very different opinion. I think that, on the contrary, we should then see dignified beauty and true grace, and that many powerful physical and moral causes would combine to produce them. It would not, admittedly, be languid beauty or the graces of helplessness; it would be the kind of beauty seen in the relics of antiquity, which seems to make us respect the human body as a majestic building, fit to receive a noble inhabitant.

I have not forgotten the popular view that the Greek statues were not modelled on nature — by which I mean not on the proportions of any one particular man — but that beautiful limbs and features were chosen from various bodies to make up a harmonious whole. This may be true to some degree. The fine ideal image formed by an exalted imagination might surpass the materials the artist found in nature, and so it might properly be called the model of mankind rather than of a man. Yet it was not a mechanical selection of limbs and features; it was the outpouring of a heated imagination that burst forth, and the artist’s fine senses and broad understanding chose the solid material that he drew into this glowing focus.

I said that it was not mechanical because a whole was produced — a model of that grand simplicity, of those combined energies, which seize our attention and command our reverence. For a slavish copy of nature, even of beautiful nature, produces only insipid, lifeless beauty. Yet, quite apart from these observations, I believe that the human form must once have been far more beautiful than it is now, because extreme idleness, barbarous bindings, and the many causes that act forcibly upon it in our luxurious state of society did not then hold back its growth or deform it. Exercise and cleanliness seem to be the surest means not only of preserving health but of promoting beauty, if physical causes alone are considered. Yet this is not enough; moral causes must work alongside them, or beauty will be merely of the rustic kind that blooms on the innocent, healthy faces of some country people whose minds have never been exercised. To make the person perfect, physical and moral beauty ought to be attained together, each giving and gaining strength through the combination. Judgment must sit upon the brow, affection and imagination shine in the eye, and humanity shape the curve of the cheek; otherwise the sparkle of the finest eye and the elegant finish of the fairest features are in vain. Meanwhile grace and modesty should appear in every movement that shows the active limbs and well-knit joints. But this fair assembly of qualities is not brought together by chance. It is the reward of efforts that support one another; for judgment can be acquired only through reflection, affection only through the performance of duties, and humanity only through the exercise of compassion towards every living creature.

Kindness to animals should be especially instilled as part of national education, for it is not at present one of our national virtues. Among the lower classes, tenderness towards the humble, dumb creatures of the household is found more often in a savage state than in a civilized one. For civilization prevents the close contact that breeds affection in the rough hut or mud cabin. It leads uncultivated minds — which are merely corrupted by the refinements prevailing in a society where the rich trample them underfoot — to tyrannize over animals in revenge for the insults they are forced to endure from their superiors.

This habitual cruelty is first picked up at school, where tormenting the wretched animals that come their way is one of the boys’ favourite sports. As they grow up, the step from cruelty to animals to domestic tyranny over wives, children and servants is a very easy one. Justice, or even benevolence, will not be a powerful motive to action unless it extends to the whole of creation; indeed, I believe it may be laid down as an axiom that those who can watch pain unmoved will soon learn to inflict it.

The common run of people are governed by their feelings of the moment and by habits they have picked up by chance; but little reliance can be placed on partial feelings, however just they may be, for when they are not strengthened by reflection, custom weakens them until they are hardly felt at all. The sympathies of our nature are strengthened by thoughtful reflection and deadened by thoughtless habit. Macbeth’s heart struck at him more for one murder, the first, than for the hundred that followed and were needed to support it. But when I used the word vulgar, I did not mean to limit my remark to the poor; for partial humanity, grounded in passing sensations or in whim, is just as conspicuous among the rich, if not more so.

The lady who weeps for the bird starved in a trap, and curses the devils in human shape who goad the poor ox to madness or whip the patient donkey as it staggers under a load beyond its strength, will nevertheless keep her coachman and horses waiting for her for whole hours while the sharp frost bites, or while the rain beats against her tightly closed windows, which do not let in a breath of air to tell her how roughly the wind is blowing outside. And she who takes her dogs to bed with her, and nurses them with a great show of sensibility when they are sick, will let her babies grow up crooked in a nursery. This illustration of my argument is taken from real life. The woman I have in mind was handsome — thought very handsome by those who do not miss the mind when the face is plump and fair — but her understanding had not been drawn away from female duties by literature, nor her innocence corrupted by knowledge. No, she was thoroughly feminine, in the masculine sense of the word; and, far from loving these spoiled animals that filled the place her children ought to have occupied, she merely lisped a pretty mixture of French and English nonsense to please the men who crowded round her. The wife, the mother and the human creature were all swallowed up by the artificial character that an improper education and the selfish vanity of beauty had produced.

I do not like to draw a distinction where there is no difference, and I confess that I have been as disgusted by the fine lady who clasped her lapdog to her bosom instead of her child as by the ferocity of a man who, while beating his horse, declared that it knew as well as a Christian when it did wrong.

This brood of folly shows how mistaken are those who, if they allow women out of their harems, do not cultivate their understanding so as to plant virtues in their hearts. For if women had good sense, they might acquire the domestic taste that would lead them to love their whole family, from the husband down to the house dog, in a reasonable order of precedence; nor would they ever insult humanity in the person of the lowliest servant by paying more attention to the comfort of an animal than to that of a fellow creature.

My observations on national education are clearly only hints; but my chief aim is to press the necessity of educating the sexes together in order to perfect both, and of letting children sleep at home so that they may learn to love home. Yet, so that private affections may support public affections instead of smothering them, children should be sent to school to mix with a number of equals; for only through the jostling of equality can we form a fair opinion of ourselves.

To make mankind more virtuous, and therefore happier, both sexes must act on the same principle; but how can that be expected when only one of them is allowed to see the reasonableness of it? Likewise, to make the social compact truly fair, and to spread those enlightening principles that alone can improve the lot of man, women must be allowed to base their virtue on knowledge; and this is hardly possible unless they are educated through the same studies as men. For at present they are made so inferior by ignorance and base desires that they do not deserve to be ranked with men; or else, by the serpentine wrigglings of cunning, they climb the tree of knowledge and gain only enough to lead men astray.

The history of every nation makes it plain that women cannot be confined to purely domestic pursuits; for they will not fulfil their family duties unless their minds range more widely, and while they are kept in ignorance they become the slaves of pleasure in the same measure as they are the slaves of man. Nor can they be shut out of great undertakings, although the narrowness of their minds often leads them to spoil what they are unable to understand.

The libertinism, and even the virtues, of superior men will always give women of a certain kind great power over them; and these weak women, swayed by childish passions and selfish vanity, will cast a false light over the very things these men see with their own eyes — men who ought to be enlightening women’s judgment. Men of imagination, and those sanguine characters who mostly steer the course of human affairs, generally relax in the company of women; and surely I need not remind even the most superficial reader of history of the many instances of vice and oppression produced by the private intrigues of female favourites, not to dwell on the mischief that naturally arises from the blundering interference of well-meaning folly. For in matters of business it is far better to deal with a knave than with a fool, because a knave sticks to some plan, and any rational plan can be seen through much sooner than a sudden flight of folly. The power that base and foolish women have held over wise men of sensibility is notorious. I shall mention only one instance.

Who ever drew a more exalted female character than Rousseau, even though he constantly tried to degrade the sex as a whole? And why was he so anxious to do so? Truly, to justify to himself the affection that weakness and virtue had led him to cherish for that fool Theresa. He could not raise her to the common level of her sex, and so he laboured to bring woman down to hers. He found her a convenient, humble companion, and pride made him resolve to find some superior virtues in the being he had chosen to live with. But did her conduct during his life and after his death not clearly show how grossly mistaken he was to call her a celestial innocent? Indeed, in the bitterness of his heart he himself complains that, when his bodily infirmities meant he could no longer treat her as a woman, she ceased to feel any affection for him. And it was very natural that she should, for, as they had so few feelings in common, what was there to hold her once the sexual tie was broken? To hold the affection of a woman whose sensibility was confined to one sex — indeed, to one man — requires good sense to turn that sensibility into the broad channel of humanity. Many women do not have mind enough to feel affection for a woman or friendship for a man. But the sexual weakness that makes woman depend on man for her living produces a kind of catlike affection, which leads a wife to purr about her husband as she would about any man who fed and petted her.

Men, however, are often gratified by this kind of doting, which is confined, in a beastly manner, to themselves; but should they ever become more virtuous, they will want to converse by their fireside with a friend once they have stopped playing with a mistress. Besides, understanding is needed to give variety and interest even to sensual pleasures; for the mind that can go on loving when neither virtue nor good sense gives a human appearance to an animal appetite stands low indeed on the intellectual scale. But good sense will always carry the greater weight; and if women are not, in general, brought more nearly to a level with men, some superior women, like the Greek courtesans, will gather the men of ability around them and draw away from their families many citizens who would have stayed at home had their wives possessed more sense, or the graces that come from exercising the understanding and the imagination, the legitimate parents of taste. A woman of talent, unless she is positively ugly, will always gain great power, heightened by the weakness of her sex; and as men acquire virtue and delicacy through the exertion of reason, they will look for both in women. But women can acquire them only in the same way that men do.

Have the women of France or Italy confined themselves to domestic life? Although they have not so far had any political existence, have they not nonetheless held great power illicitly, corrupting both themselves and the men whose passions they played upon? In short, from whatever angle I view the subject, reason and experience convince me that the only way to lead women to fulfil their particular duties is to free them from all restraint by allowing them to share in the inherent rights of mankind.

Make them free, and they will quickly become wise and virtuous, as men become more so; for the improvement must be mutual, or else the justice that one half of the human race is forced to submit to will recoil on their oppressors, and the virtue of man will be eaten away by the insect he keeps under his feet.
Let men make their choice. Man and woman were made for each other, though not to become one being; and if men will not improve women, they will corrupt them!

I am speaking of the improvement and emancipation of the whole sex. I know that the behaviour of a few women who, by accident or by following a strong natural inclination, have acquired a share of knowledge greater than the rest of their sex has often been overbearing; but there have been women who, in gaining knowledge, have not cast off modesty, nor have they always pedantically seemed to despise the ignorance they worked to clear from their own minds. The outcries that any advice about female learning commonly provokes, especially from pretty women, therefore often spring from envy. When such women happen to see that even the brilliance of their eyes and the flippant playfulness of refined coquetry will not always hold attention for a whole evening — should a woman of more cultivated understanding try to turn the conversation in a rational direction — their usual consolation is that such women seldom find husbands. What tricks have I not seen silly women use to break up, by FLIRTATION (a very telling word for such a manoeuvre), a rational conversation that had made the men forget they were pretty women!

But even granting what comes very naturally to man — that the possession of rare abilities really does tend to arouse overweening pride, which is disgusting in men and women alike — to what a state of inferiority must the female faculties have rusted, when so small an amount of knowledge as those women attained who have been sneeringly called learned women could be remarkable? Remarkable enough, that is, to puff up its owner and arouse envy in her contemporaries and in some of the other sex. Indeed, has not a little rationality exposed many women to the harshest censure? I refer to well-known facts, for I have often heard women ridiculed, and every little weakness of theirs exposed, simply because they followed the advice of certain medical men and departed from the beaten path in their way of caring for their infants. I have actually heard this barbarous dislike of innovation carried still further: a sensible woman who had wisely taken such care to preserve her children’s health was branded an unnatural mother when, in the midst of all her care, she lost one of them to one of those accidents of infancy that no prudence can prevent. Her acquaintances remarked that this was the result of newfangled notions — the newfangled notions of comfort and cleanliness. And those who claimed the authority of experience, though they had long clung to prejudices that, in the opinion of the wisest physicians, have thinned the human race, almost rejoiced at the misfortune, since it lent a kind of sanction to established custom.

Indeed, if only for this reason, the national education of women is of the greatest importance; for what a number of human sacrifices are offered to that Moloch, prejudice! And in how many ways are children destroyed by the lust of man? The lack of natural affection in many women, who are drawn away from their duty by the admiration of men, and the ignorance of others, make the infancy of man a far more dangerous state than that of animals; yet men are unwilling to place women in situations that would allow them to acquire enough understanding to know how even to nurse their babies.
This truth strikes me so forcibly that I would rest the whole drift of my reasoning upon it; for whatever tends to unfit a woman for the character of a mother takes her out of her proper sphere.

But it is useless to expect the present generation of weak mothers either to take the reasonable care of a child’s body that is needed to lay the foundation of a sound constitution — supposing that the child does not suffer for the sins of its fathers — or to manage its temper so wisely that, as it grows up, it will not have to throw off everything its mother, its first teacher, taught it directly or indirectly; and unless the mind has uncommon vigour, womanish follies will cling to the character throughout life. The weakness of the mother will be visited upon the children! And as long as women are educated to rely on their husbands for judgment, this must always be the result; for an understanding cannot be improved by halves, nor can any being act wisely by imitation, because every circumstance of life has a kind of individuality that requires an exercise of judgment to adapt general rules. The being who can think soundly along one track will soon extend its intellectual empire; and she who has judgment enough to manage her children will not submit, right or wrong, to her husband, nor submit patiently to the social laws that make a wife a nonentity.

In public schools, to guard against the errors of ignorance, women should be taught the elements of anatomy and medicine, not only so that they can take proper care of their own health but so that they become rational nurses to their infants, parents and husbands; for the bills of mortality are swollen by the blunders of self-willed old women who give remedies of their own devising without knowing anything about the human body. It is equally proper, even from a purely domestic point of view, to acquaint women with the anatomy of the mind, by allowing the sexes to share every pursuit together, and by leading them to observe the progress of the human understanding in the advancement of the sciences and arts, never forgetting the science of morality or the study of the political history of mankind.

Man has been called a microcosm, and every family might likewise be called a state. States, it is true, have mostly been governed by arts that disgrace the character of man; and the lack of a just constitution and equal laws has so confused the ideas of the worldly-wise that they more than doubt whether it is reasonable to contend for the rights of humanity. So morality, polluted in the national reservoir, sends out streams of vice to corrupt the constituent parts of the body politic. But if nobler, or rather juster, principles governed the laws — which ought to be the government of society, rather than those who carry them out — duty might become the rule of private conduct.

Besides, by exercising their bodies and minds, women would acquire the mental activity so necessary in a mother, combined with the fortitude that distinguishes steadiness of conduct from the obstinate perversity of weakness. For it is dangerous to advise the idle to be firm, because they at once become harsh, and, to save themselves trouble, severely punish faults that the patient fortitude of reason might have prevented.

But fortitude presupposes strength of mind; and is strength of mind to be gained by idle compliance? By asking advice instead of using one’s own judgment? By obeying out of fear, instead of practising the forbearance that we all need ourselves? The conclusion I wish to draw is obvious: make women rational creatures and free citizens, and they will quickly become good wives and mothers — that is, provided men do not neglect the duties of husbands and fathers.

In discussing the advantages that might reasonably be expected from a combination of public and private education such as I have sketched, I have dwelt chiefly on those that particularly concern the female world, because I believe the female world to be oppressed. Yet the gangrene produced by the vices that oppression breeds is not confined to the diseased part; it spreads through society at large. So when I wish to see my sex become more like moral agents, my heart leaps at the prospect of the general spread of that sublime contentment which only morality can spread.

chapters.title: Chapter 13. Some Instances of the Folly Which the Ignorance of Women Generates; With Concluding Reflections on the Moral Improvement That a Revolution in Female Manners May Naturally Be Expected to Produce
paragraphs: There are many follies that are, to some extent, peculiar to women: sins against reason, of commission as well as of omission; but since they all spring from ignorance or prejudice, I shall point out only those that seem harmful to their moral character. And in criticizing them I particularly wish to prove that the weakness of mind and body which men have tried, from various motives, to perpetuate prevents women from carrying out the duty peculiar to their sex: for when weakness of body will not allow them to suckle their children, and weakness of mind makes them spoil their tempers — is woman in a natural state?
SECTION 13.1.
One glaring example of the weakness that comes from ignorance claims attention first, and calls for stern rebuke.

In this capital a number of lurking leeches earn a shameful living by exploiting the credulity of women, professing to cast nativities, that is, to draw up horoscopes; and many women who, proud of their rank and wealth, regard ordinary people with sovereign contempt, prove by this very credulity that the distinction is arbitrary, and that their minds have not been cultivated enough to lift them above the prejudices of the common people. Because women have never been taught to see knowledge of their duty as the one thing necessary to know, or to live in the present by fulfilling it, they long to peep into what lies ahead, to find out what they may look forward to that will make life interesting, and to break the blank of ignorance. I must be permitted a serious word of protest to the ladies who run after these idle inventions; for ladies, mistresses of households, feel no shame at being driven in their own carriages to the fortune-teller’s door. Should any of them read this book, I entreat them to answer the following questions in their own hearts, remembering that they stand in the presence of God.
Do you believe that there is only one God, and that he is powerful, wise and good?
Do you believe that he created all things, and that all beings depend on him?

Do you trust in his wisdom, so evident in his works and in your own body, and are you convinced that he has arranged everything that lies beyond the reach of your senses in the same perfect harmony, to accomplish his purposes?

Do you acknowledge that the power to look into the future, and to see things that are not as though they were, belongs to the Creator? And if he should see fit, by an impression on the minds of his creatures, to reveal to them some event hidden in the shadows of time and not yet born, to whom would the secret be disclosed by direct inspiration? The judgment of the ages will answer this question — to venerable old men, to people known for outstanding piety.

The oracles of old were delivered in this way, by priests dedicated to the service of the god who was supposed to inspire them. The glare of worldly splendour that surrounded these impostors, and the respect shown them by crafty politicians, who knew how to make use of this handy engine for bending the necks of the strong beneath the rule of the cunning, spread a sacred, mysterious veil of holiness over their lies and abominations. Impressed by such solemn religious pageantry, a Greek or Roman lady might be excused for consulting the oracle when she was anxious to pry into the future or to ask about some uncertain event; and her inquiries, however contrary to reason, could not be counted impious. But can those who profess Christianity escape that charge? Can a Christian suppose that the favourites of the Most High, the highly favoured, would have to lurk in disguise and play the most dishonest tricks to cheat silly women out of the money that the poor beg for in vain?

Do not tell me that such questions insult common sense; it is your own behaviour, O foolish women, that brings odium on your whole sex! These reflections ought to make you tremble at your thoughtlessness and your irrational devotion, for I do not imagine that every one of you left her religion, such as it is, outside when she entered those mysterious houses. Yet, as I have all along supposed that I am addressing ignorant women — and ignorant you are, in the most emphatic sense of the word — it would be absurd to reason with you about the gross folly of wishing to know what Supreme Wisdom has chosen to conceal.

You would probably not understand me if I tried to show you that such foreknowledge would be utterly inconsistent with the great purpose of life, which is to make human creatures wise and virtuous; and that, if God sanctioned it, it would disturb the order established in creation; and if God does not sanction it, do you expect to hear the truth? Can events be foretold — events that have not yet taken on a body and so become open to mortal inspection? Can they be foreseen by a vicious worldling who feeds his appetites by preying on the foolish ones?

Perhaps, though, you piously believe in the devil and suppose — to shift the ground of the question — that he may come to the aid of his worshippers? But if you truly respect the power of such a being, the enemy of goodness and of God, how can you go to church once you have been placed under such an obligation to him? From these delusions one passes quite naturally to the still more fashionable frauds practised by the whole tribe of magnetizers; and about them, too, it is equally fitting to put a few questions to women.

Do you know anything about how the human body is constructed? If not, you ought to be told what every child should know: that when its admirable system has been upset by intemperance or idleness — I do not mean violent illnesses, but chronic diseases — it must be brought back to health by slow degrees; and, if the vital functions have not been seriously damaged, regimen (another word for temperance), air, exercise and a few medicines prescribed by people who have studied the human body are the only human means yet discovered, that will bear investigation, of recovering that priceless blessing, health.
Do you believe, then, that these magnetizers, who pretend to work a miracle by hocus-pocus tricks, are sent by God, or are helped by the one who solves all difficulties of this kind — the devil?

When, as people say, they put to flight disorders that have defeated the powers of medicine, do they work in accordance with the light of reason? Or do they achieve these wonderful cures with supernatural help?

An adept may answer: by communication with the world of spirits. A noble privilege, it must be admitted. Some of the ancients speak of familiar demons that guarded them from danger by kindly hinting (we cannot guess how) when danger was near, or showed them what they ought to undertake. Yet the men who claimed this privilege, which lies outside the order of nature, insisted that it was the reward or the result of superior temperance and piety. But today’s wonder-workers are not raised above their fellows by superior temperance or holiness. They do not heal for the love of God, but for money. They are the priests of quackery — though it is true that they lack the convenient device of selling masses for souls in purgatory, and have no churches in which to display crutches and models of limbs made sound by a touch or a word.

I am not familiar with the technical terms, nor initiated into the secrets of the art, so I may express myself improperly; but it is clear that men who will not conform to the law of reason and earn their living honestly, step by step, are very lucky to have made the acquaintance of such obliging spirits. We cannot, indeed, credit those spirits with much wisdom or goodness, or they would have chosen nobler instruments when they wished to show themselves the benevolent friends of man.
It is, however, little short of blasphemy to claim such power.

From the whole course of Providence’s dealings with us, it is plain to sober reason that certain vices produce certain effects; and can anyone insult the wisdom of God so grossly as to suppose that a miracle will be permitted to disturb his general laws, restoring the intemperate and vicious to health merely so that they may continue in the same course without penalty? Be whole, and sin no more, said Jesus. And are greater miracles to be performed by those who do not follow in the footsteps of him who healed the body in order to reach the mind?

Some of my readers may be offended that I name Christ in the same breath as such vile impostors — I respect their fervour; but they should remember that the followers of these delusions bear his name and call themselves disciples of the one who said that we should know by their works who were the children of God and who the servants of sin. I admit that it is easier to touch a saint’s body, or to be magnetized, than to curb our appetites or rule our passions; but health of body or of mind can be regained only by these means, unless we make the Supreme Judge partial and vindictive.

Is he a man, that he should change, or punish out of resentment? He, the father of us all, wounds only in order to heal, reason tells us; and because our excesses bring certain consequences, the nature of vice is forcibly brought home to us, so that, learning good from evil by experience, we may hate the one and love the other in proportion to the wisdom we gain. The poison carries its own antidote; either we mend our bad habits and cease to sin against our own bodies, in scripture’s forceful phrase, or an early death, the penalty of sin, snaps the thread of life.

Here our inquiries are brought to an awe-inspiring halt. But why should I hide my views? Considering the attributes of God, I believe that whatever punishment may follow will serve, like the pain of disease, to show the malignancy of vice for the purpose of reform. Positive punishment seems so contrary to the nature of God, as we discover it in all his works and in our own reason, that I could sooner believe the Deity paid no attention to men’s conduct than that he punished without the benevolent aim of reforming them.

Merely to suppose that an all-wise and all-powerful Being, as good as he is great, would create a creature, foreseeing that after fifty or sixty years of feverish existence it would be plunged into never-ending misery — is blasphemy. On what will the worm feed that is never to die? On folly, on ignorance, you say — I would blush with indignation at drawing the natural conclusion, could I set it down here, and would wish to withdraw myself from under the wing of my God! On such a supposition — I speak with reverence — he would be a consuming fire. We would wish, though in vain, to flee from his presence when fear had swallowed up love and darkness had wrapped all his counsels.

I know that many pious people pride themselves on submitting blindly to the Will of God, as though to an arbitrary sceptre or rod, on the same principle that leads the Indians to worship the devil. Put another way, like people in the everyday business of life, they bow to power and grovel under the foot that is able to crush them. Rational religion, on the other hand, means submitting to the will of a being so perfectly wise that everything he wills must spring from the right motive — must be reasonable.

If we respect God in this way, then, can we credit the mysterious insinuations that insult his laws? Could we believe, even if it were staring us in the face, that he would perform a miracle to authorize confusion by giving his sanction to an error? Yet we must either admit these impious conclusions, or scorn every promise to heal a diseased body by supernatural means, or to predict events that God alone can foresee.
SECTION 13.2.
Another example of that feminine weakness of character, often produced by a narrow education, is a romantic turn of mind that has very properly been called SENTIMENTAL.

Ignorance leaves women at the mercy of their sensations; taught to seek happiness in love alone, they spin refinements upon sensual feelings and take up metaphysical notions about that passion, which lead them to neglect the duties of life shamefully; and often, amid these sublime refinements, they sink into actual vice.

These are the women who delight in the daydreams of stupid novelists — writers who, knowing little of human nature, rework stale stories and paint meretricious scenes, all dealt out in a sentimental jargon, and all tending alike to corrupt the taste and to lure the heart away from its daily duties. I say nothing of the understanding, because, never having been exercised, its sleeping energies lie dormant, like the latent particles of fire which are thought to run through all matter.

Women, indeed, being denied all political privileges and, once married, allowed no civil existence except in criminal cases, naturally have their attention turned from the interest of the whole community to that of its smallest parts — although the private duty of any member of society must be very imperfectly done when it has no connection with the general good. The mighty business of female life is to please; and since political and civil oppression bars women from more important concerns, feelings become events, and reflection deepens what it ought to have effaced, and would have effaced, had the understanding been given a wider field.

But, confined to trivial occupations, they naturally absorb the opinions inspired by the only kind of reading suited to interest an innocent, frivolous mind. Unable to grasp anything great, is it surprising that they find reading history a very dry task, and treatises addressed to the understanding unbearably tedious and almost unintelligible? So they are bound to depend on the novelist for amusement. Yet when I protest against novels, I mean novels as compared with works that exercise the understanding and regulate the imagination. For I think any kind of reading better than leaving a blank still a blank, because the mind must be enlarged to some degree and gain a little strength from a slight exercise of its thinking powers; besides, even works addressed only to the imagination lift the reader a little above the gross gratification of appetites to which the mind has not lent a shade of delicacy.

This remark comes from experience; for I have known several capable housewives, and one in particular, who was a very good woman — as good as so narrow a mind would allow her to be — and who made sure that her daughters (three of them) never saw a novel. Being a woman of fortune and fashion, she had various masters come to teach them, and a sort of servant-governess to watch their every step. From their masters they learned what tables, chairs, etc. were called in French and Italian; but since the few books put in their way were either far beyond their capacities or devotional, they acquired neither ideas nor feelings, and, when they were not forced to repeat WORDS, spent their time dressing, quarrelling with one another, or talking secretly with their maids, until they were brought into society as marriageable.

Meanwhile their mother, a widow, was occupied with keeping up her connections, as she called a wide acquaintance, lest her girls should lack a proper entry into the great world. And these young ladies, their minds vulgar in every sense of the word and their tempers spoiled, went out into life swollen with notions of their own importance, and scorning anyone who could not rival them in dress and display.

As for love, nature, or their nurses, had taken care to teach them the physical meaning of the word; and since they had few topics of conversation and fewer refinements of feeling, when they spoke freely, talking of matrimony, they voiced their gross wishes in none too delicate phrases.

Could these girls have been harmed by reading novels? I nearly forgot one feature in the character of one of them: she put on a simplicity close to foolishness, and with a simper would come out with the most immodest remarks and questions, whose full meaning she had picked up while shut away from the world and afraid to open her mouth before her mother, who ruled with a high hand. All three had been brought up, as the mother boasted, in the most exemplary manner, and they read their chapters and psalms before breakfast and never touched a silly novel.

This is only one case; but I can recall many other women who, never led by degrees to suitable studies and never permitted to choose for themselves, have indeed remained overgrown children; or else, through mixing in society, have gained a little of what is called common sense — that is, a clear view of everyday occurrences taken one by one; but anything worthy of the name of intellect, the capacity to form general or abstract ideas, or even intermediate ones, was out of the question. Their minds lay idle, and whenever they were not roused by things they could see and touch and by occupations of that sort, they became low-spirited, and would weep or fall asleep.

So when I urge my sex not to read such flimsy works, my aim is to lead them to read something better; for I share the view of a wise man who, with a daughter and a niece in his charge, took quite a different course with each.

The niece, who had considerable abilities, had been allowed to read at random before she was placed under his guardianship. He tried to lead her, and did lead her, to history and moral essays; but his daughter, whom a doting, weak mother had indulged, and who was consequently averse to anything like application, he allowed to read novels; and he used to justify his conduct by saying that if she ever acquired a taste for reading them, he would have some foundation to build on, and that mistaken opinions were better than none at all.

Indeed, the female mind has been so utterly neglected that this muddy source was the only place where knowledge could be had, until some women of superior talents learned, from reading novels, to despise them.

The best way, I believe, to correct an excessive liking for novels is to ridicule them — not indiscriminately, for then it would have little effect; but if a judicious person with some sense of humour were to read several to a young girl, and show her, both by tone of voice and by apt comparisons with moving incidents and heroic characters in history, how foolishly and absurdly they caricatured human nature, sound opinions might take the place of romantic sentiments.

In one respect, however, most people of both sexes are alike, showing the same lack of taste and modesty. Ignorant women, obliged to be chaste to protect their reputation, let their imagination run riot in the unnatural, meretricious scenes drawn by the novel writers of the day, and scorn as insipid the sober dignity and matronly grace of history,* while men carry the same corrupted taste into life, and turn for amusement to the wanton, fleeing the unaffected charms of virtue and the grave respectability of good sense.

(*Footnote. I am not referring here to that superiority of mind which leads to the creation of ideal beauty, when life, surveyed with a penetrating eye, appears a tragicomedy in which little can be seen to satisfy the heart without the help of imagination.)

Moreover, novel-reading makes women, and ladies of fashion above all, much given to strong expressions and superlatives in conversation; and although the dissipated, artificial life they lead prevents them from nourishing any strong, legitimate passion, the language of passion, in affected tones, is for ever slipping off their glib tongues, and every trifle sets off those phosphorescent flashes that only imitate in the dark the flame of passion.
SECTION 13.3.

Ignorance, together with the misguided cunning that nature sharpens in weak heads as a way of protecting themselves, gives women a great love of dress. It also breeds all the vanity that such a love may naturally be expected to generate, crowding out emulation and greatness of spirit.

I agree with Rousseau that the physical part of the art of pleasing consists in ornaments; and for that very reason I would guard girls against the infectious love of dress so common among weak women, so that they do not stop at the physical part. Yet weak indeed are the women who imagine that they can please for long without the help of the mind — in other words, without the moral art of pleasing. But the moral art (if it is not a profanation to use the word “art” for the grace that is an effect of virtue, not a motive of action) is never found together with ignorance. The playfulness of innocence, so pleasing to refined libertines of both sexes, differs widely in its essence from this higher gracefulness.

A strong liking for outward ornament always shows itself in barbarous states, except that there it is the men and not the women who adorn themselves; for where women are allowed to stand so nearly level with men, society has advanced at least one step in civilization.

So the attention to dress that has been regarded as a peculiarly female tendency is, in my view, natural to mankind. But I ought to put this more precisely. Where the mind has not been opened enough to find pleasure in reflection, the body will be decorated with painstaking care, and ambition will show itself in tattooing or painting the skin.

This primitive inclination goes so far that even the hellish yoke of slavery cannot stifle the savage craving for admiration which the black heroes inherit from both their parents: a slave’s hard-won savings are commonly all spent on a little tawdry finery. And I have seldom known a good servant, man or woman, who was not especially fond of dress. Their clothes were their riches; and I reason by analogy that women’s extravagant love of dress comes from the same cause — an uncultivated mind. When men meet, their conversation turns to business, politics or literature; but, says Swift, “how naturally do women apply their hands to each others lappets and ruffles.” And very natural it is — for they have no business to occupy them and no taste for literature, and they find politics dry, because they have never learned to love mankind by turning their thoughts to those grand pursuits that lift up the human race and advance general happiness.

Besides, men pursue many different paths to power and fame, whether by chance or by choice; and though they jostle one another, since men of the same profession are seldom friends, there is still a far greater number of their fellow creatures with whom they never clash. But women stand in a very different position towards one another — for they are all rivals.

Until they marry, their business is to please men; after marriage, with a few exceptions, they keep following the same scent with all the dogged persistence of instinct. Even virtuous women never forget their sex when in company, for they are always trying to make themselves AGREEABLE. A female beauty and a male wit seem equally eager to draw everyone’s attention to themselves; and the jealousy between rival wits of the same age is proverbial.

Is it surprising, then, that when a woman’s sole ambition centres on beauty, and self-interest gives vanity extra force, endless rivalries should follow? They are all running the same race, and they would have to rise above mortal virtue not to look at one another with a suspicious and even envious eye.

An immoderate love of dress, of pleasure and of power are the passions of savages — the passions that occupy those uncivilized beings who have not yet extended the rule of the mind, or even learned to think with the energy needed to link together the abstract chain of thought that produces principles. And that women, because of their education and the present state of civilized life, are in the same condition cannot, I think, be denied. To laugh at them, then, or to satirize the follies of a being who is never allowed to act freely by the light of her own reason, is as absurd as it is cruel; for it is most natural and certain that those who are taught to obey authority blindly will try to evade it by cunning.

Yet let it be proved that they ought to obey man without question, and I will at once agree that it is woman’s duty to cultivate a love of dress in order to please, and a tendency to cunning for her own protection.

The virtues that rest on ignorance, however, must always waver — the house built on sand could not withstand a storm. There is hardly any need to draw the inference. If women are to be made virtuous by authority, which is a contradiction in terms, let them be walled up in harems and watched with a jealous eye. Do not fear that the iron will enter their souls — for souls that can bear such treatment are made of pliant stuff, just alive enough to animate the body.
“Matter too soft a lasting mark to bear, And best distinguish’d by black, brown, or fair.”

The cruellest wounds will naturally soon heal, and they may still populate the world and dress to please man — which are all the purposes that certain celebrated writers have granted they were created to serve.
SECTION 13.4.

Women are thought to have more sensibility, and even more humanity, than men, and their strong attachments and sudden surges of pity are cited as evidence. But the clinging affection of ignorance rarely has anything noble about it; for the most part it comes down to selfishness, as the affection of children and animals does. I have known many weak women whose whole sensibility was taken up by their husbands; as for their humanity, it was very faint indeed, or rather nothing more than a fleeting impulse of pity. “Humanity does not consist in a squeamish ear,” says an eminent orator. “It belongs to the mind as well as the nerves.”

This sort of exclusive affection, however, though it lowers the individual, should not be cited as evidence that the sex is inferior, since it follows naturally from narrow horizons. Even women of superior good sense, their attention fixed on small occupations and private plans, seldom rise to heroism unless love spurs them on; and love as a heroic passion, like genius, appears only once in an age. I therefore agree with the moralist who asserts “that women have seldom so much generosity as men;” and I agree that their narrow affections, to which justice and humanity are often sacrificed, make the sex appear inferior, especially as men are usually the ones who inspire those affections. But I maintain that the heart would widen as the understanding grew stronger, if women were not kept down from the cradle.

I know that a little sensibility joined to great weakness will produce a strong sexual attachment, while friendship must be cemented by reason. Consequently I grant that more friendship is to be found in the world of men than in that of women, and that men have a keener sense of justice. Women’s exclusive affections do seem, indeed, to resemble Cato’s most unjust love for his country. His wish to crush Carthage came not from a desire to save Rome but from a desire to feed its vainglory; and it is generally to principles of this kind that humanity is sacrificed, for genuine duties support one another.
And how, besides, can women be just or generous while they are the slaves of injustice?
SECTION 13.5.

The rearing of children — that is, laying a foundation of sound health in body and mind for the rising generation — has rightly been insisted on as woman’s particular calling; so the ignorance that makes women unfit for it must be contrary to the order of things. And I maintain that their minds can take in much more, and ought to, or they will never become sensible mothers. Many men who attend to the breeding of horses and oversee the running of the stable would — what a strange want of sense and feeling! — think themselves degraded by paying any attention to the nursery. Yet how many children are downright murdered by the ignorance of women! And when children escape, and are destroyed neither by unnatural neglect nor by blind indulgence, how few are properly handled as far as the infant mind is concerned! So a child whose spirit has been allowed to grow unruly at home is sent to school to have it broken; and the methods used there, which must be used to keep a number of children in order, scatter the seeds of almost every vice in soil thus violently torn up.

I have sometimes compared the struggles of these poor children — who ought never to have felt restraint, and would not have, had they always been held in with an even hand — to the desperate plunging of a spirited filly I once watched being broken on a beach: its feet sank deeper and deeper into the sand each time it tried to throw its rider, until at last it sullenly gave in.

I have always found horses, an animal I am fond of, very manageable when treated with humanity and steadiness, so I doubt whether the violent methods used to break them do not do them real harm. I am certain, however, that a child should never be tamed by force in this way after it has unwisely been allowed to run wild; for every violation of justice and reason in the treatment of children weakens their reason. And children take on a character so early that, as experience leads me to conclude, the foundation of the moral character is laid before their seventh year — the period during which women are given sole charge of them. Afterwards it too often happens that half the business of education is to correct faults they would never have acquired if their mothers had had more understanding; and the correcting is very imperfectly done if it is done in haste.

One striking example of women’s folly must not be left out: the way they treat servants in front of children, letting the children suppose that servants ought to wait on them and put up with their whims.
